item.title: [OpenRouter] LLM API Rate Limits: How to Fix OpenAI and Claude 429 Errors
item.content:encoded:
LLM API Rate Limits: How to Fix OpenAI and Claude 429 Errors

OpenRouter ·11/11/2026

A 429 Too Many Requests error means you sent more requests or tokens than your limit allows in the current time window. OpenAI, Anthropic and OpenRouter all return it, and it usually shows up the first time an app runs under real load or a batch job fans out across several workers.

Most people reach for a retry, and with default settings that often isn’t enough. When we ran a 60-prompt batch through the OpenAI Python SDK against a per-minute limit, 23 requests still failed after the SDK’s retries. The window reset 4 to 8 seconds after the SDK gave up on each one.

This guide starts from a real 429, reads its headers, and fixes it three ways: retry at the reset time the error gives you, send overflow to a fallback model, and let another provider serve the same model. We ran every example against the OpenRouter API, and the output under each code block is what we got.

Tl;dr

  • A 429 means you hit a limit in the current window. On OpenRouter, error.metadata.limit_source tells you whose limit it was.
  • With default settings, the OpenAI Python SDK retried each 429 twice and gave up within about 2 seconds. Against a per-minute limit, 23 of 60 requests in our batch still failed.
  • A retry that waits for Retry-After or X-RateLimit-Reset finished all 60 in every run, in 89 to 92 seconds in Python and 106 to 218 seconds in TypeScript.
  • A models fallback finished all 60 in 13 seconds, for $0.000066, with no waiting.
  • Pinned to one provider with failover off, up to 32 of 150 requests failed per run. With failover on, all 150 succeeded in every run.

What does a 429 rate limit error look like?

We sent 40 requests at once to poolside/laguna-s-2.1:free, a free model with a limit of 20 requests per minute. Thirty-eight succeeded, and two came back as 429 from the provider serving the model:

200: 38  429: 2  other: 0
429 limit_source: {'upstream_provider_shared_pool': 2}

A 429 from our own free-tier limit carries a different limit_source. Here’s one from a separate run:

{
  "message": "Rate limit exceeded: free-models-per-min. ",
  "code": 429,
  "metadata": {
    "headers": {
      "X-RateLimit-Limit": "20",
      "X-RateLimit-Remaining": "0",
      "X-RateLimit-Reset": "1792448640000"
    },
    "limit_source": "openrouter_free_tier_per_minute",
    "remedy_hint": "Slow down requests to free models, or retry after the per-minute window resets.",
    "provider_name": null
  }
}

The headers carry the numbers you need. X-RateLimit-Limit is the cap, X-RateLimit-Remaining is what’s left, and X-RateLimit-Reset is the earliest time a retry can succeed, as a Unix timestamp in milliseconds. The body adds limit_source, which says whose limit you hit, and a remedy_hint written for people reading logs. Branch on limit_source in your code, not on the hint text.

OpenAI and Anthropic send the same information under different names. OpenAI’s x-ratelimit-reset-requests is a duration such as 1s, and both providers can send retry-after as a number of seconds.

Why do rate limits trigger at different request counts?

Thirty-eight of 40 requests got through a limit of 20. The limiter can accept requests that arrive at the same moment before the count catches up, and most limiters don’t reset cleanly at the top of each minute. Anthropic uses a token bucket that refills continuously. OpenAI can return a 429 with the code slow_down when your traffic ramps up too fast, even while you’re under your per-minute limits.

To see how our free-model limit counts, we sent 161 more requests in different patterns. Here are three of them:

TestSucceeded in that minute
Sequential, after two idle minutes30
Sequential, the minute right after30
30 concurrent29

Two things came out of it. More than 20 requests succeeded in every minute we tested, so treat 20 as the point where 429s can start, not an exact count. When we hit it on poolside/laguna-s-2.1:free with 58 seconds left in the window, five requests to minimax/minimax-m3.1-flash:free went through right away, while Laguna stayed blocked. That doesn’t make the cap per model, though. OpenRouter applies one per-minute limiter to all free models on an account, so a request to a different free model can get the same 429.

Step 1: Read whose limit you hit

Waiting fixes a 429 only when the limit resets on a schedule, so check limit_source before you pick a fix:

limit_sourceStatusWhose limitWhat fixes it
openrouter_free_tier_per_minute429Our free-model capWait for X-RateLimit-Reset (Step 2), or fall back to a paid model (Step 3)
upstream_provider_shared_pool429The provider serving the modelAnother provider (Step 4) or a fallback model (Step 3)
openrouter_in_flight_budget402Your in-flight spending budgetWait for Retry-After and retry
openrouter_key_limit, openrouter_credits402Your key’s credit limit or your balanceRaise the key’s limit or add credits

An upstream 429 means the provider serving the model is out of capacity. Providers don’t say when that capacity will free up, so these errors carried no reset header in our runs. The free variant of Gemma 4 31B returned this:

google/gemma-4-31b-it:free is temporarily rate-limited upstream. Please retry shortly, or add your own key to accumulate your rate limits.

The same request with the paid variant as a fallback used a different provider’s capacity and succeeded at DeepInfra for $0.0000037.

Some errors that look like rate limits are about money. OpenAI and Anthropic both return a 429 when you reach a monthly spend cap, and retrying won’t fix it until the cap resets. On OpenRouter, credit problems come back as 402 instead.

Step 2: Retry at the reset time the error gives you

The OpenAI and Anthropic Python SDKs retry a 429 twice by default, with a short backoff that starts at 0.5 seconds and never waits more than 8. They follow a Retry-After header when the server sends one.

Our free-tier 429 sends X-RateLimit-Reset instead, which the SDKs don’t read, so both retries landed in the same full minute. Here’s a 60-prompt batch, 10 at a time, through the OpenAI SDK (openai 3.26.1) with default settings:

openai 3.26.1 | max_retries default: 2
finished in 12s  (HTTP requests sent: 112)
succeeded: 37  RateLimitError after retries: 23
slowest failure gave up after 2.3s
message: Rate limit exceeded: free-models-per-min.  | limit_source: openrouter_free_tier_per_minute
  limit_source=openrouter_free_tier_per_minute  x-ratelimit-reset: 1792444980000  retry-after: None  window reset 8s after the SDK gave up
  limit_source=openrouter_free_tier_per_minute  x-ratelimit-reset: 1792444980000  retry-after: None  window reset 7s after the SDK gave up
  ...
  limit_source=openrouter_free_tier_per_minute  x-ratelimit-reset: 1792444980000  retry-after: None  window reset 4s after the SDK gave up

The SDK sent 112 HTTP requests for 60 prompts, and 23 still failed. Raising max_retries would eventually get through, but only by sending a request into a full window every 8 seconds, and OpenAI’s docs note that failed requests still count toward your per-minute limit. A better retry waits until the time the server gives you. To run all 60 prompts, use an account with at least 60 free-model requests left for the day, because accounts that haven’t bought 10 credits get 50 a day:

import email.utils
import os
import random
import time
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor

import requests

URL = "https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/chat/completions"
HEADERS = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['OPENROUTER_API_KEY']}"}

def retry_delay(headers, attempt):
    """Seconds to wait after a 429: Retry-After, then X-RateLimit-Reset, then backoff."""
    retry_after = headers.get("Retry-After")
    if retry_after:
        if retry_after.replace(".", "", 1).isdigit():
            return float(retry_after)
        when = email.utils.parsedate_to_datetime(retry_after).timestamp()
        return max(0.0, when - time.time())
    reset = headers.get("X-RateLimit-Reset")  # Unix time in milliseconds
    if reset:
        # Spread clients over a few seconds after the reset, so they don't all retry at once.
        return max(0.0, int(reset) / 1000 - time.time()) + random.uniform(1, 5)
    return min(2 ** attempt, 60) * random.uniform(0.5, 1)  # exponential backoff with jitter

def chat(body, max_attempts=6):
    for attempt in range(max_attempts):
        r = requests.post(URL, headers=HEADERS, json=body, timeout=120)
        source = None
        if r.status_code in (402, 429):
            source = r.json()["error"].get("metadata", {}).get("limit_source")
        if source == "openrouter_free_tier_daily":  # resets at UTC midnight, so don't sleep until then
            r.raise_for_status()
        # A 402 from the in-flight budget clears after Retry-After; other 402s need credits.
        if r.status_code != 429 and source != "openrouter_in_flight_budget":
            r.raise_for_status()
            return r.json()
        if attempt == max_attempts - 1:
            break  # out of attempts, so don't wait before failing
        wait = retry_delay(r.headers, attempt)
        print(f"{r.status_code} ({source}), attempt {attempt + 1}: waiting {wait:.1f}s")
        time.sleep(wait)
    r.raise_for_status()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    def job(i):
        return chat({
            "model": "poolside/laguna-s-2.1:free",
            "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": f"Reply with the number {i}."}],
            "max_tokens": 16,
        })

    t0 = time.time()
    with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=10) as pool:  # the same batch job: 60 prompts, 10 at a time
        results = list(pool.map(job, range(60)))
    print(f"{len(results)} of 60 completed in {time.time() - t0:.0f}s")
429 (openrouter_free_tier_per_minute), attempt 1: waiting 19.3s
429 (openrouter_free_tier_per_minute), attempt 1: waiting 19.1s
429 (openrouter_free_tier_per_minute), attempt 1: waiting 18.8s
429 (openrouter_free_tier_per_minute), attempt 1: waiting 17.2s
429 (openrouter_free_tier_per_minute), attempt 1: waiting 19.7s
429 (openrouter_free_tier_per_minute), attempt 1: waiting 15.6s
429 (openrouter_free_tier_per_minute), attempt 1: waiting 14.8s
429 (openrouter_free_tier_per_minute), attempt 1: waiting 16.4s
429 (openrouter_free_tier_per_minute), attempt 2: waiting 61.7s
429 (openrouter_free_tier_per_minute), attempt 2: waiting 58.9s
429 (openrouter_free_tier_per_minute), attempt 2: waiting 60.1s
429 (openrouter_free_tier_per_minute), attempt 2: waiting 57.8s
60 of 60 completed in 89s

All 60 requests finished, but the batch took 89 seconds instead of 12. Nothing fails with this approach, and every request that hits the limit waits out the window.

retry_delay checks Retry-After first because it’s the server’s direct instruction, while X-RateLimit-Reset only marks when the window rolls over. The random 1 to 5 seconds keeps the 10 workers from retrying at the same instant and filling the new window at once.

Even so, four requests in this run retried after the new window had already filled, so they waited a second time. If you wrap an SDK call in a loop like this, set max_retries=0 on the client, or each of your attempts turns into three requests.

The same retry in TypeScript

retry.ts follows the same order: Retry-After, then X-RateLimit-Reset, then backoff. It uses the built-in fetch, so it needs no packages. We ran it on Node 24 with npx tsx retry.ts:

const URL = "https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/chat/completions";
const HEADERS = {
  Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.OPENROUTER_API_KEY}`,
  "Content-Type": "application/json",
};

const sleep = (ms: number) => new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, ms));
const randomBetween = (min: number, max: number) => min + Math.random() * (max - min);

/** Seconds to wait after a 429: Retry-After, then X-RateLimit-Reset, then backoff. */
export function retryDelay(headers: Headers, attempt: number): number {
  const retryAfter = headers.get("Retry-After");
  if (retryAfter) {
    const seconds = Number(retryAfter);
    if (!Number.isNaN(seconds)) return seconds;
    const when = Date.parse(retryAfter); // HTTP date
    if (!Number.isNaN(when)) return Math.max(0, (when - Date.now()) / 1000);
  }
  const reset = headers.get("X-RateLimit-Reset"); // Unix time in milliseconds
  if (reset) {
    // Spread clients over a few seconds after the reset, so they don't all retry at once.
    return Math.max(0, (Number(reset) - Date.now()) / 1000) + randomBetween(1, 5);
  }
  return Math.min(2 ** attempt, 60) * randomBetween(0.5, 1); // exponential backoff with jitter
}

export async function chat(body: object, maxAttempts = 6): Promise<any> {
  let res: Response | undefined;
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < maxAttempts; attempt++) {
    res = await fetch(URL, { method: "POST", headers: HEADERS, body: JSON.stringify(body) });
    if (res.status !== 402 && res.status !== 429) {
      if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}: ${await res.text()}`);
      return res.json();
    }
    const error = (await res.json()).error;
    const source = error?.metadata?.limit_source;
    // A 402 from the in-flight budget clears after Retry-After; other 402s need credits.
    if (res.status === 402 && source !== "openrouter_in_flight_budget") {
      throw new Error(`HTTP 402: ${JSON.stringify(error)}`);
    }
    if (source === "openrouter_free_tier_daily") {
      throw new Error(`HTTP 429: ${JSON.stringify(error)}`); // resets at UTC midnight, so don't sleep until then
    }
    if (attempt === maxAttempts - 1) break; // out of attempts, so don't wait before failing
    const wait = retryDelay(res.headers, attempt);
    console.log(`${res.status} (${source}), attempt ${attempt + 1}: waiting ${wait.toFixed(1)}s`);
    await sleep(wait * 1000);
  }
  throw new Error(`Still rate limited after ${maxAttempts} attempts`);
}

// The same batch job: 60 prompts, 10 at a time.
async function main() {
  const prompts = Array.from({ length: 60 }, (_, i) => i);
  const results: any[] = [];
  const worker = async () => {
    for (let i = prompts.shift(); i !== undefined; i = prompts.shift()) {
      results[i] = await chat({
        model: "poolside/laguna-s-2.1:free",
        messages: [{ role: "user", content: `Reply with the number ${i}.` }],
        max_tokens: 16,
      });
    }
  };

  const t0 = Date.now();
  await Promise.all(Array.from({ length: 10 }, worker));
  const completed = results.filter(Boolean).length;
  console.log(`${completed} of 60 completed in ${Math.round((Date.now() - t0) / 1000)}s`);
}

main();
429 (openrouter_free_tier_per_minute), attempt 1: waiting 34.9s
429 (openrouter_free_tier_per_minute), attempt 1: waiting 34.6s
429 (openrouter_free_tier_per_minute), attempt 1: waiting 35.1s
429 (openrouter_free_tier_per_minute), attempt 1: waiting 33.5s
429 (openrouter_free_tier_per_minute), attempt 2: waiting 60.5s
429 (openrouter_free_tier_per_minute), attempt 2: waiting 58.6s
429 (openrouter_free_tier_per_minute), attempt 2: waiting 60.6s
60 of 60 completed in 106s

The total time depends on where the window is when the batch starts and on how busy the model’s provider is. Our two TypeScript runs took 218 and 106 seconds, and our two Python runs took 92 and 89. All four finished every request.

Step 3: Send overflow to a fallback model

If an answer from a second model is acceptable, you don’t have to wait at all. A provider rate limit applies to one model at one provider, so a different model uses separate capacity. The free-tier cap is the exception, because every :free model on your account shares it. With the models parameter, we try each model in order and move to the next on any error, including a 429, before anything reaches your code:

import os
import time
from collections import Counter
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor

import requests

URL = "https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/chat/completions"
HEADERS = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['OPENROUTER_API_KEY']}"}

def job(i):
    r = requests.post(URL, headers=HEADERS, timeout=120, json={
        # Try the free model first; if it is rate limited, OpenRouter sends the request to the next one.
        "models": ["poolside/laguna-s-2.1:free", "deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash"],
        "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": f"Reply with the number {i}."}],
        "max_tokens": 16,
    })
    data = r.json()
    return r.status_code, data.get("model"), data.get("usage", {}).get("cost", 0)

t0 = time.time()
with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=10) as pool:  # the same batch job: 60 prompts, 10 at a time
    results = list(pool.map(job, range(60)))
print(f"finished in {time.time() - t0:.0f}s")
print(Counter((status, model) for status, model, _ in results))
print(f"total cost: ${sum(cost for *_, cost in results):.6f}")
finished in 13s
Counter({(200, 'poolside/laguna-s-2.1:free'): 52, (200, 'deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash'): 8})
total cost: $0.000066

The free model served 52 requests, and the paid model served the other 8. No request waited, and you pay only for the paid ones. The response’s model field records which model answered, and that’s the model you’re billed for.

Choose a fallback that has its own capacity. Every :free model on your account shares the free-model cap, so another free model isn’t a reliable fallback when that cap is the cause. Free models also run out of provider capacity often, so a paid fallback is the more reliable choice.

Here are the three runs of the same batch side by side:

RunCompletedTimeCost
OpenAI SDK, default retries37 of 6012 s$0
Retry that waits for the reset60 of 6089 s$0
Models fallback60 of 6013 s$0.000066

If the job can wait, retry at the reset. If it can’t, and a second model’s answer is good enough, add a fallback.

Step 4: Let another provider serve the same model

Steps 2 and 3 handle our free-model cap. Paid models run into a different kind of limit: the capacity of whichever provider is serving them. Most models on OpenRouter are served by several providers, each with its own rate limits. When one provider returns a 429, we retry the request at the next provider before the error reaches you. This is on by default.

We sent 300 requests to google/gemma-4-31b-it, 50 at a time, and checked the provider_responses list in each request’s GET /api/v1/generation record, which shows every provider we tried:

300 requests, 50 at a time, in 11s
status codes: Counter({200: 300})
generation records read: 300 of 300
served by: {'CoreWeave': 177, 'DeepInfra': 118, 'Novita': 1, 'Venice': 1, 'ModelRun': 1, 'Parasail': 2}
requests that needed more than one provider: 0
failed attempts, by provider and status: []
total cost: $0.00130

Spread across six providers, no request needed a second try. Then we pinned the same model to Crusoe with “provider”: {“order”: [“crusoe”]} and sent 150 requests, 50 at a time. Here’s one run with fallbacks on:

150 requests, 50 at a time, in 5s
status codes: Counter({200: 150})
generation records read: 150 of 150
served by: {'CoreWeave': 79, 'Crusoe': 71}
requests that needed more than one provider: 79
failed attempts, by provider and status: [(('Crusoe', 429), 79)]
total cost: $0.00056

Crusoe rate-limited 79 requests, CoreWeave answered all 79, and the client saw 150 successes. We repeated the pinned run several times with allow_fallbacks off and on:

allow_fallbacksRunsSucceeded per run429s per run
false4150, 147, 118, 1360, 3, 32, 14
true3150, 150, 1500

Crusoe’s capacity changed from minute to minute, so the failures with fallbacks off ranged from none to 32. With fallbacks on, Crusoe rate limited 21, 41 and 79 requests across the three runs, and the client never saw one of them. Anything that narrows which providers can serve a request leaves less capacity to absorb a burst. If you still see provider 429s on OpenRouter, check for allow_fallbacks: false, a short only list or a tight max_price. To prefer one provider without losing failover, set order and leave allow_fallbacks at its default.

The same 300-request burst to anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5 and openai/gpt-6-luna had no failed attempts. When a closed model’s own API runs out of capacity, the error is usually a 529 rather than a 429, which the Claude 529 overloaded guide covers.

How do you avoid hitting rate limits at all?

The fixes above deal with a 429 after it happens. These habits make one less likely:

  • Cap concurrency at what the limit allows. Concurrency is what pushed our first test over the limit. Pacing requests just under the limit loses less time than waiting out a full window after a 429.
  • Set max_tokens close to the answer length you expect. OpenAI counts max_tokens toward your tokens-per-minute limit, so a generous value uses up the limit faster than the answers do.
  • Check your key before a large job. GET /api/v1/key reports the daily free-model counter. Ours read {‘used’: 585, ‘limit’: 1000, ‘remaining’: 415} after these runs. The daily limit is 50 free-model requests until you’ve bought at least 10 credits, and 1,000 after that.
  • Use paid variants in production. The 20-per-minute cap applies only to :free models.

Frequently asked questions

How do I increase my OpenAI API rate limit?

OpenAI raises your limits automatically as your organization’s total credit purchases pass each usage tier threshold. You can see your current limits under Settings > Organization > Limits in the OpenAI dashboard. Through OpenRouter, provider routing spreads a model’s traffic across every provider that serves it, so one provider’s limit doesn’t cap you.

Why does Claude say “rate limit reached”?

On the Claude API, it means your organization used up its requests or tokens per minute for that model, and the retry-after header says how many seconds to wait. If the 429 comes from your monthly spend cap, there’s no retry-after header, and retrying won’t help until access resumes. In Claude Code on a subscription, the message usually means the plan’s usage limit. See Hit your Claude Code usage limit?.

Do more API keys get around rate limits?

No. On OpenRouter, extra API keys or accounts don’t change your rate limits, because we govern capacity globally. Provider limits apply per model, which is why a fallback model works, but every :free model on your account shares one free-tier cap. With BYOK, requests that use your own provider key count against your limits at that provider.

Is Retry-After in seconds or milliseconds?

Seconds, or an HTTP date. Our X-RateLimit-Reset is different. It’s a Unix timestamp in milliseconds. The retry_delay function in Step 2 handles all three forms.

Next steps

  • Limits: free-model caps, the X-RateLimit-* headers and how to handle 402 and 429 errors.
  • Provider routing: order, allow_fallbacks, only and sorting.
  • Model fallbacks: the models parameter and how fallback requests are billed.
  • Free LLM APIs compared: free-tier limits across providers.

item.title: [OpenRouter] LLM Quantization: What fp8 and fp4 Do to Quality and Price
item.content:encoded:
LLM Quantization: What fp8 and fp4 Do to Quality and Price

OpenRouter ·11/11/2026

When you call an open-weight model through an API, several providers may serve it at different precisions, such as 16-bit bf16, 8-bit fp8 or 4-bit fp4. The precision can affect both the answers and the price. LLM quantization creates these versions by storing a model’s weights in fewer bits, so the model needs less memory and hardware, at some cost in accuracy.

This post explains the formats and reports what we measured on OpenRouter on October 20, 2026, across 1,455 provider endpoints and six endpoints serving Qwen3.8 27B. On our test, we didn’t detect an accuracy difference between fp8, fp4 and fp16, so the precision label alone didn’t predict accuracy. Lower precision was usually cheaper, but not for every model.

TL;DR

  • We didn’t detect an accuracy difference between fp8, fp4 and fp16 on our 240 scored tasks. All six endpoints scored between 98.3% and 99.2%.
  • On 40 more multiplication tasks, one fp4 endpoint scored lowest, by a gap too small to rule out chance.
  • 8-bit was cheaper than 16-bit for 14 of the 24 models served at both, and more expensive for 7. 4-bit was cheaper than 8-bit for 26 of 33.
  • provider.quantizations pins the precision you get. List every precision you’d accept, so the router has more than one endpoint to fall back to.

What is LLM quantization?

LLM quantization means storing a large language model’s numbers with fewer bits than it was trained with. Most LLMs today use FP16 or BF16, which are 16-bit formats. fp8 halves the memory each weight takes, and fp4 or int4 quarters it, so the same GPU holds a bigger model or serves more requests. The cost is accuracy, because each weight is rounded to the nearest value the smaller format can store.

FormatBits per weightWeights for a 27B modelWhere you see it
bf16 / fp161654 GBThe precision most models are released in
fp8827 GBThe most common labeled precision on OpenRouter
fp4, nvfp4, mxfp4, int4413.5 GBCheaper endpoints, local runs, some lab releases

These figures cover weights only. A running model also needs memory for its KV cache, the stored attention state for each token in the context.

There are two main types of quantization. Post-training quantization converts a finished model’s weights. It can be dynamic, computing the range of each activation at run time, or static, computing those ranges in advance by passing sample data through the model. Quantization-aware training simulates the rounding during training so the weights learn to tolerate it. The Hugging Face Optimum concept guide explains both, and the Transformers quantization overview covers the quantization methods you can run yourself.

fp8 vs bf16: what’s the difference?

Floating-point formats split their bits between a sign, an exponent and a mantissa. The exponent sets the range of values, and the mantissa sets how finely values within that range are resolved.

bf16 has 1 sign bit, 8 exponent bits and 7 mantissa bits, so it has the same range as 32-bit fp32 with less precision. fp16 splits its 16 bits as 5 exponent and 10 mantissa bits. The OCP 8-bit floating point spec defines two fp8 encodings, E4M3 (4 exponent bits, 3 mantissa bits) and E5M2 (5 exponent bits, 2 mantissa bits). fp8 gives up both range and precision, so quantized models store a scale factor per tensor or per block of weights. MXFP4 shares one scale across each block of 32 values, and NVFP4 uses one fp8 scale per 16 values.

For an API user, fp8 vs bf16 shows up as a different label and price on the same model. In our test, we didn’t detect a difference between the three fp8 endpoints and the fp16 endpoint.

How much quality is lost with fp8 and fp4?

We didn’t detect a quality loss at fp8 or fp4 in our test. All six endpoints scored between 98.3% and 99.2%, and a test this size can’t rule out a gap of a point or two.

We ran 280 tasks with exact answers through qwen/qwen3.8-27b, pinned to six endpoints. Cerebras serves it at fp16. Parasail, CoreWeave and AkashML serve it at fp8, and Darkbloom and ModelRun serve it at fp4. Each request set provider.only, quantizations and allow_fallbacks: false, so it could only reach the endpoint we named, at temperature 0 with reasoning off. The tasks were multi-step arithmetic with working, Python programs to trace, lists of 20 to 30 numbers to sort, a key to find among 240 or 1,200 entries (about 4,000 and 20,000 tokens), and a four-step lookup chain through about 9,000 tokens. We generated every task, so each has an exact answer and no judge is needed. Another 40 tasks asked for the product of two four-digit numbers with no working, scored separately.

Task familyTasksfp16 Cerebrasfp8 Parasailfp8 CoreWeavefp8 AkashMLfp4 Darkbloomfp4 ModelRun
Arithmetic with working50484948494950
Short code traces50505050505050
Long code traces30302929292928
Sorting 20 to 30 numbers30302929292930
Recall at 4,000 tokens20202020202020
Recall at 20,000 tokens20202020202020
Four-hop recall40394040403940
Total24098.8%98.8%98.3%98.8%98.3%99.2%
Multiplication, no working40303331322630

Source: OpenRouter, Qwen3.8 27B, October 20, 2026. The 95% confidence intervals on the totals run from 95.8% to 99.8%, and all six overlap.

No task family separated the precisions. Each endpoint missed at most two tasks in any family, and the misses were ordinary slips, such as a number dropped from a sorted list. The fp8 endpoints disagreed with each other on 2 to 5 of the 240 tasks, and the two fp4 endpoints on 4. Darkbloom disagreed with the fp16 and fp8 endpoints most often, on 7 or 8 tasks, yet its total was within half a point of fp16.

The one place a gap showed was multiplication with no working. Darkbloom at fp4 got 26 of 40 products exactly right, against 30 to 33 on the other five endpoints, including 30 on ModelRun at fp4. A two-proportion z-test against the best endpoint (33), a comparison we chose after seeing the results, puts the chance of a gap that large arising with no real difference at about 7.5%, so we can’t call it a precision effect. Wrong products were close at every precision, with the median miss off by less than 0.01%.

We ran all 280 tasks twice on Cerebras, and both runs returned identical text on every task. The small differences between endpoints can come from precision, from each provider’s hardware and inference software, or from run-to-run variation on the other endpoints, and at this size we can’t separate them. Cerebras is the only fp16 endpoint, so fp16 has no second endpoint to compare it with.

This test covers one model, 280 tasks and six endpoints on one day. It doesn’t show that 4-bit is safe for every model or workload, so test your own prompts before you move traffic to a 4-bit endpoint.

Which precision do API providers serve?

fp8 is the most common labeled precision, and most endpoints don’t report a precision at all. We pulled every model’s endpoints from our endpoints API, which returned 1,455 endpoints across 470 models.

Reported precisionEndpointsShare of allShare of labeled
unknown86559.5%
fp834323.6%58.1%
fp41238.5%20.8%
bf16704.8%11.9%
int4201.4%3.4%
nvfp4130.9%2.2%
mxfp4120.8%2.0%
fp1680.5%1.4%
fp3210.1%0.2%

Source: OpenRouter (openrouter.ai/api/v1/models/{author}/{slug}/endpoints), as of October 20, 2026.

610 of the 865 unknown endpoints belong to closed-weight models with no labeled endpoint at all, including every Claude and Gemini model and every OpenAI model except gpt-oss. Of the other 255, 253 are on open-weight models whose providers don’t label precision. Only 54 of the 163 models with a labeled endpoint have a 16-bit one, so for most open-weight models, 8-bit or 4-bit is the only labeled option.

Is a quantized endpoint cheaper?

Usually, but not always. For each model, we compared the cheapest endpoint at each precision, at a blended price of three input tokens to one output token.

ComparisonModelsLower precision cheaperWithin 2%Lower precision more expensiveMedian price ratio
8-bit vs 16-bit2414370.94
4-bit vs 8-bit3326340.76
4-bit vs 16-bit119020.73

Source: OpenRouter endpoints API, list prices including provider discounts, as of October 20, 2026.

Here’s the cheapest endpoint at each precision for five models, in dollars per million blended tokens. Two are exceptions. gpt-oss-120b costs more at 8-bit than at 16-bit, and MiniMax M3 costs more at 4-bit than at 8-bit.

Model16-bit8-bit4-bit
Qwen3.8 27B$0.581$0.342$0.140
Kimi K2.6$1.400$1.079$0.825
Gemma 4 31B$0.205$0.200$0.160
gpt-oss-120b$0.067$0.100$0.060
MiniMax M3None$0.388$0.412

Source: OpenRouter endpoints API, as of October 20, 2026.

The provider affects the price more than the precision does. Where one model has several endpoints at the same precision, the most expensive was a median 1.72 times the cheapest. For Qwen3.8 27B, the ten fp8 endpoints ranged from $0.342 to $1.137 per million blended tokens. To send a request to the cheapest endpoint that passes your precision filter, add :floor to the model slug, as our lowest-cost inference guide explains. With quantizations: [“fp8”], qwen/qwen3.8-27b:floor went to Chutes, the cheapest fp8 endpoint, on both of our tries.

In our test, the cheapest full 280-task run was at fp4 and the most expensive at fp16, but the order in between didn’t follow precision. One run cost $0.58 on Darkbloom (fp4), $0.72 on AkashML (fp8), $0.77 on ModelRun (fp4), $0.81 on Parasail (fp8), $1.19 on CoreWeave (fp8) and $1.24 on Cerebras (fp16). Speed didn’t follow precision either. Cerebras (fp16) and ModelRun (fp4) answered in a median 1.3 and 2.4 seconds, against 8.4 to 15.0 seconds for the other four. Across all endpoints, median 24-hour uptime was 99.8% or higher at every labeled precision except fp32, which has one endpoint.

How do you choose the precision you get?

Check what a model’s endpoints serve, then set provider.quantizations on your requests. A GET to https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/models/qwen/qwen3.8-27b/endpoints returns one entry per endpoint with its quantization, price, context length and uptime. It answered without an API key when we called it, and the model’s providers tab shows the same list. For Qwen3.8 27B it listed 21 endpoints, with one bf16, one fp16, ten fp8, three fp4 and six unknown. Check the count for the precision you want before you pin it, because that count is how many endpoints can take over when one fails.

To keep requests at 8 bits or higher, list the precisions you accept.

import os
import requests

response = requests.post(
    "https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/chat/completions",
    headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['OPENROUTER_API_KEY']}"},
    json={
        "model": "qwen/qwen3.8-27b",
        "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "What is the capital of Australia? One word."}],
        "reasoning": {"enabled": False},
        "provider": {"quantizations": ["fp8", "bf16", "fp16"]},
    },
    timeout=120,
)
data = response.json()
if "error" in data:
    raise RuntimeError(data["error"])
print(data["provider"], data["choices"][0]["message"]["content"], f'${data["usage"]["cost"]:.6f}')

We ran it three times, and each run printed the same line.

Reka Canberra $0.000007

The provider routing quantization docs list every accepted value and explain how quantizations combines with only, order and sort.

quantizations filters the list of endpoints. We drop every endpoint whose precision isn’t in the list, then load-balance across the rest, weighted toward the lowest price, and fall back to the next endpoint if a provider fails. Nothing in the filter guarantees the same provider each time, so log the response’s provider field if you track quality. The docs also note that fp4 includes mxfp4 and nvfp4, and fp8 includes mxfp8.

Common problems with precision filters and how to fix them

The filter runs before any provider is contacted, so an empty candidate list fails fast. Asking Qwen3.8 27B for int8, which no endpoint serves, returned a 404 in 0.4 seconds.

{"error":{"message":"No endpoints found for the request with quantization: int8. To learn more about provider routing, visit: https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/provider-selection","code":404,"metadata":{"routing_funnel":[{"step":"Initial Endpoints","endpoint_count":21}],"failed_routing_step":"Filter by Quantization"}}}

The routing_funnel field shows how many endpoints survived each step, and failed_routing_step names the step that left none. {“quantizations”: [“fp8”], “only”: [“cerebras”]} returned the same 404 with quantization: fp8, because Cerebras serves fp16, so the funnel went from 21 endpoints to 1 to none.

The slower failure happens when only one endpoint matches. Cerebras is the only fp16 endpoint for Qwen3.8 27B. During our test, which pinned Cerebras with allow_fallbacks: false, 93 of the first 280 requests failed three times in a row with this error (abridged).

{"message":"Provider returned error","code":429,"metadata":{"raw":"qwen/qwen3.8-27b is temporarily rate-limited upstream. Please retry shortly, or add your own key to accumulate your rate limits: https://openrouter.ai/settings/integrations","provider_name":"Cerebras","limit_source":"upstream_provider_shared_pool","retry_after_seconds":59}}

We retried them until all 280 completed. quantizations: [“fp16”] on its own leaves the same single candidate, so a rate limit there has nowhere else to go. Widening the list to [“fp16”, “bf16”] gave the router a second candidate, and the same request went to DeepInfra.

A provider failure can also arrive with an HTTP 200 status, because we send the status as soon as the provider accepts the request. Check the body for error, not only the status code.

Sort endpoints by quality signals with Exacto

Quantized quality depends “on the method used”, and each provider runs its own inference software, so two endpoints with the same label aren’t guaranteed to match. For requests with tools, Auto Exacto already moves endpoints with lower throughput, tool-calling success rates and benchmark scores to the back of the list. To apply that ordering to requests without tools, add :exacto to the model slug. Exacto ranks endpoints on tool-calling signals, not on accuracy at your task, so run your own prompts against the endpoints you’re considering. How to evaluate LLM provider performance covers how to compare their latency, throughput and uptime.

Frequently asked questions

Is higher or lower quantization better?

More bits keep more of the original model’s precision and take more memory. In our test of Qwen3.8 27B on October 20, 2026, we didn’t detect an accuracy difference between fp8, fp4 and fp16 endpoints on 240 tasks with exact answers. That covers one model on one day, so test 4-bit on your own workload before you commit to it.

Why doesn’t quantization destroy an LLM’s accuracy?

Not all weights matter equally. AWQ found that protecting about 1% of the most important weights greatly reduces quantization error, and LLM.int8() uses mixed precision, keeping outlier values at 16-bit while multiplying more than 99.9% of values in 8-bit. Our test of Qwen3.8 27B can’t show which methods the providers use, but the fp16 endpoint missed 3 of 240 tasks and the fp8 and fp4 endpoints missed 2 to 4.

When should you quantize a model?

Quantize when the model doesn’t fit your hardware at 16-bit, or when you need more throughput from the same GPUs. In our test we didn’t detect a loss at fp8, and fp8 rounds each weight less than 4-bit does, so it’s the smaller step. Test either one on your own tasks first. Through an API you don’t quantize the model yourself. You choose an endpoint on OpenRouter that serves the precision you want, with provider.quantizations.

What does “unknown” quantization mean on a provider?

It means the provider hasn’t reported a precision for that endpoint. On OpenRouter, 865 of 1,455 endpoints were unknown on October 20, 2026, and 610 of those belong to closed-weight models such as Claude and Gemini. unknown is also an accepted value in provider.quantizations, so you can include or exclude those endpoints.

item.title: [OpenRouter] MCP vs CLI vs Skills: What Each Costs in Context
item.content:encoded:
MCP vs CLI vs Skills: What Each Costs in Context

OpenRouter ·11/11/2026

Every tool you give an agent sends its definition to the model on every request, and you pay for it as input tokens. A Model Context Protocol (MCP) server can add tens of thousands of tokens to the context window. The usual alternatives are a command-line tool (CLI) or a skill.

We measured it on one GitHub task with the GitHub MCP server, the gh CLI, and a gh skill, on Claude Haiku 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5, GPT-6 Luna, and Gemini 3.8 Flash. On Sonnet 5.5, all three answered correctly, but the input tokens they used were very different. The CLI used 1,421, the skill used 3,315, and the MCP server used 59,417 with its default tools loaded. Here’s where the tokens go and how to cut them with our Tool Search server tool.

TL;DR

  • The GitHub MCP server’s 46 default tools add 19,436 tokens to every request on Claude Sonnet 5.5.
  • On Sonnet 5.5, one tool result, GitHub’s release object, cost about 20,400 tokens, more than all 46 definitions.
  • Tool Search cut the up-front cost of 46 tools to under 600 tokens. Over the whole task, it halved the cost on Sonnet 5.5 and raised it on Claude Haiku 5.5.

What is the difference between MCP, a CLI, and a skill?

All three give a model a capability. They differ in what the model reads before it can use it.

What the model sees up frontWhat it sees when it acts
MCP serverEvery tool’s name, description, and JSON schema, on every requestThe tool’s result, in whatever shape the server returns
CLIA shell tool and a line saying the CLI existsThe command’s output, which you shape with flags such as —json
SkillA one-line description of each skillThe skill’s SKILL.md file, once, then the command output

A CLI relies on the model already knowing the tool. A skill teaches the model how to use a tool, and the model loads the full instructions only when a task needs them.

How many tokens does an MCP server add to every request?

The reliable way to count them is to ask the model. Each provider writes tool definitions into the prompt in its own format before counting tokens, which a local tokenizer misses. Send the same request with and without the tools, and the difference in usage.prompt_tokens is what the tools cost on every turn.

Save this as mcp_cost.py. It speaks the 2025-06-18 version of MCP, which the GitHub server accepts.

"""How many prompt tokens does an MCP server add to every request? Ask the model."""
import json
import os
import subprocess
import sys

import requests

API = "https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/chat/completions"
HEADERS = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['OPENROUTER_API_KEY']}"}

def list_mcp_tools(command):
    """Start a stdio MCP server, run the handshake, and return its tools/list result."""
    proc = subprocess.Popen(command, stdin=subprocess.PIPE, stdout=subprocess.PIPE,
                            stderr=subprocess.DEVNULL, text=True)

    def rpc(method, params, id=None):
        msg = {"jsonrpc": "2.0", "method": method, "params": params}
        if id is not None:
            msg["id"] = id
        proc.stdin.write(json.dumps(msg) + "\n")
        proc.stdin.flush()
        while id is not None:
            reply = json.loads(proc.stdout.readline())
            if reply.get("id") == id:
                return reply["result"]

    rpc("initialize", {"protocolVersion": "2025-06-18", "capabilities": {},
                       "clientInfo": {"name": "mcp-cost", "version": "1"}}, id=1)
    rpc("notifications/initialized", {})
    tools, cursor, id = [], None, 2
    while True:  # follow nextCursor so servers that paginate tools/list are fully counted
        page = rpc("tools/list", {"cursor": cursor} if cursor else {}, id=id)
        tools += page["tools"]
        cursor, id = page.get("nextCursor"), id + 1
        if not cursor:
            break
    proc.kill()
    return tools

def prompt_tokens(model, tools=None):
    body = {"model": model, "max_tokens": 16, "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Say ok."}]}
    if tools:
        body["tools"] = tools
    if model.startswith("google/"):
        # Google Vertex and Google AI Studio count the same tools differently, so pin one.
        body["provider"] = {"only": ["google-vertex"]}
    r = requests.post(API, headers=HEADERS, json=body, timeout=120)
    r.raise_for_status()
    return r.json()["usage"]["prompt_tokens"]

if __name__ == "__main__":
    mcp_tools = list_mcp_tools(sys.argv[1:])
    # What an MCP client sends the model: each tool's name, description and input schema.
    tools = [{"type": "function", "function": {"name": t["name"], "description": t.get("description", ""),
                                               "parameters": t["inputSchema"]}} for t in mcp_tools]
    print(f"{len(tools)} tools")
    for model in ["anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5", "openai/gpt-6-luna", "google/gemini-3.8-flash"]:
        added = prompt_tokens(model, tools) - prompt_tokens(model)
        print(f"{model:30} +{added:,} prompt tokens on every request")

Pass the server’s start command as arguments, as here for the GitHub MCP server v2.0.2.

$ python mcp_cost.py github-mcp-server stdio --toolsets=default
46 tools
anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5     +19,436 prompt tokens on every request
openai/gpt-6-luna              +8,903 prompt tokens on every request
google/gemini-3.8-flash        +8,525 prompt tokens on every request

The cost grows with each tool you add. On Haiku 5.5, the issues toolset has 10 tools and adds 5,801 tokens. The users toolset has one tool and adds 619.

The model you use changes the count too. The same 46 tools cost 19,436 tokens on Haiku 5.5 but 8,903 on GPT-6 Luna, so measure on the model you plan to run.

Even the provider serving the model can change it. On Gemini 3.8 Flash, the 46 tools cost 8,525 tokens through Google Vertex and 13,010 through Google AI Studio. That’s why the script always sends Gemini requests to Google Vertex.

What does the same task cost with a CLI, a skill, and MCP?

We asked each model, “What is the latest release of the GitHub repository cli/cli, and what are the three most recently opened open issues in that repository with the label bug?” Each approach ran as a tool-calling loop on our Responses API, and we added up usage.input_tokens across requests.

  • CLI. One run_shell tool and the line “The GitHub CLI gh is installed and authenticated.”
  • Skill. The same tool, plus a one-line index pointing at a 1,492-character SKILL.md of gh recipes.
  • MCP. The server’s tools, scoped to the 2 the task needs, the default 46, or all 91.

We ran each combination three times on October 20, 2026, and show medians. Haiku 5.5 counts a prompt exactly as Sonnet 5.5 does, but it took extra turns in some runs, so we show Sonnet’s steadier tokens and billed cost.

ApproachSonnet 5.5 tokensSonnet 5.5 cost per taskGPT-6 Luna tokensGemini 3.8 Flash tokens
CLI1,421$0.00756275,292
Skill3,315$0.01181,5426,107
MCP, 2 tools23,228$0.055214,47917,267
MCP, 46 default tools59,417$0.1274116,28235,409
MCP, all 91 tools101,351$0.2113135,23853,289
MCP, 2 tools, results capped at 4,000 characters5,357$0.01912,7262,943

Every run in this table answered correctly. The failures came with Tool Search, covered below. On Sonnet 5.5, the default MCP server used 42 times the CLI’s input tokens and cost 17 times as much, $127 against $7.50 per 1,000 tasks. Output tokens cost five times as much as input on Sonnet 5.5, and the CLI run’s 463 output tokens were $0.0046 of its $0.0075.

The skill cost more than the bare CLI because the file stays in the conversation once the model reads it. For a CLI tool the model knows well, a skill is optional. For your own CLI, the skill is how the model learns the commands.

Why do MCP tool results cost as much as the definitions?

get_latest_release returned GitHub’s full release object, 42,182 characters, and 87% of it described the 22 download files. The model needed the tag and date, which is all gh release view returned.

$ gh release view -R cli/cli --json tagName,publishedAt
{"publishedAt":"2026-09-30T02:40:02Z","tagName":"v2.102.0"}

That object stays in the context window and is resent with every later request, and on Sonnet 5.5 it added about 20,400 tokens. Scoping the server to two tools cut the first request from 19,487 tokens to 1,406. The whole task still cost 23,228.

The table shows two fixes. First, expose only the tools the agent needs, with —tools=get_latest_release,list_issues or —toolsets=issues,repos. Second, shrink results in your client before the model sees them. A 4,000-character cap brought the scoped route to 5,357 tokens with every run correct, because GitHub puts the tag and date near the top.

The cap worked only because of where the fields happened to sit. Combined with Tool Search, the cap left Gemini 3.8 Flash and Haiku 5.5 with one correct answer in three runs each, and Gemini once hit our 12-request limit while retrying.

Keep whole fields instead, as —json does for the CLI. The GitHub server’s list_issues takes a fields argument, and asking for only number, title, and creation date cut its result from 8,336 characters to 714. Without it, the model decides the size. In four of six runs with 46 or 91 tools loaded, GPT-6 Luna asked for 100 issues with their full text and got 281,963 characters back.

Does Tool Search fix MCP’s context problem?

Tool Search removes most of the cost of tool definitions. You mark tools defer_loading: true and add {“type”: “openrouter:tool_search”}. We withhold the deferred definitions and send the search tool, plus any tools you left loaded. The model searches tool names and descriptions with a regular expression and calls a match on its next turn. It’s in beta and works with any model and provider on the Responses and Messages APIs.

With all 46 GitHub tools deferred, the cost before any search was 578 tokens on the Claude models, 144 on GPT-6 Luna, and 130 on Gemini 3.8 Flash.

This script sends one question with all 46 tools loaded, then deferred. Save it next to mcp_cost.py, since it reuses list_mcp_tools.

"""Send the same MCP tools with defer_loading and openrouter:tool_search, and compare prompt tokens."""
import os
import sys

import requests

from mcp_cost import list_mcp_tools

API = "https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/responses"
HEADERS = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['OPENROUTER_API_KEY']}"}
QUESTION = "What is the latest release of the GitHub repository cli/cli?"

def ask(model, tools):
    r = requests.post(API, headers=HEADERS, timeout=300,
                      json={"model": model, "input": QUESTION, "tools": tools})
    r.raise_for_status()
    return r.json()

mcp_tools = list_mcp_tools(sys.argv[1:])
# The Responses API takes function tools flat: type, name, description, parameters.
tools = [{"type": "function", "name": t["name"], "description": t.get("description", ""),
          "parameters": t["inputSchema"]} for t in mcp_tools]
deferred = [{"type": "openrouter:tool_search"}] + [{**t, "defer_loading": True} for t in tools]

for model in ["anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5", "openai/gpt-6-luna"]:
    for label, tool_list in [("all loaded", tools), ("tool search", deferred)]:
        res = ask(model, tool_list)
        steps = [f"search {o['query']!r}" if o["type"] == "openrouter:tool_search" else f"call {o['name']}"
                 for o in res["output"] if o["type"] in ("openrouter:tool_search", "function_call")]
        print(f"{model:28} {label:12} {res['usage']['input_tokens']:>6,} input tokens  {' -> '.join(steps)}")
$ python tool_search.py github-mcp-server stdio --toolsets=default
anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5   all loaded   19,464 input tokens  call get_latest_release
anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5   tool search   7,069 input tokens  search 'github|release' -> search 'latest release|list_releases|get_latest_release' -> call get_latest_release
openai/gpt-6-luna            all loaded    8,923 input tokens  call get_latest_release
openai/gpt-6-luna            tool search   4,453 input tokens  search 'github repository latest release cli cli' -> search 'github' -> search 'search web internet browser' -> search 'release' -> call get_latest_release

To try it on your agent, mark your MCP tools defer_loading: true, add {“type”: “openrouter:tool_search”}, and compare usage.input_tokens before and after.

The Tool Search rows vary with how the model searches. In five separate runs of this script, Haiku 5.5 used 2,134 to 13,225 tokens, rising with each search. GPT-6 Luna wrote phrases instead of patterns, made three to six searches, and once gave up without calling the tool. Our docs suggest keeping your three to five most-used tools loaded.

Over the whole task, the result depended on the model.

ModelMCP, 46 tools loadedTool Search, 46 deferredTool Search, 91 deferred
Claude Sonnet 5.559,41730,33431,615
GPT-6 Luna116,28225,54457,975
Gemini 3.8 Flash35,40937,56838,445
Claude Haiku 5.599,319154,62331,781

GPT-6 Luna’s loaded figure includes the 100-issue request described above.

On Sonnet 5.5, 91 deferred tools cost 1,281 tokens more than 46, where loading all 91 cost about 42,000 more. Tool Search doesn’t shrink tool results, and the release object still filled most of Sonnet’s second request.

Haiku 5.5 cost more with 46 deferred tools than with all loaded. In all three runs it asked list_issues for a field the tool doesn’t offer, then retried three or four times with arguments of the wrong type, such as labels as a string instead of an array. With all tools loaded, Haiku made the same mistake in two of three runs and fixed it on its next call. Cap the requests in your loop, and check tool errors when a run’s cost jumps.

Tool Search reveals tools by widening tool_choice, so a request that also forces a tool call fails.

400 tool_choice conflicts with openrouter:tool_search. Deferred tools are revealed through tool_choice, so it must be omitted or set to {“type”: “allowed_tools”, …}. Remove tool_choice, or drop defer_loading from your tools to use it as-is.

Chat Completions doesn’t accept openrouter:tool_search and returns a 400, so move that agent to the Responses or Messages API first.

MCP vs CLI vs skills: which should you use?

Use a CLI when one exists and your agent can run commands. When it can’t, use MCP, scoped and with small results.

Your situationUseFrom our runs on Sonnet 5.5
A well-known CLI exists and the agent can run commandsThe CLI1,421 tokens per task
Your own CLI, or one the model uses inconsistentlyThe CLI plus a skill3,315 tokens, same commands every run
No CLI, no shell, or you need the server’s auth and permissionsMCP, scoped to the tools you need23,228 tokens with 2 tools, against 59,417 with 46
A large tool library across many serversMCP with Tool SearchOn Sonnet 5.5, 91 deferred tools cost about what 46 did
Any MCP routeTrim tool results to the fields you need23,228 down to 5,357 tokens

If your agent has no shell, our Shell server tool gives any model a sandboxed one. In our Agent SDK, MCP Tools connects remote MCP servers, and the skills loader example adds a skill’s instructions only after the model asks for it.

We tested one server on one task, so run mcp_cost.py on yours before you decide.

Frequently asked questions

What is a CLI in an AI agent context?

A CLI (command-line interface) is a program you run with typed commands. An agent gets a shell tool and writes the commands itself. In our tests, the gh CLI used 1,421 input tokens on a GitHub task, against 59,417 for the GitHub MCP server.

What is the difference between an MCP server and a connector?

An MCP server exposes tools over the Model Context Protocol. A connector is what an app such as Claude calls its link to a remote MCP server. Our Agent SDK can connect remote MCP servers through MCP Tools.

Are skills replacing MCP?

No. A skill is instructions, usually for a CLI, that load only when a task needs them. MCP gives typed tools with their own auth and works without a shell. On OpenRouter, Tool Search lets you keep MCP and load each tool only when needed.

Does prompt caching fix MCP’s token cost?

It lowers the price of those tokens but doesn’t remove them. As of October 2026, on OpenRouter, cached input costs a tenth of the normal rate on Claude Haiku 5.5 and GPT-6 Luna, per our live model prices, and still fills the context window.

How many MCP tools is too many?

Our Tool Search docs suggest deferring tools once definitions pass roughly 10,000 tokens or about 10 tools. The GitHub MCP server’s 46 default tools came to 19,436 tokens on Claude.

Next steps

  • Tool Search covers every option, including max_results.
  • Build a Reliable Tool-Calling Agent Loop shows the kind of loop our runs used, with an iteration cap.
  • OpenRouter Prompt Caching explains what cached tokens cost.

item.title: [Amazon Bedrock] Introducing Kimi K3.1 Pro on Amazon Bedrock
item.content:encoded:
Artificial Intelligence

Introducing Kimi K3.1 Pro on Amazon Bedrock

Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed from Moonshot AI is now available on Amazon Bedrock. Part of Moonshot AI’s new K3.1 series, it’s a post-trained version of Kimi K3 with the same 3T-class open-weight architecture and 1-million-token context window, trained with substantially more post-training compute. According to Moonshot AI, that extra training targets long-horizon agentic work and fewer factual errors. It also improves professional tasks such as financial modeling and office documents, and coding for game engines, 3D scenes, and computer-aided design (CAD) scripts. Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed generates output tokens at a higher rate and Moonshot AI reports 2–3 times the speed of Kimi K3.1 Pro.

Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed uses the same endpoint, APIs, and features as Kimi K3 on Amazon Bedrock. If you already build with Kimi K3, you can try it by changing the model ID in your existing code.

Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed supports tool calling, structured output, configurable reasoning, image input, and streaming. You can adopt Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed without changing your security posture. Your data is processed within the AWS data boundary, isn’t shared with Moonshot AI, and isn’t used to train the model. Zero data retention is always enabled for inference requests, and with zero operator access, AWS operators can’t view your prompts and completions during inference.

In this post, we show you how to get started with Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed on Amazon Bedrock. We also cover how to lower costs with the Flex tier, explicit prompt caching for repeated context, and how to use the model as a coding assistant in OpenCode.

Get started with Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed on Amazon Bedrock

To try the model without writing code, open the Amazon Bedrock console, choose Test, then Playground, and select Kimi K3.1.

From code, Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed is available on the bedrock-runtime endpoint through the OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions and Responses APIs, and through the Amazon Bedrock Converse and Invoke APIs. We recommend the Chat Completions API. You reach the model through cross-Region inference profiles:

  • global.moonshotai.kimi-k3.1 routes requests to any supported commercial AWS Region, and costs less per token than the geographic profiles. We recommend it for most workloads.
  • us.moonshotai.kimi-k3.1 keeps processing within US Regions, and in.moonshotai.kimi-k3.1 keeps it within India Regions, for workloads with data residency requirements.

Prerequisites

To follow the examples, you need:

  • An AWS account with access to Amazon Bedrock.
  • Python 3.11 or later, with the OpenAI SDK, aws-bedrock-token-generator, and boto3 installed (pip install -U openai aws-bedrock-token-generator boto3).
  • An AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) identity allowed to call bedrock:InvokeModel and bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream on the Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed inference profiles. Add bedrock:CallWithBearerToken if you authenticate with a bearer token.

Call Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed with the Chat Completions API

If your application already uses the OpenAI SDK, point it at the Amazon Bedrock endpoint and change the model name. The following example creates a short-term bearer token from your AWS credentials and sends one request:

from openai import OpenAI
from aws_bedrock_token_generator import provide_token

REGION = "us-west-2"
MODEL_ID = "global.moonshotai.kimi-k3.1"

# A short-term token derived from your AWS credentials, so no long-lived key is stored in code
client = OpenAI(
    base_url=f"https://bedrock-runtime.{REGION}.amazonaws.com/openai/v1",
    api_key=provide_token(region=REGION),
)

completion = client.chat.completions.create(
    model=MODEL_ID,
    messages=[
        {"role": "system", "content": "You are a concise senior engineer."},
        {"role": "user", "content": "When should I prefer a queue over a stream?"},
    ],
    reasoning_effort="high",
)
print(completion.choices[0].message.content)

Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed always reasons before it answers. With reasoning_effort, you control how much: low, high, or max. If you don’t set it, the model uses max, so a lower value is the most direct way to reduce latency and output tokens on simpler tasks.

Call Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed with the Responses API

The same client works with the Responses API, which uses reasoning.effort for the same setting:

response = client.responses.create(
    model=MODEL_ID,
    input="Summarize the trade-offs between optimistic and pessimistic locking.",
    reasoning={"effort": "low"},
)
print(response.output_text)

Call Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed with the Converse API

If you already use the Amazon Bedrock Converse API, the change is the model ID:

import boto3

bedrock = boto3.client("bedrock-runtime", region_name="us-west-2")
response = bedrock.converse(
    modelId="global.moonshotai.kimi-k3.1",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": [{"text": "Explain idempotency keys in two sentences."}]}],
)

# The model can return a reasoning block before the answer, so pick the text block
content = response["output"]["message"]["content"]
print(next(block["text"] for block in content if "text" in block))

Lower costs with the Flex tier

The Flex tier serves Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed at half the Standard price, in exchange for potentially longer response times. It’s well suited to workloads where cost efficiency is a higher priority than response time, such as model evaluations, content summarization, and background tasks in agentic workflows. Because you choose the tier for each request, one application can mix tiers. For example, the same application could use Priority for latency-critical requests, Standard for everyday traffic, and Flex for cost-sensitive work. Your on-demand quota is shared across the Standard, Priority, and Flex tiers.

To use Flex, set service_tier to flex. The following example reuses the Chat Completions client from earlier:

completion = client.chat.completions.create(
    model=MODEL_ID,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "List edge cases to test in a function that parses ISO 8601 dates."}],
    service_tier="flex",
)
print(completion.choices[0].message.content)
print(completion.service_tier)  # The tier that served the request

On the Converse API, set serviceTier to {"type": "flex"} instead. To see how much of your traffic each tier served, use the ServiceTier and ResolvedServiceTier dimensions in Amazon CloudWatch. We recommend starting with a small share of your traffic on Flex and comparing latency and cost before you move more.

Optimize inference with explicit prompt caching

Agents and coding assistants resend the same large prefix on every turn: system instructions, tool definitions, repository conventions, and reference documents. Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed caches repeated prefixes automatically, and with explicit prompt caching, you can mark where the stable prefix ends to improve your cache hit rate. Later requests reuse that prefix instead of processing it again, which lowers both latency and input cost for long, repeated context.

A few rules apply:

  • Explicit caching works on the Chat Completions, Responses, and Invoke APIs, but not on Converse.
  • A prompt_cache_breakpoint must follow at least 256 tokens of stable content.
  • Cached content is retained for at least 30 minutes.
  • Cache writes are billed at a higher rate than standard input. Cache reads are billed at a discounted rate and don’t count toward your input tokens-per-minute quota.

The following example caches a long system prompt and adds a second breakpoint after the user content, so a follow-up question on the same document can reuse both layers:

from pathlib import Path

LONG_STATIC_PROMPT = Path("repo_guidelines.md").read_text()  # stable content, at least 256 tokens
QUESTION = "Which of these guidelines apply to database migrations?"

def cached_text(text):
    # Marks the end of a cacheable prefix
    return {"type": "input_text", "text": text, "prompt_cache_breakpoint": {"mode": "explicit"}}

response = client.responses.create(
    model=MODEL_ID,
    extra_body={"prompt_cache_options": {"mode": "explicit"}},
    input=[
        {"type": "message", "role": "system", "content": [cached_text(LONG_STATIC_PROMPT)]},
        {"type": "message", "role": "user", "content": [cached_text(QUESTION)]},
    ],
)
details = response.usage.input_tokens_details
print(f"Cache read: {details.cached_tokens} tokens")  # greater than 0 on a cache hit

For more information, refer to Prompt caching for faster model inference.

Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed in practice: Coding with OpenCode

OpenCode is an open source, model-agnostic coding agent that runs in your terminal. You can connect it to Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed through the Amazon Bedrock Chat Completions API, using OpenCode’s OpenAI-compatible provider and an Amazon Bedrock API key. To create a key, open the Amazon Bedrock console in the AWS Region that you set in baseURL, then choose API keys. Short-term keys last up to 12 hours, work only in the Region where you generate them, and are recommended for production use. Long-term keys are intended for exploration.

Add the following to ~/.config/opencode/opencode.json, replacing the Region in baseURL with your own:

{
  "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
  "providers": {
    "amazon-bedrock-chat-completions": {
      "name": "Amazon Bedrock (Chat Completions)",
      "package": "@opencode/ai/providers/openai-compatible",
      "settings": {
        "baseURL": "https://bedrock-runtime.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/openai/v1"
      },
      "models": {
        "global.moonshotai.kimi-k3.1": {
          "name": "Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed",
          "capabilities": {
            "reasoning": { "supported": true, "effort": ["low", "high", "max"] }
          }
        }
      }
    }
  },
  "model": "amazon-bedrock-chat-completions/global.moonshotai.kimi-k3.1"
}

Start OpenCode in your project directory, enter /connect, choose Amazon Bedrock (Chat Completions), and paste your API key as shown in Figure 1. OpenCode stores the key, so you connect once per key. To switch between Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed and other models during a session, enter /models.

Figure 1: Connecting OpenCode to the Amazon Bedrock (Chat Completions) provider

The capabilities entry in the configuration lists the reasoning effort levels that the model supports, so OpenCode offers low, high, and max as variants of the model, as shown in Figure 2:

Figure 2: Reasoning effort variants for Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed in OpenCode

Output speed matters most in agentic coding. To complete a single task, a coding agent makes many model calls in a row. It reads files, plans a change, edits code, runs tests, and fixes what fails. Each call has to finish before the next one starts, and much of that time is spent generating reasoning and code. A higher output-token rate shortens every step, so the whole edit-test-fix loop finishes sooner and you wait less between iterations.

Availability

Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed is available on Amazon Bedrock through the global.moonshotai.kimi-k3.1, us.moonshotai.kimi-k3.1, and in.moonshotai.kimi-k3.1 cross-Region inference profiles. For supported Regions and model details, refer to the Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed model card and Regional availability. For pricing, refer to Amazon Bedrock pricing.

To get started, try Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed on the Amazon Bedrock console. To discuss your use case with the Amazon Bedrock team, connect with us.

About the authors

item.title: [Anthropic Claude] Introducing Claude Whiteboards, Claude Sheets, and Claude Da…
item.description: Full title: Introducing Claude Whiteboards, Claude Sheets, and Claude Data
item.content:encoded:
Today we’re launching Claude Whiteboards and Claude Sheets in beta, and Claude Dashboards (opens in new tab) becomes generally available as Claude Data. Whiteboards is a shared board where your team brainstorms with Claude, Sheets is a spreadsheet Claude builds and edits with you, and Claude Data adds data stories, certified queries, and live sharing. These are available on all paid plans.

Working with Claude on a project often meant moving the output over to another tool or program, where Claude didn’t have live access to follow progress and changes. Now, your documents, boards, sheets, and dashboards can stay in Claude, with access for your team to continue editing together. When ready, you can bring the outputs directly into tools from our partners and continue working there.

Claude Whiteboards

Many people use Claude as a thought partner, but brainstorming with it has typically meant copy-pasting the results elsewhere so you can then start brainstorming or collaborating with your coworkers. Now, you can talk through a messy plan out loud with Claude, and Claude can turn it into a board with a timeline with owners and dates, so you and your team can collaborate in real time. In a retro meeting, for example, everyone can add their notes, and Claude can group them by theme and draft the action items for each person. You can focus on any part of the board by dragging a box around it and asking Claude questions. When you’re done brainstorming, Claude can turn the board into a doc or deck, or bring it into tools like Lucid, Miro, or Vani by Zoho, where you can continue working on it with your team.

Claude Sheets

Claude can now generate spreadsheets with tabs, formulas, formatting, and drop-downs, often from just a prompt like asking for a campaign tracker or a hiring budget. It can edit in the cells, outlining each new edit so you can track changes. You can share sheets with your team, so you and Claude can work on them together.

For now, sheets have simple spreadsheet functionality, but we are working on adding more. When you need the full functionality of Excel, you can export your file to .xlsx or CSV, or use Claude for Excel (opens in new tab). You can also continue working in partner tools including Airtable, Asana, monday.com, and Smartsheet.

Claude Data

Claude Dashboards (opens in new tab) launched in beta in October, enabling teams to ask quick questions of their company’s data in tools like Amazon Redshift, BigQuery, and ClickHouse. Starting today, it’s generally available as Claude Data. We changed the name because the way companies use their data is broader than dashboards, and the product now covers how they work more broadly. Certified queries and live sharing are in beta. Here are some ways teams can use Claude Data:

  • Create certified definitions of metrics. Your data team can certify the queries everyone should use, so you don’t end up building or working on dashboards with conflicting data. Charts built on these metrics carry a "certified" badge showing they’re certified.
  • Craft stories from data. You can work with Claude in Claude Data to draft data stories or narrated videos from your metrics, for you to review before sharing.
  • Share current numbers with everyone. With live sharing, your colleagues can see up-to-date numbers when they open a shared dashboard, even if they don’t have access to the connectors that keep that data current. Viewers see the results of the queries you’ve approved, and can’t run others with your access.
  • Match your look-and-feel. Design systems are now supported in Claude Data.
  • Get faster loading with caching. Previously, every dashboard would reload on every load. Now, dashboards support caching, and refresh cadences can be set on a per-dashboard basis.
  • Track changes over time. Claude Data now has tracked changes, so you can see who has made edits and roll back to a specific version if needed.

Our partners for Claude Data include Amplitude, Mixpanel, Omni, PostHog, and Sigma.

Work in your other tools, too

Starting today, interactive connectors (opens in new tab) can open as full apps beside your conversation or in full screen, so you can work in tools like Adobe, Atlassian, Box, and Notion yourself, or ask Claude to make changes with you.

Getting started

Claude Whiteboards, Sheets, and Data work on web, desktop, and mobile. Claude Data needs a data connector, such as a warehouse or CRM.

For admins: On Team plans, all three are on by default. On Enterprise plans, Claude Whiteboards and Sheets are off by default, and Claude Data turns on by default on November 19, 2026. You can change these anytime in Organization settings > Artifacts.

item.title: [Anthropic Claude] Your apps can now open in Claude, and Claude can work in the…
item.description: Full title: Your apps can now open in Claude, and Claude can work in them
item.content:encoded:
Earlier this year, we launched interactive connectors (opens in new tab) to bring a small live view of tools into Claude. Starting today, where a connector supports it, you can open a tool beside your conversation or expand it to full screen, and ask Claude to work alongside you and make changes directly.

This is rolling out on the web and in the Claude desktop app on all plans, as part of the new Claude experience (opens in new tab) that brings chat and Cowork together. You’ll see these features once your account is updated with the new Claude or your organization turns it on.

What’s new:

  • Claude can work in your open tools. You can ask Claude to make changes to a page, row, or file that you have open and approve its actions the same way you approve a connector’s actions. Changes appear in the tool as Claude makes them, so you can keep working right alongside it.
  • The whole tool opens next to your conversation. You can work in the tool and hide the chat or go full screen when you need room. For tools like Confluence or Notion, that means you get the full editor, signed into your own account, rather than a limited preview.
  • Open a connected tool directly, without having to write a Claude prompt. When you want Claude’s help, you can ask from the same screen.
  • Pin the tools you use most. You can arrange them alongside your artifacts and access them with one click in your sidebar and the + menu.

Work with Claude in the tools you use

We’re starting with a small group of tools from our directory, including Asana, Canva, Carta, Dropbox, monday.com, Smartsheet, Vercel, and Webflow.

Here’s what you can do with some of the tools available in Claude today:

  • Adobe. Ask Claude to retouch, edit and add effects to photos; highlight, edit and redact PDFs.
  • Atlassian. Open a Confluence page beside your chat, ask Claude to write and edit, and review its changes live on the page.
  • Box. Open a Box file beside your chat, ask Claude to revise it, and compare the versions side by side before you keep the changes.
  • HubSpot. Prioritize pipeline tasks and follow-ups, then act on them in Claude.
  • Notion. Ask Claude to create a Notion doc or database. Build as you chat, or edit it yourself, without leaving Claude.

Figma, Harvey, and Shopify are also building integrations, and we encourage other developers to do the same.

For developers: built on MCP Apps

Interactive connectors run on MCP Apps, the open extension to the Model Context Protocol (opens in new tab) that lets an MCP server bring its own interface into AI applications. An MCP App you build isn’t limited to Claude and can run in any AI application that supports the extension (opens in new tab).

Until now, MCP Apps in Claude have mainly appeared as interactive views in the conversation. Claude now supports more of the extension, such as app tools, along with embedded sites, so a developer’s full app can run inside Claude.

Support for these capabilities is in public preview for developers. Developers can start building with them today. Read our docs (opens in new tab) to start building.

Getting started

You can connect the tools we mention above from the directory (opens in new tab), then open any tool from your chat or pin it to your sidebar.

For admins: If your organization already allows all of a connector’s tools, its new features appear as they roll out. Admins can restrict a connector’s tools the same way they do today.
