item.title: [Anthropic Claude] How Curative is building a national provider network with ag…
item.description: Full title: How Curative is building a national provider network with agents on Claude
item.content:encoded:
In our series, How startups build with Claude, we highlight how startups are transforming their industries with AI. In this article, we share how Curative built a hierarchy of agents on Claude to sign provider contracts about 50 times faster than its team did in 2025.

The quick pitch
NameCurative
Founded2020; launched its health plan in 2022
FoundersFred Turner (CEO), Isaac Turner (CTO), Tami Wilson-Ciranna (President)
StackClaude Platform, Claude Code, bespoke claims system
Growth$150M Series B at a $1.275B valuation. 165,000+ members and 1,200+ employers (Dec 2025). 23,000 provider contracts signed with Gwen. 2,000 to 2,400 new contracts a week, up from 2,100 in all of 2025.

Curative sells health insurance to employers, with $0 copays and $0 deductibles for in-network care once members complete a Baseline Visit. Curative didn’t start out in insurance. It started as a lab startup and ended up processing 10% of all US COVID-19 tests according to their internal estimates. As a result, they started working with nearly every insurer in the country.

Its British founders, used to a system where patients don’t pay for care, saw inefficiencies and set out to build a payer focused on prevention. They realized they had significantly underestimated how hard building a national network would be.

“Sometimes naivety is good in startups, because you don’t know that it’s impossible. And then along the way you figure out a way to make it not impossible,” said Curative CEO Fred Turner. “Last year we signed 2,100 contracts, twice as many as we did the year before, but at 2,000 a year, we realized it would still be a 30-year build. There is a reason there are only a handful of national networks and they were all built about 30 years ago.”

Curative needed to accelerate contract signings, but hiring alone couldn’t close a gap that size.

Their solution: Gwen, an agent that works one provider deal from initial outreach to signature, surrounded by smaller agents that review its rates, check its messages, answer its questions, and escalate to humans for non-standard pricing.

Here is how they built it and what broke along the way.

Gwen: the provider contracts agent

Gwen works both inbound and outbound leads. Each run of Gwen handles a single provider, mostly on Claude Opus, so nothing from other deals influences it.

For example, if a practice fills in the form on Curative’s website, Gwen will research the practice and reply with proposed rates based on a purchased claims data set and price-transparency files payers are now required to publish. Gwen will show providers these market rate data to help with negotiations.

The rate reviewer runs on Sonnet. When Gwen wants to exceed its standard rate template, it writes out why, and the reviewer decides whether the rate makes sense.

“For a long time there was a big approval queue where Gwen had to get rates approved if she wanted to go a certain amount above the template, but we relaxed over time. Having a second agent review rates worked better than just giving Gwen more authority,” said Fred.

The Sonnet rate reviewer clears about two-thirds of Gwen’s requests and then anything non-standard goes to Fred for approval.

“The requests I see are from a big medical group or someone with a weird request that would come to me even if this wasn’t an agent-led motion,” said Fred.

Outbound deals take more persistence, because practices are busy. Some providers’ replies come after the fourteenth email and the ninth fax.

Image used with permission from Curative.

A judge, which runs on Haiku, reads every communication before it’s sent. Curative added it after Gwen copied providers on internal notes about how high it could go. A blocked message comes back with the reason, so Gwen can rewrite it and try again.

Each contract takes about 20 million tokens to complete, roughly a tenth of the original cost. These efficiencies enable one of Curative’s core strategies: signing smaller providers that have often been overlooked by larger networks.

“The agent will happily give you the same level of attention whether you are a large hospital system or if you’re a solo provider,” Fred explained. “From that agent’s perspective, this provider is its only focus.”

During negotiations, Gwen checks practice redlines against Curative’s policy document, then writes Python to merge both sides’ changes into a final document.

From form to signature, the process can be as quick as an hour. Once the contract is signed, a separate credentialing agent checks the provider’s licenses, and agents load the provider’s data and contract so claims can price against it.

Curative’s contracting team has grown from 45 to about 55 people since Gwen launched, each about 2.5 times as productive. They hand Gwen cold outreach and paperwork and take over warm leads by phone. Curative pays its contracting team on Gwen’s deals too, so people and agents share one target.

“People’s work becomes more about the relationship and less about paperwork,” said Fred.

Fred also believes faster contracting helps small practices stay independent. “If you start a medical practice and it takes three months to get in network and credentialed, you’re just not getting paid for three months,” he said.

Gwen is not Curative’s only agent. Brad, another Opus-based agent, helps sell Curative’s plan to employers, mainly through brokers. Brad follows up with brokers on each quote and helps underwriters move faster by pulling employee data out of the spreadsheets underwriters used to scrub by hand.

Using human-agent teams, Curative can now answer emailed or faxed claims disputes in under 30 minutes, with a letter specific to that claim. “Claims dispute responses used to take about 90 days and now take under 30 minutes by email or fax,” said Fred. “Most payers use a set of templates that are mail-merged together. That leaves a provider deeply unsatisfied, because usually the template doesn’t actually explain what’s going on. Now providers get a customized letter that explains the specifics of the individual claim, what’s happening, and why.”

All of their agents sit on bespoke claims, prior authorization, and finance systems that 13 engineers rebuilt this year with Claude Code. The team had once sized building a claims system alone at 100 engineer-years.

“We’re not trying to plug [these agents] into a claim system,” Fred said. “The claim system is Python running in AWS, and it has an MCP and it has an API, and Claude wrote it, so it understands it.”

What Curative learned from building agents that negotiate with people

Here’s what the Curative team learned about how to build agents that negotiate with people.

  • Start with one general tool. “We started off with, ‘Oh, we’ll have tools,’ and that doesn’t work that well, because redlining is quite complex,” Fred said. “What we found works best is that the model just has one tool, which is run Python, and it does all the redlining with a docx library. It works beautifully.”
  • Meet people on their channel. A fax tool more than doubled Gwen’s win rate. Many providers now handwrite on a printed fax and fax it back. “It’s meeting people where they are,” said Curative CTO Isaac Turner. “Yes, they have email, but really they’re comfortable in fax.”
  • Keep each run isolated. One Gwen run sees one provider and keeps no memory across deals. Brad, Curative’s sales agent, does keep memories, which works but needs care. “You can end up making notes that are wrong and then get into these doom loops, where it has a bad memory that can never be cleared,” Fred noted.
  • Improve the system from outside the run. Every few days, Fred gives Claude Code the same prompt: sample the last 10,000 runs, flag anything weird, and open a PR to fix it. “The improvement loops come from running Claude Code over lots of historic conversations and asking how could this have gotten better,” he said.
  • Experiment away from PHI first. For a long time Gwen was barred from protected health information (PHI), so early mistakes were in lower-risk settings. Where agents touch PHI now, back-end controls limit what enters a conversation, and agent activity is logged for audit. “We learned how to do it there and then transferred it over into PHI land,” said Fred. Signing Business Associate Agreements (BAAs), the contracts HIPAA requires before a vendor can handle PHI, has gotten easier too. “Anthropic especially has been very good about getting HIPAA-compliant versions of the latest services out very quickly,” said Isaac. “We’ve been able to onboard these new technologies very quickly despite it being regulated.”
  • Watch what the agent starts doing on its own and make sure it matches your risk profile. When providers asked for a flyer to share internally, Gwen made one with its Python tool, with no policy telling it to. When a front desk turned away a member at an in-network practice, Gwen asked the office to train its staff, then checked that the member got in.

Where Curative is going next

Next, Curative plans to bring agents to care navigation, extending the reach of the 130 people who guide and coach its members.

Fred expects agents on the provider side too. A large share of claims disputes already appear to be written by agents, and he hopes providers will use agents to negotiate contracts. “There’s a clearing price, and the faster you find the clearing price, everybody can get on with providing care,” he said.

Best practices from the Curative team
How much authority should an agent start with?Less than you think it can handle. Gwen began with a human approval queue for any rate above the template. Curative loosened the limits in steps and for more deterministic decisions, then added the rate reviewer, with Fred still approving what it doesn’t clear.
What happens when the agent gets it wrong?Plan for it, and compare it with the alternative. “The bar isn’t perfect,” Isaac said. “The bar is, if you had a thousand people signing contracts, how many mistakes would they make that you regret?”
How do you audit hundreds of thousands of messages?Log everything, put a judge agent on every outbound message, and have Claude Code sample the runs.

Start building with the Claude Platform today.

item.title: [Anthropic Claude] More ways to work with Claude: Sheets, Whiteboards, and Inte…
item.description: Full title: More ways to work with Claude: Sheets, Whiteboards, and Interactive Connectors
item.content:encoded:
We've seen Claude Code change how developers work. Engineers went from manually coding line by line, to describing ideas and reviewing what Claude built. It reconnected them with the joy of building. Our goal is to bring that magic to every team, and today we're expanding what Claude makes possible. We're introducing new artifact types with Claude Sheets, Claude Whiteboards, and Claude Data. We're also making it easier to work in your most-used apps with an upgrade to interactive connectors. Claude Meetings is coming soon.

All your connectors and context

In Claude Code, the context Claude needs is already in the codebase. For other teams, context sprawls across emails, apps, and drives. Claude reaches it through connectors built on the Model Context Protocol (opens in new tab) (MCP), the open standard we introduced for connecting AI to the tools you use. Claude Marketplace lists more than 9,000 connectors and plugins, including community-built ones.

Interactive connectors (opens in new tab) take this further. Starting today, partners can embed their apps directly in Claude, so you can work in Adobe, Atlassian, and others without switching tabs. Plugins from Salesforce (beta), NetSuite, and Workday (beta) come with built-in skills, so sellers can prep for a call, accountants can analyze financial data, and HR teams can handle time off and expenses.

Bring ideas to life faster, together

Starting today, Claude can build spreadsheets, whiteboards, and dashboards with your team. These work with its existing abilities to create documents, slide decks, and designs (opens in new tab), and with Claude Motion (opens in new tab) (beta), which helps you turn content into short animations. In each one, Claude quickly picks up what you need, so your thinking sets the pace of work:

  • New artifact types (opens in new tab):In Claude Sheets, your team and Claude build spreadsheets together, collaboratively organize data, create and edit formulas, and work across multiple tabs.Claude Whiteboards is a digital whiteboard that your team can use to lay out and organize ideas together in a meeting, then ask Claude to summarize the findings.Claude Data (formerly Dashboards) connects to tools like Snowflake and Salesforce and can use definitions your data team certifies (beta) to create dashboards, visual data stories, or narrated short videos.

You can also ask Claude to build custom artifacts for the way your team works, like an account tracker, a daily briefing, a project status board, or a contract review table. Since Claude carries the same context through every step, an idea can carry over from a whiteboard to a spreadsheet to a dashboard, without the need to reiterate the details.

Coming soon, Claude Meetings will let you add Claude to a call to take notes and update the documents your team is working on during the conversation.

Teams already working this way

Inside Anthropic, non-technical teams are starting to get as much out of Claude as our engineers. Our legal team worked with Claude to build a Slack-based legal review tool that automatically draws redlines from the team’s own playbook. This brought marketing reviews from three days down to 24 hours, and easy fixes are made before a lawyer reviews the draft. Our finance team turned a long business update document for executives into an interactive page, and now the whole team updates it together with Claude.

Neither of these teams writes code, but they're experts in their fields. They used Claude to turn that knowledge into tools that saved them time, and that others can use. Our customers are working this way too:

“At Datadog, Claude has extended from coding to knowledge work. Our product managers are using Claude to move from an idea to a feature brief, PRD, and testable prototype much faster, giving them more time to focus on customer needs, product judgment, and the right problems to solve. When someone builds something good with Claude at Datadog, it spreads fast.”

Yanbing Li, Chief Product Officer, Datadog

1/5

Built for and with enterprises

As Claude starts to connect to more tools, businesses need better ways to oversee its access and actions. We build in security and compliance controls to help enterprises meet their own requirements, and we use the same Claude for our own most sensitive work. On Enterprise plans, admins decide who can use which products and connectors, and set spend limits for the organization at a granular level.

That control applies to the tools Claude connects to. With Claude auto-connect (opens in new tab), now in beta on eligible Team and Enterprise plans, connecting an app like Notion, Atlassian, or Dropbox is a one-time setup. Employees are then connected to the tool the first time they use it in Claude, instead of connecting each one individually.

Whichever way a tool is connected, Claude works within your existing permissions. Admins can also limit what each connector does, meaning that Claude might be able to read Slack but not send messages on your behalf.

Protecting sensitive business data is core to how we build, and we're continuing to harden those protections as Claude takes on longer, more complex work:

  • Data from Enterprise organizations (opens in new tab) is encrypted in transit and at rest.
  • On Enterprise plans, security teams can see how Claude is being used (opens in new tab), through audit logs and a Compliance API that works with more than 100 security and compliance tools, including Splunk and CrowdStrike.
  • In the new Claude experience on Enterprise, each cloud session runs in its own isolated virtual machine (opens in new tab), with connector credentials kept outside it.

Work that keeps up with your ideas

Modern work is set up around software, but Claude works around you. It knows your team's work through the tools you connect, helps you bring ideas to life in the formats you need, and runs within the controls your admins set. That leaves you more time to focus and make progress on big goals.

item.content:encoded:
Today Anthropic, PBC launched the roadshow for its proposed initial public offering of its Class A common stock.

The proposed offering consists of 825,000,000 shares of Class A common stock. Of these, 801,351,354 shares are being offered by Anthropic and 23,648,646 shares are being offered by certain existing stockholders. Anthropic will not receive any proceeds from the sale of shares by the selling stockholders. Anthropic also expects to grant the underwriters a 30-day option to purchase up to an additional 123,750,000 shares of its Class A common stock.

The initial public offering price is expected to be between $70.00 and $78.00 per share. Anthropic has applied to list its Class A common stock on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the symbol “ANT.”

The proposed offering will be made only by means of a prospectus. Copies of the preliminary prospectus may be obtained from: Goldman Sachs & Co. LLC, Attention: Prospectus Department, 200 West Street, New York, NY 10282, by telephone at (866) 471-2526, or by email at prospectus-ny@ny.email.gs.com; or Morgan Stanley & Co. LLC, Attention: Prospectus Department, 180 Varick Street, 2nd Floor, New York, NY 10014.

A registration statement relating to these securities has been filed with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission but has not yet become effective. These securities may not be sold, nor may offers to buy be accepted, prior to the time the registration statement becomes effective. Today’s announcement does not constitute an offer to sell or the solicitation of an offer to buy these securities, nor shall there be any sale of these securities in any state or jurisdiction in which such offer, solicitation, or sale would be unlawful prior to registration or qualification under the securities laws of any such state or jurisdiction.

item.title: [Hugging Face] Pay for Hugging Face Hub with your Google Cloud Account
item.content:encoded:
Back to Articles

Pay for Hugging Face Hub with your Google Cloud Account

Published November 10, 2026

Update on GitHub

9

Zaïd Alhadad

zaid-alhadad

Pierric Cistac

pierric

Simon Pagezy

pagezyhf

Michelle Habonneau

michellehbn

You can now link your Hugging Face organization to your Google Cloud account, so that your Hugging Face usage shows up on your Google Cloud bill instead of being charged to a credit card. Get started on the Google Cloud Marketplace.

Why pay through Google Cloud?

Hugging Face is where teams find, build and run open models: from hosting private models and datasets, to running GPU workloads with Jobs, deploying models with Inference Endpoints, calling thousands of models through Inference Providers, or hosting demos on GPU Spaces.

If your company already runs on Google Cloud, adding a new vendor and a corporate credit card just to use these services can slow things down. By linking your organization through the Google Cloud Marketplace:

  • One bill: your Hugging Face usage appears on your existing Google Cloud invoice, next to the rest of your cloud spend.
  • No new vendor to onboard: purchases go through your existing Google Cloud billing account and procurement process.
  • Everything is covered: upgrading your org to a Team or Enterprise subscription, pay-as-you-go compute (Jobs, Inference Endpoints, Inference Providers, GPU Spaces, ZeroGPU quota extension), and additional storage at public Hugging Face pricing.

If you're an admin of your Hugging Face organization, here's how to set it up, step by step.

1. Subscribe to Hugging Face on the Google Cloud Marketplace

Go to the Hugging Face Hub listing on the Google Cloud Marketplace, select the Google Cloud project you want to use, and click on "Subscribe".

You are now on the subscription page. Select the billing account to be charged, review and accept the terms, then click "Subscribe".

Once the order is placed, Google Cloud asks you to finish setting up your account with Hugging Face. Click on "Sign up with Hugging Face" to be redirected to Hugging Face.

2. Link your Hugging Face organization

You are now on Hugging Face, where you can select the organization you want to link to your Google Cloud account. Only organizations where you are an admin are listed. Select it and confirm.

You are then redirected to the billing settings of your organization. The payment method section now shows the linked Google Cloud account, with a pending status.

Every cloud marketplace subscription is reviewed by the Hugging Face team before paid usage starts being billed through it. While the subscription is pending, usage keeps being billed to the organization's existing payment method, if any.

3. Subscription approved

Once your subscription is approved, you will receive an email confirming that your Google Cloud account and Hugging Face organization are linked. Organizations that already have a credit card on file switch to cloud marketplace billing at the start of their next billing period. Organizations on the free tier with no credit card on file usually switch immediately, so their paid usage is billed through the cloud marketplace right away.

To confirm it, open the billing settings of your organization: the Google Cloud account is now shown as the organization's active payment method.

Congratulations!

Your organization is now billed through your Google Cloud account. All members of your organization can use Hugging Face compute services, and the usage will show up on your Google Cloud bill.

A few things worth knowing:

  • Google Cloud replaces the credit card as the organization's payment method. Usage is metered and reported to Google Cloud, so adding credits is not available while the organization is billed through the marketplace.
  • Included credits still apply: if your organization has a Team or Enterprise subscription, the monthly included credits are applied before any pay-as-you-go usage is reported to Google Cloud.
  • Monitor your usage at any time from the billing section of your organization settings, and find the charges in the Billing reports of the Google Cloud console.
  • Linking and unlinking are audited: both actions are recorded in your organization's audit logs.

Thanks for reading! You can find more details in the billing documentation. If you have any questions, please contact us at billing@huggingface.co.

item.title: [Hugging Face] Decision Models in Hugging Face
item.content:encoded:
Back to Articles

Decision Models in Hugging Face

Published November 10, 2026

Update on GitHub

53

Aritra Roy Gosthipaty

ariG23498

Lysandre

lysandre

Pedro Cuenca

pcuenq

Tom Aarsen

tomaarsen

Large Language Models (LLMs) are exceptionally good at generating text. We use them to answer questions, write code, reason about problems, and so much more. But not every problem requires generating text.

Consider a customer support system receiving the following message:

"I was charged twice for my subscription. I need a refund today."

The system needs to determine which team should handle the request, how urgent it is, and whether the customer is requesting a refund.

We could ask an LLM to return a JSON object containing these answers.

llama cli -hf ggml-org/gemma-4-e4b-it-GGUF:Q4_0

> We have the following customer support ticket, "I was charged twice for my subscription. I need a refund today.", which team should handle the request, how urgent it is, and whether the customer is requesting a refund. Give the answers in JSON.

[Start thinking]
...
[end thinking]

{ "team_to_handle": "Billing", "urgency": "High", "request_refund": true }


But what if the model could directly evaluate the available options and return a probability distribution over them, *without generating any text*?

from transformers import pipeline

decide = pipeline("decision", model="autotrust/GEV-26B-Decide") decision = decide( { "state": "I was charged twice for my order and want a refund.", "questions": { "department": { "type": "choice", "instructions": "Which team should handle this?", "criteria": { "billing": "Payments and refunds", "technical": "Bugs and technical issues", "sales": "Pricing and subscriptions" } }, } } )

{

'department': {

'type': 'choice',

'choice': 'billing',

'confidence': 0.9974000453948975,

'probabilities': {

'billing': 0.9982666969299316,

'technical': 0.0010246571619063616,

'sales': 0.0007087149424478412

}

}

}


This is the key idea behind **decision models**.

## What are decision models?

A decision model takes some input context (state), evaluates a question with a set of predefined possible answers (primitives), and returns a structured decision along with probabilities. Instead of asking a model to generate an answer token by token, we ask it to assign probabilities to the answers that our application already understands.

[![state and primitives for the decision models](https://huggingface.co/datasets/huggingface/documentation-images/resolve/main/blog/decision/decision-models.png)](https://huggingface.co/datasets/huggingface/documentation-images/resolve/main/blog/decision/decision-models.png)

[TypeSafe AI introduced Jev](https://typesafe.ai/blog/introducing-system-one-models-and-jev), describing it as a [*System One model*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thinking,_Fast_and_Slow). The name draws inspiration from the distinction between fast, intuitive thinking (System 1) and slower, deliberative thinking (System 2).

> The community has converged to the term decision model, because it describes the model's computational role rather than invoking a particular theory of cognition. In the rest of the post we will refer to the models as "decision models" instead of "system one models". (A poll on twitter deciding what we should be calling such models)

For a decision model, the fundamental interface is:

State + Questions + Allowed Answers → Decisions + Probabilities


## Why not use LLMs for everything?

We could simply prompt an LLM to return a JSON object containing our decisions. In fact, this is how many applications already use language models for classification, routing, and other structured tasks.

However, there are a few problems with this approach.

- LLMs are not guaranteed to follow the requested schema: Even with explicit instructions, a model might produce invalid JSON, introduce unexpected keys, or return an answer outside the allowed choices.
- Constrained decoding helps, but does not eliminate the computational overhead: Libraries such as [Outlines](https://github.com/dottxt-ai/outlines) and [XGrammar](https://github.com/mlc-ai/xgrammar) can enforce grammars or JSON schemas by restricting which tokens the model is allowed to generate at each step. This ensures the output follows the supported structural constraints, but introduces additional work.
- Why generate an entire response: LLMs are designed for open-ended generation, but when our application only needs to choose between predefined answers, autoregressive decoding can be unnecessary work.

## How are decision models different from classification models?

Before understanding the interface of a decision model, it is useful to revisit two closely related approaches namely traditional classification and zero-shot classification.

### Traditional classification

Suppose we train a classifier that routes customer-support requests to three departments:

- Billing
- Technical support
- Sales

A conventional classification model learns a mapping from an input to a predefined set of labels. During training, the model learns to predict these labels from examples. A classification head typically produces one logit per class, and softmax turns those logits into a probability distribution.

The limitation here is that ***the output classes are baked into the model's classification head***.

If we introduce a fourth department, such as Legal, the existing classifier does not automatically acquire a corresponding output class. We may need to modify the head, collect training data, and **retrain** or adapt the model.

### Zero-shot classification

[Zero-shot classification](https://huggingface.co/tasks/zero-shot-classification) addresses an important part of this limitation. Instead of requiring the classifier to be trained specifically on every output category, we supply the candidate labels at inference time.

For example:

from transformers import pipeline

classifier = pipeline( "zero-shot-classification", model="facebook/bart-large-mnli", )

classifier( "My payment was deducted twice.", candidate_labels=["billing", "technical support", "sales"], )

{'sequence': 'My payment was deducted twice.',

'labels': ['billing', 'sales', 'technical support'],

'scores': [0.8466812372207642, 0.0962134450674057, 0.05710534751415253]}


Unlike a conventional fixed-label classifier, the categories can change from one request to another. Let’s add another department, such as “Legal”, and see the model outputs.

from transformers import pipeline

classifier = pipeline( "zero-shot-classification", model="facebook/bart-large-mnli", )

classifier( "My payment was deducted twice.", candidate_labels=["billing", "technical support", "sales", "legal"], )

{'sequence': 'My payment was deducted twice.',

'labels': ['billing', 'sales', 'technical support', 'legal'],

'scores': [0.8185835480690002, 0.09302053600549698, 0.05521026626229286, 0.03318570926785469]}


One common implementation uses a model trained for natural language inference (NLI). Each candidate label is converted into a hypothesis, and the model measures how strongly the input entails that hypothesis.

This already sounds quite similar to a decision model. And in many ways, it is.

### Where decision models differ

Decision models extend this idea beyond simply assigning an input to a category. A decision model can accept several named questions about the same state, with different answer types. The types can be choosing between alternatives (choice), scoring an ordered scale (score), or estimating the probability that a statement is true (noul).

More importantly, its interface is designed around the **probability distribution over possible decisions**.

Consider these three approaches:

| Property | Classification | Zero-shot classification | Decision model |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Probability over choices | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| Labels defined at inference | No | Yes | Yes |
| Multiple typed questions | No | No | Yes |
| Ordered scoring and yes/no decisions | Task-specific | Possible with adaptation | Native primitives |

The advantage of decision models is not that they invented runtime-defined labels or probabilistic classification. It is that they organize these capabilities into a consistent interface, potentially backed by architectures and training procedures optimized specifically for decisions.

## The decision model interface

A decision model request has the following two components:

- state
- questions

### State

The state is the information the model should evaluate. It may be a string, a structured JSON object, or, other modalities for supported omni-modal models.

For example:

{ "customer_message": "I was charged twice. Please refund me today.", "subscription": "pro", "previous_tickets": 2 }


### Questions and their primitives

Questions describe what we want to know about the state. In the decision models interface, three fundamental primitives represent different forms of decisions:

- **Choice:** Select one of several possible answers.
- **Score:** Evaluate something on an ordered scale.
- **Noul:** Answer a yes/no question probabilistically.

Let's go over them one by one.

#### Choice: A probability distribution over options

Choice is the most intuitive primitive and the closest to traditional classification.

Suppose we ask:

> Which department should handle this customer request?

The available options are Billing, Technical support, and Sales.

from transformers import pipeline

decide = pipeline("decision", model="autotrust/GEV-26B-Decide") decision = decide( { "state": "I was charged twice for my order and want a refund.", "questions": { "department": { "type": "choice", "instructions": "Which team should handle this?", "criteria": { "billing": "Payments and refunds", "technical": "Bugs and technical issues", "sales": "Pricing and subscriptions" } }, } } )

{

'department': {

'type': 'choice',

'choice': 'billing',

'confidence': 0.9974000453948975,

'probabilities': {

'billing': 0.9982666969299316,

'technical': 0.0010246571619063616,

'sales': 0.0007087149424478412

}

}

}


The model assigns a logit to each option. For logits ($z_1,\ldots,z_K$), (with K classes) we can obtain the probabilities using softmax:

pi=exp⁡(zi/T)∑j=1Kexp⁡(zj) p_i=\frac{\exp(z_i/T)}{\sum_{j=1}^{K}\exp(z_j)}

Here, (K) is the number of choices.

Consider this illustrative distribution:

| Choice | Probability |
| --- | --- |
| Billing | 0.998 |
| Technical support | 0.001 |
| Sales | 0.001 |

The probabilities sum to one:

∑i=1Kpi=1. \sum_{i=1}^{K}p_i=1.

The model chooses the option with the largest probability:

y^=arg⁡max⁡ipi \hat y=\arg\max_i p_i

In this case, the choice is Billing, with the probability of 0.998, but the remaining probabilities are useful too. They tell us how the model distributes its belief among the alternatives.

#### Score: The expectation of an ordered distribution

Choice works when there are several distinct alternatives. But what if we want to measure something on an ordered scale?

Consider the question:

> How urgent is this customer request?

We define three levels:

- 0: Low urgency
- 1: Medium urgency
- 2: High urgency

from transformers import pipeline

decide = pipeline("decision", model="autotrust/GEV-26B-Decide") decision = decide( { "state": "I was charged twice for my order and want a refund.", "questions": { "urgency": { "type": "score", "instructions": "How urgent is the request?", "criteria": ["low", "medium", "high"] }, } } )

{

'urgency': {

'type': 'score',

'score': 1.7053890228271484,

'legend': {

'0': 'low',

'1': 'medium',

'2': 'high'

},

'confidence': 0.5580834252759814,

'probabilities': {

'0': 0.014908230863511562,

'1': 0.26479458808898926,

'2': 0.7202972173690796

}

}

}


The model again produces a probability distribution:

| Level | Probability |
| --- | --- |
| 0 — Low | 0.01 |
| 1 — Medium | 0.26 |
| 2 — High | 0.72 |

Rather than returning only the most likely level, the Score primitive computes the **expected value of the level index**.

For a random variable (X) representing the level, the expectation is:

E[X]=∑i=0K−1ipi \mathbb{E}[X]=\sum_{i=0}^{K-1}ip_i

For our example:

E[X]=0(0.01)+1(0.26)+2(0.72)=1.7 \mathbb{E}[X] = 0(0.01)+1(0.26)+2(0.72)=1.7

The reported score is therefore `1.7`.

This does not mean that the model selected a fictional level halfway between medium and high. It means that the expectation of its probability distribution is 1.7.

#### Noul: A Bernoulli decision

The third primitive is Noul, which represents a binary question.

For example:

> Is the customer requesting a refund?

from transformers import pipeline

decide = pipeline("decision", model="autotrust/GEV-26B-Decide") decision = decide( { "state": "I was charged twice for my order and want a refund.", "questions": { "refund": { "type": "noul", "instructions": "Is the customer requesting a refund?" } } } )

{

'refund': {

'type': 'noul',

'noul': 0.9947046637535095

}

}


Rather than defining a list of choices, we ask the model to return the probability that the answer is true. We can understand this using the Bernoulli distribution (noul comes from Bernoulli).

Let (Y) represent a binary outcome:

Y∼Bernoulli⁡(p) Y\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p)

where

P(Y=1)=p,P(Y=0)=1−p. P(Y=1)=p,\qquad P(Y=0)=1-p.

If the model returns:

{"type": "noul", "noul": 0.92}


it assigns a probability of `0.92` to Yes and `0.08` to No.

The model is not randomly sampling a binary answer here. It returns the probability parameter itself, leaving the application to decide how to act on it.

#### Confidence: How certain is the model?

So far, we have obtained probability distributions from the model. But the decision model interface also returns a field called `confidence` for Choice and Score.

The full distribution might contain several possible answers, and it is useful to summarize how concentrated the model's belief is. With `confidence` we achieve just that.

For a Choice with (K) options, the confidence is:

pmax⁡−1K1−1K \frac{p_{\max}-\frac{1}{K}}{1-\frac{1}{K}}

where ($p_{\max}$) is the largest predicted probability.

The intuition here is:

- A uniform distribution has confidence 0. ($p_{\max} = \frac{1}{K}$). This means the model estimates that all choices are equally likely.
- A distribution concentrated entirely on one option has confidence 1. ($p_{\max} = 1$)
- The larger the winning probability relative to a uniform distribution, the higher the confidence.

In our previous three-choice example, Billing had probability 0.80:

C=3(0.99)−12=0.98 C=\frac{3(0.99)-1}{2}=0.98

Notice that the winning probability is 0.99, but the reported confidence is 0.98. The confidence normalizes the largest probability relative to the number of available options. In contrast, the ordered Score example only had a confidence of 0.558.

## Decision models in the Hugging Face ecosystem

Decision models are a young and fast-moving space. Each one makes decisions differently under the hood (heads that score the whole schema jointly, separate readouts on top of LLM backbones, edge-sized and multimodal variants, etc). This variety is healthy, but it comes at a cost. If every model exposes its own interface, every tool around it needs model-specific adaptations.

Our goal at Hugging Face is to agree on a common **interface** without forcing a common **implementation**. A decision model should be free to work however it likes internally, as long as it accepts the same state and questions and returns the same typed decisions. Once that contract exists, the rest of the ecosystem can build on it once:

- inference engines like llama.cpp can serve any decision model through the same API
- the Hub can package and surface them consistently
- and training tools can target shared primitives instead of individual architectures

The rest of this section walks through each of these pieces.

### 1. Serving with Transformers

Transformers now supports the `DecisionPipeline`, `AutoModelForDecision`, and the `DecisionConfig` classes. These follow the same overall structure of the pipeline and model classes in `transformers` but are tailor made for decision models.

from transformers import pipeline

decide = pipeline("decision", model="autotrust/GEV-26B-Decide") print(decide)

DecisionPipeline: {'model': 'JevForDecision', 'dtype': 'bfloat16', 'device': 'cuda', 'input_modalities': 'text'}


One can also inspect the configuration and the model like so:

from transformers import AutoModelForDecision, DecisionConfig

model_id = "autotrust/GEV-26B-Decide" config = DecisionConfig.from_pretrained(model_id) model = AutoModelForDecision.from_pretrained(model_id)


[Transformers also supports the `/v1/systemone` endpoint](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/serve-cli/serving#v1systemone).

We can start a local server using the serving dependencies:

pip install "transformers[serving]" transformers serve


Using a compatible version of Transformers, we can then send a decision request:

curl http://localhost:8000/v1/systemone \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "model": "autotrust/GEV-26B-Decide", "state": "I was charged twice. Please refund me today.", "questions": { "department": { "type": "choice", "instructions": "Which team should handle this?", "criteria": { "billing": "Payments and refunds", "technical": "Bugs and technical issues", "sales": "Pricing and subscriptions" } }, "urgency": { "type": "score", "instructions": "How urgent is the request?", "criteria": ["low", "medium", "high"] }, "refund": { "type": "noul", "instructions": "Is the customer requesting a refund?" } } }'


The response contains three named answers with the corresponding typed results and probabilities.

{ "model":"autotrust/GEV-26B-Decide", "answers":{ "department":{ "type":"choice", "choice":"billing", "confidence":0.9974000453948975, "probabilities":{ "billing":0.9982666969299316, "technical":0.0010246571619063616, "sales":0.0007087149424478412 } }, "urgency":{ "type":"score", "score":1.7525686174631119, "legend":{"0":"low","1":"medium","2":"high"}, "confidence":0.6288529792800546, "probabilities":{ "0":0.014000383205711842, "1":0.2194305807352066, "2":0.7665690183639526 } }, "refund":{ "type":"noul", "noul":0.9953224062919617 } }, "usage":{"input_tokens":148,"output_tokens":0} }


> An interesting detail is that the above APIs works with compatible autoregressive language models too. Transformers constructs the decision prompts, evaluates the answer label logits in a batched forward pass, and applies softmax without generating response text. This means we can experiment with the decision interface without necessarily training a new model.

### 2. Serving with llama.cpp

[llama.cpp also supports decision models](https://huggingface.co/blog/ggml-org/decision-models-in-llamacpp) using the same `/v1/systemone` API.

For example, we can launch a GGUF decision model from the Hub:

llama serve -hf ggml-org/Kev-4B-GGUF


The default server runs on port 9931.

We can then send a request containing the same state and questions, using `http://localhost:9931/v1/systemone`. With the model selected by the server, we can omit the `model` field from the request.

The useful property is interface compatibility.

curl http://localhost:9931/v1/systemone \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "model": "ggml-org/Kev-4B-GGUF", "state": "I was charged twice. Please refund me today.", "questions": { "department": { "type": "choice", "instructions": "Which team should handle this?", "criteria": { "billing": "Payments and refunds", "technical": "Bugs and technical issues", "sales": "Pricing and subscriptions" } }, "urgency": { "type": "score", "instructions": "How urgent is the request?", "criteria": ["low", "medium", "high"] }, "refund": { "type": "noul", "instructions": "Is the customer requesting a refund?" } } }'


### 3. Discovering models on the Hugging Face Hub

Hugging Face introduced a dedicated [`decision-model` tag](https://huggingface.co/models?other=decision-model&sort=trending) for discovering compatible models. This is useful because decision models do not have to share a single backbone or architecture.

For example, the ecosystem includes models based on encoder architectures such as ModernBERT, as well as models derived from larger generative language-model backbones.

### 4. Training decision models using Hugging Face tooling

Once we understand inference, the next question is whether we can adapt a decision model. Since decision models are integrated in transformers, we can fine-tune them with the `Trainer` API.

Below is a toy example that fine-tunes `JEV-9B` to route support requests. It is intentionally small, but it shows the parts that matter:

- each example is a decision request (a `state` plus `questions`) paired with the gold answer.
- `model.decision_config.prepare_inputs` turns the request into model inputs, the same way it does at inference time.
- the model returns one logit per option, so a `choice` question is trained with a plain cross-entropy loss over the options.

import os; os.environ["CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES"]="2" import torch import torch.nn.functional as F from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForDecision, Trainer, TrainingArguments

checkpoint = "autotrust/JEV-9B" tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(checkpoint) model = AutoModelForDecision.from_pretrained(checkpoint)

examples = [ ("I was charged twice. Please refund me.", "refund"), ("My package has not arrived.", "shipping"), ("The application crashes when I open it.", "technical"), ("I want my money back.", "refund"), ("Where is my delivery?", "shipping"), ("I cannot log into my account.", "technical"), ]

options = { "refund": "Billing issues and refunds", "shipping": "Orders and deliveries", "technical": "Software and account issues", }

def preprocess(text, label): request = { "state": text, "questions": { "category": { "type": "choice", "instructions": "Classify the support request.", "criteria": options, } }, } (inputs, questions), = model.decision_config.prepare_inputs( request, tokenizer ) inputs["marks"] = inputs["marks"].unsqueeze(0) inputs["num_options"] = torch.tensor([[len(questions[0].options)]]) inputs["question_type_ids"] = torch.tensor([[1]]) # choice inputs["labels"] = torch.tensor( [questions[0].options.index(label)] ) return inputs

dataset = [preprocess(text, label) for text, label in examples]

class DecisionTrainer(Trainer): def compute_loss(self, model, inputs, return_outputs=False, kwargs): inputs = inputs.copy() labels = inputs.pop("labels") logits = model(inputs)

logits = logits.unsqueeze(0) # [3] -> [1, 3] loss = F.cross_entropy(logits.float(), labels)

return (loss, logits) if return_outputs else loss

trainer = DecisionTrainer( model=model, args=TrainingArguments( output_dir="./decision-toy", max_steps=30, per_device_train_batch_size=1, learning_rate=1e-3, logging_steps=5, save_strategy="no", report_to="none", remove_unused_columns=False, ), train_dataset=dataset, data_collator=lambda batch: batch[0], )

trainer.train()


First-class support for training decision models is also coming to TRL ([huggingface/trl#8040](https://github.com/huggingface/trl/pull/8040)), so we won't have to write this plumbing by hand. At the time of writing, the PR is still open.

If we want to go further and turn a generative LLM into a decision model, [Unsloth provides a recipe](https://unsloth.ai/docs/basics/train-your-own-decision-model-with-unsloth) that fine-tunes models such as Qwen with LoRA and a decision-scoring head.

## Final thoughts

Decision models are interesting not because classification is new, but because they make **decisions and probabilities first-class outputs for software**.

Traditional classifiers already produce probabilities, and zero-shot classifiers already allow runtime-defined categories. Decision models bring these ideas into a typed interface with multiple question primitives, non-generative scoring, and the possibility of specialized training for reliable, calibrated decisions.

### Community

Upload images, audio, and videos by dragging in the text input, pasting, or clicking here.

Tap or paste here to upload images

· [Sign up](https://huggingface.co/join?next=%2Fblog%2Fdecision) or [log in](https://huggingface.co/login?next=%2Fblog%2Fdecision) to comment

Upvote

item.title: [OpenRouter] Best OCR Model for Scanned Documents, Measured
item.content:encoded:
Best OCR Model for Scanned Documents, Measured

Kenny Rogers ·11/10/2026

Turning scanned documents into reliable text is hard. Classic OCR engines such as Tesseract fail on faded print, handwriting and faxes. Vision models read those pages well, but sometimes write values that aren’t on the page. We made eight test pages from text we wrote, so every character could be checked, and ran them through 15 vision models and Mistral OCR on OpenRouter, plus Tesseract.

The best OCR model in our test was Claude Opus 5.5, with 262 of 264 key values right at $16.42 per 1,000 pages. Mistral OCR was the best value: 258 of 264 for $2.02. This post shows the results, the errors to watch for, and code to catch them.

These results are a starting point. Our eight pages aren’t your documents, so the only real way to know which model is best for your workflow is to test the candidates on your own scans.

Tl;dr

  • Most accurate: anthropic/claude-opus-5.5. Best value: mistral-ocr. Cheapest good result: inclusionai/ling-3.0-flash-vl with reasoning off, 254 of 264 for $0.04 per 1,000 pages.
  • On a faded receipt, GPT-6 Luna and GPT-6.1 Sol made up card digits, wifi passwords and a server name. Error rates don’t show this, so check the values you’ll actually use.
  • Turning reasoning off made four of five models we tested faster and cheaper, with no key values lost.
  • Flagging the words where two cheap models from different labs disagreed caught 34 of 35 wrong words, for $0.62 per 1,000 pages.

How we tested

We rendered each page from known text, then degraded it like a scan: a small rotation, blur, noise and JPEG compression. Five pages are ordinary: a receipt, a letter with two deliberate misspellings, a form with a ticked box, a two-column newsletter and a neat handwritten note. Three are built to be hard: a faded thermal receipt, fast cramped handwriting, and a low-resolution fax of 12 serial numbers made from look-alike characters (0/O, 1/I/L, 5/S, 8/B), so a model can’t guess them from context.

We scored each transcript two ways. The character error rate (CER) is the edit distance to the true text divided by its length, ignoring line breaks and Markdown. The key values are 88 strings a pipeline would use, 10 to 15 per page, such as totals, dates, card digits, serials and the misspelled words. Each has to appear exactly in each of three runs, which gives 264 checks per model. Costs are the billed usage.cost of each request. Models are from the OpenRouter catalog as of October 8, 2026.

Which OCR model is most accurate on scanned documents?

The table is sorted by key values correct.

RouteKey values correctCER, all pagesCER, 3 hard pagesCost per 1,000 pagesMedian seconds
anthropic/claude-opus-5.5262 of 2640.02%0.06%$16.427.2
mistral-ocr (PDF engine)258 of 2640.14%0.26%$2.023.8
anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5256 of 2641.34%3.49%$7.684.2
google/gemini-3.8-flash254 of 2640.15%0.28%$7.509.3
stepfun/step-5-preview254 of 2640.42%1.11%$5.489.3
inclusionai/ling-3.0-flash-vl254 of 2641.05%2.56%$0.127.2
anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5253 of 2641.19%2.89%$0.463.8
x-ai/grok-4.7252 of 2640.13%0.35%$12.8511.3
z-ai/glm-5.3-flashx252 of 2640.33%0.86%$1.455.5
openai/gpt-6.1-sol252 of 2640.65%1.74%$6.038.4
deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash248 of 2640.20%0.48%$0.204.8
qwen/qwen3.8-flash248 of 2640.74%1.49%$0.298.1
qwen/qwen3.8-27b246 of 2640.92%2.31%$1.5410.8
xiaomi/mimo-v2.6-flash246 of 2642.02%5.34%$0.583.1
mistralai/mistral-large-4-0240 of 2644.61%12.19%$6.8047.9
openai/gpt-6-luna232 of 2641.49%3.95%$0.547.8
Tesseract 5.5 (local, 1 run)46 of 8826.06%64.39%$058.1

On the five ordinary pages every vision model scored under 0.3% CER, and all 15 transcribed the neat handwriting perfectly. Most of the spread comes from the faded receipt. Opus 5.5 and Mistral OCR got all 33 checks on it, while GPT-6 Luna got 16. Models count image tokens differently (a median page was 1,070 prompt tokens for DeepSeek and 3,314 for Grok), so measure cost on your own pages.

Which OCR model fits your work

If most of your work isStart withWhy
Hard scans where every value mattersClaude Opus 5.5262 of 264 key values, at $16.42 per 1,000 pages
High volume at a fair priceMistral OCR (the mistral-ocr PDF engine)258 of 264 key values, at $2.02 per 1,000 pages
The lowest costLing 3.0 Flash VL with reasoning off254 of 264 key values, at $0.04 per 1,000 pages
Serial numbers and IDs with look-alike charactersClaude Haiku 5.5 checked by DeepSeek V4.1 FlashThe pair flagged 34 of 35 wrong words, for $0.62 per 1,000 pages
Clean typed pages, offlineTesseract 5.5Perfect on the letter and the newsletter, and free, but it returned nothing for the faded receipt

What goes wrong when a vision model reads a hard scan?

The most serious error was a value that looks plausible but isn’t on the page. Here’s the bottom of the faded receipt as printed, followed by one GPT-6 Luna run:

CONTACTLESS 32.95
CARD ****9026
SERVED BY: PRIYA
WIFI: verdigris-guest / tide2026
NET                                 27.46

CONTACTLESS
CARD **** 9027

SERVED BY: SHEVA
WIFI: verdigris_guest / 1freecoffee

There’s no NET line on the receipt. The card ends in 9026, and the name and password are invented. GPT-6 Luna changed the server’s name and the year in all three runs. GPT-6.1 Sol wrote a different made-up password in each run (flatwhite24, flat9am!, flatleaf). We also asked models to write [?] instead of guessing. It didn’t help: four of seven models never used the marker.

The other errors that repeated:

  • O and 0: Two fax serials were wrong in at least one run from 13 of the 15 models. Only Claude Sonnet 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol read them correctly every time.
  • Spelling fixes: The letter is signed “Senior Assosiate”, and the prompt says to copy spelling exactly. 16 of 45 transcripts “corrected” it anyway.
  • Ticked boxes: Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Haiku 5.5 copied the form’s checkbox labels but dropped which box was ticked.

Step 1: Send the scan to a vision model

A vision model generates its transcript the same way a language model generates any text, so it tends to write what text usually says rather than exactly what’s printed. The prompt asks it to copy exactly. That reduces the problem but doesn’t remove it: 16 of 45 transcripts still corrected the letter’s deliberate misspelling. You need an OpenRouter API key in OPENROUTER_API_KEY. The image goes in as a base64 image_url part (see image inputs), so every vision model on OpenRouter takes this same request. Save it as transcribe.py, since steps 3 and 4 import from it:

import base64
import mimetypes
import os

import requests

API = "https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/chat/completions"
HEADERS = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['OPENROUTER_API_KEY']}"}
PROMPT = ("Transcribe all of the text in this scanned document, in reading order. "
          "Copy spelling, numbers and punctuation exactly as they appear, even if they "
          "look wrong. Return plain text only, with no Markdown and no commentary.")


def transcribe(path, model="deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash", reasoning={"effort": "none"}):
    mime = mimetypes.guess_type(path)[0] or "image/jpeg"
    with open(path, "rb") as f:
        image = f"data:{mime};base64," + base64.b64encode(f.read()).decode()
    body = {
        "model": model,
        "max_tokens": 16000,
        "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": [
            {"type": "text", "text": PROMPT},
            {"type": "image_url", "image_url": {"url": image}},
        ]}],
    }
    if reasoning:
        body["reasoning"] = reasoning
    response = requests.post(API, headers=HEADERS, json=body, timeout=300)
    response.raise_for_status()
    data = response.json()
    choice = data["choices"][0]
    if choice["finish_reason"] != "stop":
        raise ValueError(f"finish_reason={choice['finish_reason']}: the transcript is incomplete")
    return choice["message"]["content"], data["usage"]["cost"]


if __name__ == "__main__":
    text, cost = transcribe("receipt.jpg")
    print(text)
    print(f"\n${cost:.5f}")
HARBOR LANE MARKET
1180 Harbor Lane, Unit 4
Portland OR 97209
Tel (503) 555-0148
...
TOTAL 62.86
VISA ****4471 62.86
AUTH 08813C
...

$0.00022

Every character came back right, for about two hundredths of a cent. The data URL takes its type from the file extension, so PNG and WebP scans work too. To compare models, change only the model string, and pass reasoning=None for the models in step 2 that can’t turn reasoning off.

The finish_reason check is there because reasoning tokens count against max_tokens. With a limit of 4,000, Gemini 3.8 Flash spent 3,841 tokens reasoning about the fax on every run and stopped partway through serial number 4. The request still returned 200 OK with finish_reason: "length", so without the check a pipeline stores short transcripts without noticing.

Step 2: Turn reasoning off for transcription

Reasoning helps when a model has to plan an answer. Copying text from a page doesn’t need a plan, so the extra tokens mostly add cost and time. That’s why transcribe sends "reasoning": {"effort": "none"} by default (see reasoning tokens). We reran the full test with reasoning off for every model that allows it:

ModelKey values, on → offCER, on → offCost per 1,000 pages, on → offMedian seconds, on → off
mistralai/mistral-large-4-0240 → 2494.61% → 0.15%$6.80 → $1.6847.9 → 5.6
inclusionai/ling-3.0-flash-vl254 → 2541.05% → 0.19%$0.12 → $0.047.2 → 4.0
openai/gpt-6-luna232 → 2321.49% → 1.08%$0.54 → $0.227.8 → 3.8
deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash248 → 2490.20% → 0.23%$0.20 → $0.164.8 → 4.5
qwen/qwen3.8-27b246 → 2440.92% → 2.28%$1.54 → $0.7710.8 → 8.9

With reasoning on, one Mistral Large 4 request reasoned for 626 seconds and returned no text (finish_reason: "error"). Qwen3.8 27B did better with reasoning on, so test your own pages. Gemini 3.8 Flash, Grok 4.7 and GLM 5.3 FlashX don’t allow reasoning to be turned off, so pass reasoning=None to leave the field out. Otherwise the request fails with:

400 {"error":{"message":"Reasoning is mandatory for this endpoint and cannot be disabled.","code":400,"metadata":{"provider_name":null}}}

Step 3: Cross-check two models from different labs

Look-alike characters such as O and 0 are hard to tell apart in a blurry image. Each model decides based on its own training, so two models from different labs rarely make the same wrong choice. Where their transcripts differ is usually where the image is unclear. We tested every pair among six models. The best was Claude Haiku 5.5 checked by DeepSeek V4.1 Flash. Haiku made 35 word errors in 2,964 words, and DeepSeek, with reasoning off as in step 2, disagreed on 34 of them, with 10 false alarms. The pair costs $0.62 per 1,000 pages, a third of Mistral OCR. Both use the same API, so the check is one extra call. Haiku is called with reasoning=None because that’s how it ran in our table:

import difflib

from transcribe import transcribe  # the function from step 1

a, _ = transcribe("fax.jpg", model="anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5", reasoning=None)
b, _ = transcribe("fax.jpg", model="deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash")
a, b = a.split(), b.split()
for tag, i1, i2, j1, j2 in difflib.SequenceMatcher(None, a, b, autojunk=False).get_opcodes():
    if tag != "equal":
        print("check:", " ".join(a[i1:i2]), "vs", " ".join(b[j1:j2]))
check: 8LI5-QS0B5O vs 8LI5-QS0B50
check: 30HY-1OHLG7 vs 30HY-10HLG7

Those are the two serials most models got wrong. If both models misread a character the same way, nothing is flagged. That happened once in our runs, with an O both read as a zero, so validate IDs against a list or a checksum where you can. The comparison also assumes both models read the page in the same order. In one of three runs the models listed the fax’s two columns in different orders, and every serial showed up as a disagreement.

Step 4: Use Mistral OCR as a dedicated engine

Mistral OCR is a model trained only for document OCR. On OpenRouter it runs as an engine in the file-parser plugin, which accepts PDFs, at $2 per 1,000 pages. The plugin OCRs the file before your model sees it. It returns the text as a file annotation on the response, so the model you name only has to reply. Wrap the scan in a one-page PDF and send it with any cheap model:

import base64
import html
import io
import os

import requests
from PIL import Image, ImageSequence

from transcribe import API, HEADERS  # from step 1


def mistral_ocr(path):
    if path.lower().endswith(".pdf"):  # scanned PDFs go as they are
        with open(path, "rb") as f:
            raw = f.read()
    else:  # wrap an image in a PDF in memory, one page per frame of a multipage TIFF
        pages = [p.convert("RGB") for p in ImageSequence.Iterator(Image.open(path))]
        buf = io.BytesIO()
        pages[0].save(buf, "PDF", save_all=True, append_images=pages[1:])
        raw = buf.getvalue()
    pdf = "data:application/pdf;base64," + base64.b64encode(raw).decode()
    pdf_name = os.path.splitext(os.path.basename(path))[0] + ".pdf"
    body = {
        "model": "upstage/solar-mini4",  # any cheap text model; it only has to reply
        "max_tokens": 5,
        "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": [
            {"type": "text", "text": "Reply OK."},
            {"type": "file", "file": {"filename": pdf_name, "file_data": pdf}},
        ]}],
        "plugins": [{"id": "file-parser", "pdf": {"engine": "mistral-ocr"}}],
    }
    response = requests.post(API, headers=HEADERS, json=body, timeout=300)
    response.raise_for_status()
    data = response.json()
    parts = data["choices"][0]["message"]["annotations"][0]["file"]["content"]
    texts = [p["text"] for p in parts if p.get("type") == "text"]  # skip extracted image parts
    text = "\n".join(t for t in texts if not t.startswith(("<file", "</file")))
    return html.unescape(text), data["usage"]["cost"]


text, cost = mistral_ocr("receipt_faded.jpg")
print(text)
print(f"\n${cost:.5f}")
CAFE VERDIGRIS
22 Quayside Row
Bristol BS1 4QA
VAT No. GB 318 7742 09

27/09/2026 08:17 TILL 2 CHK 0193
...
|  CONTACTLESS | 32.95  |
|  CARD ***9026 |   |

SERVED BY: PRIYA
WIFI: verdigris-guest / tide2026

$0.00202

Every value on the faded receipt came back right, including the card digits and password. Mistral OCR is built to keep layout, so its output is Markdown: receipt lines become tables, headings get ##, and & comes back as &. That’s why the function unescapes the HTML entities. Strip the Markdown if you need plain text, or keep it if an LLM reads the result next.

Is an LLM better than Tesseract for OCR?

Yes, except on clean typed pages. Tesseract 5.5 reads character shapes line by line, so it holds up on crisp print and breaks down on noise and handwriting. It transcribed the letter and the newsletter perfectly. It returned nothing for the faded receipt, 1 of 11 values on the messy handwriting and 4 of 15 on the fax.

Frequently asked questions

Which LLM is best for OCR?

Claude Opus 5.5 in our test. Gemini 3.8 Flash and Grok 4.7 had error rates almost as low but missed more serials. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and Ling 3.0 Flash VL came close for under $0.20 per 1,000 pages.

How do I OCR a scanned PDF?

Send it with the mistral-ocr engine as in step 4. Alternatively, render each page to an image for a vision model, or send the PDF directly to a model that reads PDFs. A free text parser won’t work on a scan, because a scan has no text layer.

What is the most accurate OCR model?

Claude Opus 5.5 got 262 of 264 key values right and had a 0.02% character error rate across our eight scans. Mistral OCR was second with 258 of 264, at an eighth of the cost.

How much does OCR with an LLM cost?

In our test it ran from $0.04 per 1,000 pages (Ling 3.0 Flash VL with reasoning off) to $16.42 (Claude Opus 5.5). Mistral OCR costs $2 per 1,000 pages. Models count image tokens differently, so measure cost on your own pages.

Is Mistral OCR better than a vision model?

It was the best value in our test: 258 of 264 key values for $2.02 per 1,000 pages, behind only Claude Opus 5.5. It returns Markdown that keeps the layout, while a vision model returns whatever format you ask for.

Can an LLM read handwriting?

Yes. All 15 vision models transcribed our neat note perfectly. On messy handwriting most stayed above 99% character accuracy, and the misses were mostly names (“Ackterberg” for “Achterberg”).

Next steps

  • Image inputs covers sending images by URL or base64, and our vision API guide covers detail levels.
  • PDF inputs lists the PDF engines and explains how to reuse parsed results.
  • The vision models collection lists every model that takes images.
  • To turn a transcript into typed fields, see structured outputs.

item.title: [OpenRouter] How to Build a Voice AI Agent
item.content:encoded:
How to Build a Voice AI Agent

OpenRouter ·11/10/2026

A voice agent needs to do more than generate a good answer. It must understand what someone said, decide what to do, call any needed tools, and start speaking again before the pause gets awkward.

In this tutorial, we’ll build that full loop in Python. Our example is a restaurant booking agent that transcribes a caller, checks table availability with tools, and turns the response back into speech. Speech-to-text, the LLM, and text-to-speech all run through one OpenRouter API key, and we stream each completed sentence to TTS instead of waiting for the entire reply.

Across all 12 turns in three test conversations, the overall median server-side time to first audio was 1.9 seconds, while a four-turn conversation cost about $0.013 per minute of processed speech at the promotional prices available during our October 8 test.

TL;DR

  • Text-to-speech accounted for roughly 90% of the measured model cost, making spoken response length an important cost factor for this agent.
  • Server-side time to first audio was an estimated 1.4 seconds for plain turns and 2.4 seconds for tool turns in our test, counting one LLM request per turn. The example code makes extra LLM requests, and network and playback add time.
  • Names were harder to transcribe than phone numbers. Have callers confirm important details before taking action.
  • Sending completed sentences to text-to-speech (TTS) can reduce the wait for spoken output, but real-time playback and interruptions need additional orchestration.

How a voice AI agent turn works

A voice agent takes a caller’s speech, converts it into text, passes it to an LLM to decide what to do, and turns the response back into speech. Here’s how the process works:

For example, when someone calls our restaurant to book a table, the LLM may need to call check_availability before responding. Your application executes the function, sends the available times back to the model, and waits for it to generate a response. This extra round trip adds to the caller’s wait time.

To reduce that wait, we can start generating speech before the LLM finishes its entire response. Instead of waiting for the full text, we’ll stream the response, split it into sentences, and send each completed sentence to TTS while the model continues generating the rest.

For this build, we’ll use our speech-to-text API to transcribe the caller, Chat Completions with tool calling to handle the conversation and bookings, and our text-to-speech API to generate the spoken response.

The transcription API returns text as JSON, while the speech API returns audio bytes. Our Python example will save the generated audio as WAV files, and later we’ll use LiveKit to handle live audio and interruptions.

Build the voice agent in Python

Let’s build the restaurant booking agent using three models: elevenlabs/scribe-v2 for transcription, openai/gpt-6-luna for the conversation and tool calls, and elevenlabs/eleven-flash-v2.5 for speech generation.

You’ll need Python 3.10 or later and an OpenRouter API key. Install the requests library and set your API key as an environment variable:

python -m pip install requests
export OPENROUTER_API_KEY="your-api-key"

To make the example easy to reproduce, we’ll use a second TTS voice to simulate four caller turns rather than connecting a microphone. We’ll also use mock booking data so the agent can check availability and return reservation details without a real booking system.

Save the following code as voice_agent.py:

import base64
import io
import json
import os
import re
import wave
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
from datetime import date

import requests

API = "https://openrouter.ai/api/v1"
AUTH = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['OPENROUTER_API_KEY']}"}

STT = "elevenlabs/scribe-v2"
LLM = "openai/gpt-6-luna"
TTS = "elevenlabs/eleven-flash-v2.5"
PCM_RATE = 24000

def system_prompt():
    today = date.today()  # read per call, so a long-running agent stays on the right day
    return (
        "You are the phone receptionist for Luigi's restaurant. "
        f"Today is {today:%A, %B} {today.day}, {today.year}. Keep answers short and spoken: "
        "no markdown, and say times in words. Check availability before "
        "offering a table. Only book after the caller agrees and provides a name. "
        "Do not claim to send confirmation texts."
    )

def tool(name, description, properties):
    return {
        "type": "function",
        "function": {
            "name": name,
            "description": description,
            "parameters": {
                "type": "object",
                "properties": properties,
                "required": list(properties),
            },
        },
    }

DATE = {"type": "string", "description": "YYYY-MM-DD"}
TIME = {"type": "string", "description": "HH:MM, 24-hour"}
PARTY = {"type": "integer", "minimum": 1}

TOOLS = [
    tool(
        "check_availability",
        "Find open tables near the requested time",
        {"date": DATE, "time": TIME, "party_size": PARTY},
    ),
    tool(
        "book_table",
        "Book only after the caller accepts a time and gives a name",
        {
            "date": DATE,
            "time": TIME,
            "party_size": PARTY,
            "name": {"type": "string"},
        },
    ),
]

def run_tool(name, args):
    # Mock booking service; replace with a real reservation backend.
    if name == "check_availability":
        return {
            "open_times": (
                ["17:45", "20:15"]
                if args["party_size"] >= 5
                else [args["time"]]
            )
        }

    if name == "book_table":
        allowed = (
            ["17:45", "20:15"]
            if args["party_size"] >= 5
            else [args["time"]]
        )
        return (
            {"booked": True, "reference": "XJ47Q"}
            if args["time"] in allowed
            else {"booked": False, "error": "Time unavailable"}
        )

    return {"error": f"Unknown tool: {name}"}

def to_wav(pcm, rate):
    if len(pcm) % 2:
        raise ValueError("PCM audio must contain whole 16-bit samples")
    output = io.BytesIO()
    with wave.open(output, "wb") as wav:
        wav.setnchannels(1)
        wav.setsampwidth(2)
        wav.setframerate(rate)
        wav.writeframes(pcm)
    return output.getvalue()

def speak(text, voice="sarah"):
    if not text.strip():
        return b"", PCM_RATE

    with requests.post(
        f"{API}/audio/speech",
        headers=AUTH,
        stream=True,
        timeout=60,
        json={
            "model": TTS,
            "input": text,
            "voice": voice,
            "response_format": "pcm",
            "provider": {
                "options": {
                    "elevenlabs": {"output_format": "pcm_24000"}
                }
            },
        },
    ) as response:
        response.raise_for_status()
        if not response.headers.get("Content-Type", "").startswith("audio/pcm"):
            raise ValueError("Expected raw PCM audio from TTS")
        pcm = b"".join(response.iter_content(4096))
        if not pcm:
            raise ValueError("TTS returned no audio")
        return pcm, PCM_RATE

def transcribe(wav):
    response = requests.post(
        f"{API}/audio/transcriptions",
        headers=AUTH,
        timeout=60,
        json={
            "model": STT,
            "language": "en",
            "input_audio": {
                "data": base64.b64encode(wav).decode("ascii"),
                "format": "wav",
            },
        },
    )
    response.raise_for_status()
    return response.json()["text"].strip()

def choose_tool_calls(messages):
    # Resolve possible tools before starting any paid TTS requests.
    response = requests.post(
        f"{API}/chat/completions",
        headers=AUTH,
        timeout=60,
        json={
            "model": LLM,
            "messages": messages,
            "tools": TOOLS,
            "tool_choice": "auto",
            "reasoning": {"effort": "none"},
            "max_tokens": 300,
        },
    )
    response.raise_for_status()
    message = response.json()["choices"][0]["message"]
    return message.get("tool_calls") or []

def stream_reply(messages):
    # This request has no tools, so sentences can safely go to TTS.
    pending, finish = "", None
    with requests.post(
        f"{API}/chat/completions",
        headers=AUTH,
        stream=True,
        timeout=60,
        json={
            "model": LLM,
            "messages": messages,
            "reasoning": {"effort": "none"},
            "max_tokens": 300,
            "stream": True,
        },
    ) as response:
        response.raise_for_status()
        response.encoding = "utf-8"

        for line in response.iter_lines(decode_unicode=True):
            if not line or not line.startswith("data: {"):
                continue

            chunk = json.loads(line[6:])
            if chunk.get("error"):  # a provider error mid-stream, after some text may have arrived
                raise RuntimeError(f"stream error: {chunk['error']}")
            choices = chunk.get("choices")
            if not choices:
                continue

            finish = choices[0].get("finish_reason") or finish
            pending += (choices[0].get("delta") or {}).get("content") or ""
            # Wait for whitespace; a buffer ending in "3." may still become "3.14".
            while match := re.search(r"[.!?]\s", pending):
                sentence = pending[:match.end()].strip()
                if sentence:
                    yield sentence
                pending = pending[match.end():]

    if finish == "length":  # hit max_tokens, so don't speak the clipped tail or save the reply as a full answer
        raise RuntimeError("reply cut off at max_tokens")
    if pending.strip():
        yield pending.strip()

def run_turn(caller_wav, messages):
    heard = transcribe(caller_wav)
    messages.append({"role": "user", "content": heard})

    # Tool selection can repeat when the model needs several tool results.
    for _ in range(4):
        calls = choose_tool_calls(messages)
        if not calls:
            break

        messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": None, "tool_calls": calls})
        for call in calls:
            try:
                args = json.loads(call["function"]["arguments"])
                result = run_tool(call["function"]["name"], args)
            except (ValueError, TypeError, KeyError) as exc:
                result = {"error": str(exc)}
            messages.append({
                "role": "tool",
                "tool_call_id": call["id"],
                "content": json.dumps(result),
            })
    else:
        raise RuntimeError("Too many tool calls")

    sentences, jobs = [], []
    with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=3) as pool:
        for sentence in stream_reply(messages):
            sentences.append(sentence)
            jobs.append(pool.submit(speak, sentence))
        audio = [job.result() for job in jobs]

    if not sentences:
        raise RuntimeError("LLM returned no spoken response")

    rates = {rate for _, rate in audio}
    if rates != {PCM_RATE}:
        raise ValueError("Inconsistent TTS sample rates")

    spoken = " ".join(sentences)
    messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": spoken})
    pcm = b"".join(chunk for chunk, _ in audio)
    return heard, spoken, to_wav(pcm, PCM_RATE)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    caller_lines = [
        "Hi, do you have a table for six this Saturday at seven thirty?",
        "Eight fifteen works. The name is Siobhan Okafor.",
        "Can you text the confirmation to four one five, "
        "five five five, zero one eight two?",
        "No, that's everything. Thanks, bye.",
    ]

    messages = [{"role": "system", "content": system_prompt()}]
    for turn, line in enumerate(caller_lines, 1):
        pcm, rate = speak(line, voice="george")
        heard, said, reply = run_turn(to_wav(pcm, rate), messages)
        with open(f"agent_{turn}.wav", "wb") as file:
            file.write(reply)
        print(f"caller: {heard}\nagent:  {said}\n")

The script connects the three APIs through run_turn(), which transcribes each caller message, passes the transcript to the LLM, and processes the response. If the LLM requests a tool, the function executes it, adds the result to the conversation history, and makes another request so the model can continue.

Look at how stream_reply() handles tool calls. The model streams function names and arguments in fragments, so we assemble them before executing the tool. For spoken replies, we send completed sentences to TTS through a thread pool, allowing speech generation to overlap with the remaining LLM output.

We then combine the audio in sentence order and save it as a WAV file. We’ll handle actual playback and interruptions when we introduce LiveKit.

You can run the script with this command:

python voice_agent.py

It should create four audio files, agent_1.wav through agent_4.wav, and print the conversation. Here’s an excerpt from one of our test runs. The caller lines show the transcribed audio, so the numbers may differ from how they were spoken.

caller: Hi, do you have a table for six this Saturday at 7:30?

agent:  We don't have seven-thirty available for six,
        but I can offer five forty-five or eight fifteen.
        Would either work for you?

caller: 815 works. The name is Siobhan Okafor

agent:  You're booked for six at eight fifteen this
        Saturday under Siobhan Okafor.
        Your reference is XJ47Q.

caller: Can you text the confirmation to 415-555-0182?

agent:  I can't send texts from here, but your
        reservation is confirmed under Siobhan Okafor
        for six at eight fifteen this Saturday,
        reference XJ47Q.

The example shows the agent checking availability before offering another time, then calling book_table after the caller accepts. It also refuses to promise a text confirmation because we haven’t provided a tool for sending one.

Why this design works, and what breaks it

A response can look perfectly fine in a chat window but sound strange when read aloud. Times, phone numbers, and markdown are good examples. That’s why our system prompt asks the LLM to keep responses short, avoid formatting, and write times as spoken words, such as “eight fifteen” instead of 8:15.

The same issue can happen in reverse. In our test, speech-to-text converted “eight fifteen” into 815, but the LLM correctly understood the caller’s response because it had the earlier conversation for context. We maintain that history in messages and send it with each request, since Chat Completions doesn’t automatically retain previous turns. As a result, the prompt grew from approximately 290 tokens on the first turn to 490 on the fourth.

Another important consideration is making sure the agent only confirms actions that have actually happened. In an earlier version without book_table, the agent could tell callers their reservation was confirmed even though the application hadn’t created one.

This is why the booking tool needs to do more than return a response. When connected to a real reservation system, it should verify availability, save the booking, and return a confirmation only when the operation succeeds.

How fast is a voice AI agent?
