For details on evaluation methodology, see the Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 System Card. Scores for Fable 5.2, Fable 5.1, and Opus 5.5 show results with safeguards on unless otherwise noted. All scores show each model’s highest-available effort unless otherwise noted. † On CyScenarioBench, each lab’s scores are based on unique tasks. ‡ RoboDojo Sim shows the highest-available effort and was run internally.

Effort and efficiency. On Medium effort (the default in Claude apps and Claude Code), Fable 5.2 can accomplish challenging tasks with fewer tokens than Fable 5.1. In early testing on the FrontierCode 2.0 evaluation, Fable 5.2 at High effort scored about level with Opus 5.5 at Max effort, for roughly half the cost per task. At Xhigh effort, it also scored the highest of any released model tested.

Agentic coding: FrontierCode 2.0Agentic search: WANDRHardware engineering: BenchCAD 2.1Multidisciplinary reasoning: Humanity’s Last ExamVisual chart recognition: Chartography

FrontierCode 2.0Accuracy vs. cost

FrontierCode measures whether a model’s code changes would be merged by the maintainers of open-source repositories. At High effort, Fable 5.2 scores about the same as Opus 5.5’s best score (45.3% vs. 45.5%) for roughly half the cost per task, and ahead of GPT-6 Astra’s best score (42.8%) at about the same cost. At Xhigh effort, Fable 5.2 reaches 49.1%, the highest score of any released model we’ve tested.

WANDR (relaxed score)Accuracy vs. cost

Perplexity’s WANDR benchmark measures agents on large data-collection tasks. At Medium effort, Fable 5.2 matches Opus 5.5’s top score for about 40% of the cost per task.

BenchCAD 2.1 (with tools)Accuracy vs. cost

BenchCAD 2.1 measures hardware engineering, specifically how closely a model’s designs match reference geometry and circuits, and is scored 0–100 with partial credit. At Max effort, Fable 5.2 scores 83.5, ahead of Opus 5.5 (65.3) and Fable 5.1 (44.4).

Humanity’s Last Exam (with tools)Accuracy vs. cost

Humanity’s Last Exam (HLE) is a test of expert-level academic knowledge and reasoning. At Low effort, Fable 5.2 matches Opus 5.5’s top score for less than one-tenth of the cost per task.

Chartography (no tools)Accuracy vs. cost

Chartography tests how accurately a model can read charts and figures. At Medium effort, Fable 5.2 scores 66.4%, ahead of Opus 5.5 at Max effort (64.4%) for less than one-tenth of the cost per task.

Coding

Over 90% of the changes merged into Anthropic’s core codebase are now written by Claude (with human guidance). We’ve used Fable 5.2 to fix stubborn bugs in minutes, optimize performance across all of our services, and complete high-value software projects that would otherwise have been too slow or too costly to attempt. A team of agents running an earlier version of Fable 5.2 migrated a critical production service from Python to Rust—the service is now more efficient, more reliable, and starts about 26 times faster. We’ve found that Fable 5.2 exercises strong engineering judgment and can produce high-quality results from even ambiguous requests.

As an experiment, one Anthropic engineer gave Fable 5.2 the task of designing a prototype operating system. Starting from an empty folder, the model coordinated over 1,000 subagents, working around the clock for eight days writing, testing, and reviewing code. It produced a working operating system that boots on a laptop, with its own core that runs the machine, drivers for the disk, keyboard, and network, permanent file storage, windows, a login screen, an installer, and built-in Claude functionality (see the video below).

Early testers have been impressed at how successfully Fable 5.2’s coding skills can be applied to a wide range of tasks:

VercelShopifyDatadogUnityUberOracleiGentSnowflakeCognition

Quote

“The model is in my head. It understands the intent behind every prompt I’ve given it. I haven’t had to say ‘No, I meant…’ a single time. Projects we’ve been pushing along with other models for weeks got finished and approved by our teammates in a few days with Claude Fable 5.2, and the humans reviewing its code had less to say.”

CompanyVercel

AuthorJoe Haddad, Member of Technical Staff

Quote

“Claude Fable 5.2 is great for taking a loose idea and refining it. Its answers are really well-considered, and within a few turns I can almost always say ‘ok, go do that,’ and trust that it’ll complete it with little intervention. It feels like working with another staff-level engineer.”

CompanyShopify

AuthorTom Pritchard, Staff Engineer

Quote

“You can just throw Claude Fable 5.2 at new, ambiguous systems it has never seen before, and it will figure out how to actually work within them. It’s almost like an incident commander that can send out faster models to get quick signals and coordinate, which removes that burden from me as an operator.”

CompanyDatadog

AuthorMatt Lee, Senior Staff Engineer

Quote

“Claude Fable 5.2 can complete tasks that previous models struggled with. The clearest examples so far are building higher-quality 3D scenes from scratch and rebuilding an experience from a visual reference. It’s very strong on the harder game-dev tasks, where it keeps iterating and improving instead of getting stuck.”

CompanyUnity

AuthorSam Zhang, Creative Technologist

Quote

“I had Claude Fable 5.2 run a 10–12 hour security audit. It sent out about 170 reviewer agents and came back with a write-up, fix pull requests and a policy proposal. It works until the job is actually complete instead of stopping at a plausible checkpoint. Its self-correction and honesty about gaps impressed me. At High effort, I’d use this over what I run today for long unattended audits and doc-heavy work.”

CompanyUber

AuthorAndrew Mager, Staff Engineer, Agentic Systems

Quote

“In one test combining country debt summaries, repayment history, and regional benchmarks, Claude Fable 5.2 generated SQL that returned the expected results. The SQL generated by two other models also ran successfully, but incorrectly summed country-level summary amounts, producing values 5–8x the expected amounts. Getting these business calculations right is why we see value in using Fable 5.2 for enterprise SQL generation.”

CompanyOracle

AuthorLiyu Gong, Senior Manager of Machine Learning

Quote

“In a single session, Claude Fable 5.2 built a hypervisor, the software that walls off virtual computers sharing one machine. Its core is mathematically proven to keep them apart. More than 3,500 machine-checked proofs cover every case, not just the ones you test. It’s the first model I’ve seen break a problem this large into pieces it can prove, fit them together, and keep taking on more ambitious work. A very clear upgrade from Fable 5.1.”

CompanyiGent

AuthorSean Ward, Co-Founder and CEO

Quote

“Claude Fable 5.2 is the strongest model we have measured on data-eng-bench, our open-source benchmark of 103 data-engineering tasks. It solved tasks consistently across repeated runs and passed every interactive coding task we gave it.”

CompanySnowflake

AuthorBala Kasiviswanathan, VP of AI and Developer Experience

Quote

“Claude Fable 5.2 says it doesn’t know things instead of hallucinating. At one point it told me its last estimate was wrong and that it wouldn’t give a number until it had measured the change. Very impressive!”

CompanyCognition

AuthorAdhyyan Sekhsaria, Member of Technical Staff

Cybersecurity

Claude Mythos 5.2 is our most capable model for cybersecurity engineering. It catches more vulnerabilities than our previous models, and is better at reproducing and fixing them (note that Claude Fable 5.2’s safeguards will block most cybersecurity-related tasks). A security company found that one in six confirmed bugs found by Claude Mythos 5.2 were missed by all of the other frontier models they tested. On our internal evaluation, CVE Rediscovery,¹ Claude Mythos 5.2 found 10.2% more vulnerabilities than Claude Opus 5.5 and 14.4% more than Claude Mythos 5.1. Claude Mythos 5.2 also shows better judgment and calibration—one tester found that previous models had overstated the seriousness of about 1 in 20 findings, whereas Claude Mythos 5.2 hadn’t overstated any.²

CVE RediscoveryAccuracy vs. cost

CVE Rediscovery is an internal cybersecurity evaluation that assesses how many published CVEs (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) a model can independently find when given a snapshot of the project before a CVE was fixed. Our October 2026 run against 1,829 CVEs showed Claude Mythos 5.2 outperformed Claude Mythos 5.1 and Claude Opus 5.5 at every effort level.

Claude Mythos 5.2’s cyber capabilities are accessible through our Cyber Verification Program, which we’re continuing to expand and improve. Claude Enterprise customers (even if they aren’t members of the Cyber Verification Program) can access Claude Security, which scans codebases for vulnerabilities using our most capable models—which now includes Claude Mythos 5.2. A recent update to Claude Security helps it watch repositories as code is updated, track any findings to ensure they’re fixed, learn from additional context, and connect to a user’s tools through an API and MCP.

RubrikMozilla

Quote

“We have worked closely with Anthropic’s new model, Claude Mythos 5.2, to do a next round of high-fidelity threat discovery and elimination within our own systems for potential issues we did not uncover with earlier Mythos models. The output is more readable and empowered our team to spot-check faster and more easily. We built our Code Guardian harness with Mythos 5.1, and we’d switch to Mythos 5.2 to give our customers more powerful cyber capabilities.”

CompanyRubrik

AuthorArvind Nithrakashyap, Co-Founder and Chief Technology Officer

Quote

“Claude Mythos 5.2 is astonishingly good. We’ve worked closely with the Anthropic team all year to harden Firefox with successive generations of Claude models, and each round has left fewer, subtler bugs to find. Even so, Mythos 5.2 roughly doubled the vulnerability discovery metrics of Mythos 5.1 across respective scanning campaigns.”

CompanyMozilla

AuthorBrian Grinstead, Distinguished Engineer

Science and engineering

Important tasks in science, engineering, and mathematics increasingly depend on coding: analyzing data, modeling molecules, designing parts, and controlling instruments are all done through software. Below, we discuss how Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 have helped researchers make progress on difficult problems in these areas.

Theoretical physics

Claude Fable 5.2 solved two open problems in theoretical physics. Both concern black holes, and the effort to unite the two linchpin theories of modern physics, relativity, and quantum mechanics.

Both of Claude’s results rely on holographic duality, the idea that certain universes containing gravity can be precisely described by a quantum theory containing no gravity at all. In the first problem, physicists in 1983 had shown that as these universes heat up, black holes form abruptly, like water boiling; but their method worked only in large universes that were big enough for relativity to apply. A calculation to determine whether the same was true in very small universes, where only the quantum description can be used, was laid out in 2003 but was too laborious to complete. Fable 5.2, working largely autonomously, completed it and found the transition is abrupt there, too. In the second problem, Fable 5.2 found the exact limit of a technique physicists have used for more than 15 years to rule out candidate theories of quantum gravity in a simplified universe. Read more about these results in their respective preprints, here and here.

Protein folding

Adeno-associated viruses are small, harmless viruses whose protein shell, the capsid, can be used to deliver gene therapies. The protein structure of the capsid is important—for example, it affects whether the therapy will be blocked by a patient’s immune system—but it’s also highly complex. Existing protein-folding models like AlphaFold can predict individual proteins, but a capsid is built from dozens of them. Building on two open-source protein-folding models, Claude Mythos 5.2 found a novel way to accurately predict a whole capsid’s structure. It wrote code that ran these models on overlapping groups of protein chains, and used the information on the known symmetries of the capsid to merge them together.

Claude’s method worked across several capsids, both natural and engineered (in our tests, it accurately modeled 28 of the 34 it attempted).³ Three computational biologists shared the following reflections on how Claude’s skills could be used to speed up their research into gene therapies:

Dyno TherapeuticsColumbia UniversityBiohub

Quote

“This acceleration could save meaningful time and cost from our capsid folding pipeline, enabling us to deploy compute more efficiently across many capsid properties that are needed for a genetic medicine. We are excited to help Anthropic push the reasoning capabilities further to reduce the cost of designing capsids overall.”

CompanyDyno Therapeutics

AuthorSam Sinai, Cofounder and Head of AI

Quote

“Large protein assemblies, including capsids, remain an open problem for protein modeling, due to the complexity of accurately predicting and positioning the structures of dozens of individual macromolecules, not to mention the inordinately high computational costs involved. Claude’s approach cleverly tackles this problem for symmetric assemblies, making it possible for individual scientists to model systems on personal workstations that would otherwise require dedicated clusters.”

CompanyColumbia University

AuthorMohammed AlQuraishi, Assistant Professor of Systems Biology and Computer Science

Quote

“Biohub’s goal in open-sourcing ESMFold2 was to enable the scientific community to build on the biology it has learned. We are excited to see Claude prototype a new sampling procedure that enables predictions of large, symmetric complexes such as AAV capsids—a protein used to deliver gene therapies. We will continue to incorporate such contributions from the community that extend our tools to important application domains.”

CompanyBiohub

AuthorZeming Lin, Principal Research Scientist

Mathematics

Mathematical formalization. Formalization is the process of translating a mathematical proof into a language that a computer can check step by step. It can help human mathematicians gain confidence in results without having to check them by hand (this matters even more when AI models generate results that are hard for humans to verify). Because formalization is such a laborious process, if AI could assist with it, mathematicians could spend more time exploring novel ideas.

Our first formalization of Fermat’s Last Theorem, performed by an unreleased research version of Claude, took 11 days. It relied on a purpose-built harness along with guidance from a human researcher. By contrast, a team of 1,000 Fable 5.2 agents fully formalized the theorem in just 30 hours, with minimal human intervention. Fable 5.2 started from minimal prompts, built its own ways to coordinate, and used no mathematical references, only a list of intermediate theorem statements to score progress. It needed one-third as many action tokens as our first formalization and produced a proof seven times shorter. As can be seen in the figure below, Opus 5.5 (with the same 1,000-agent setup) completed only 26% of the formalization in 18 hours, and barely made any more progress after 30.

Read more about the formalization here.

Fermat’s Last Theorem proof formalizationCompletion over time

Formalizing the proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem in the mathematical programming language Lean. Each line shows the proportion of the full formalization that Fable 5.2 (green line) and Opus 5.5 (orange line) had completed over 30 hours with about 1,000 agents, and a single run per model. At the dashed line (18 hours), both teams resumed from their last save with 12 more hours.

Hardware and robotics

Many of AI’s potential benefits—for example, in speeding up laboratory research—depend on it being able to act in the physical world. Claude Fable 5.2 continues our models’ trend of increasing usefulness in the real world, showing promising results on tasks such as designing hardware devices and substantial advances in controlling physical robots.

Hardware engineering. We tested Fable 5.2’s skills in hardware engineering, asking it in a one-paragraph prompt to design and produce three working electronic devices with their own circuit boards, 3D-printed enclosures, and software. The devices, shown below, were a home voice-assistant hub, a USB speakerphone, and a handheld virtual pet. We collaborated on this project with Diode, a company that designs and manufactures circuit boards.

Claude wrote its own specifications, selected available electronic components from US distributors, routed each device’s four-layer circuit board, modeled the enclosures with computer-aided design, and programmed the devices’ software. Each board was ready for manufacturing in under a day, with minimal human input. Once Diode had built the boards, Claude guided the company’s engineers through the testing and assembly of the devices. All three devices worked without needing any electrical modifications. Read more about Claude’s hardware engineering skills here.

Robotics. Compared with earlier Claude models, Fable 5.2 shows substantially improved skills in controlling physical robots—even for robotics tasks on which it has never explicitly been trained. The video below shows robots controlled by Fable 5.2 completing a variety of tasks, including solving a puzzle cube, unscrewing a bottle cap, and drawing a picture of a robot. On the public RoboDojo benchmark, which tests how AIs can control a simulated two-arm robot from camera images, Fable 5.2 outperformed other frontier models that were run on the same harness, as well as most AI systems built specifically to control robots.

RoboDojo (average)Max score by model

  • Gemini 4 Argon
  • GPT-6 Astra
  • Fable 5.1
  • Opus 5.5
  • Fable 5.2

RoboDojo Sim tests control of a simulated two-arm robot. Scores are based on our internal runs for each model using the highest available effort level. At Max effort, Fable 5.2 scores 64.9%, more than double GPT-6 Astra (29.8%) and Fable 5.1 (27.6%).

Research and analysis

Early testers using Claude Fable 5.2 for research and analysis tasks found that it can handle more ambiguous, data-heavy tasks than previous models and has better judgment on ambiguous tasks—particularly those that require abstract reasoning and design. Proprietary trading firm Jump Trading tested Fable 5.2 on proxy evaluations that resemble some of its quantitative research tasks, embedding it in a harness similar to the one the firm uses for its own research. In one run, Fable 5.2 effectively played all the necessary roles: code-writer, coordinator, planner, and job-submitter. Previous models had required substantial investments of time to manually rebalance roles to accommodate different models’ strengths and weaknesses.

Other testers from research and analysis organizations sent us the following statements on their experiences with Fable 5.2:

Jump TradingBalyasny Asset ManagementDiscovered MaterialsIMCHarveyFundamental Research LabsXTX MarketsBox

Quote

“Claude Fable 5.2 is incredible at playing every major role within a research system: defining questions, interpreting, coordinating, and of course finding and implementing the key ideas. Definitely one of the strongest on taste and judgment that we’ve seen. In an internal research automation benchmark, it achieved a full 10% lower error than the next best model.”

CompanyJump Trading

AuthorLucas Baker, Head of LLM R&D

Quote

“In a recent evaluation, we asked Claude Fable 5.2 to investigate how one organization tested a new integration in its core technology systems. It traced the answer to the right sources and didn’t overstate what the evidence showed. It also flagged that the question’s framing could be misleading. In investment research, that restraint makes clear what remains unknown and where the market may be mispricing risk or opportunity.”

CompanyBalyasny Asset Management

AuthorAshish Malik, AI Researcher

Quote

“Phonon calculations are one of the most expensive routine steps in computational materials science, which is why labs often skip stability checks when screening new materials. Claude Fable 5.2 made Quantum ESPRESSO’s phonon code about 36 times faster on average than stock on the same GPU, taking our 13 benchmark cases from 3.3 hours to under four minutes. That beats Fable 5.1’s speedup by 3–4 times.”

CompanyDiscovered Materials

AuthorAkash Ramdas, Co-Founder

Quote

“With Fable 5.1 we saw the first glimmers of a model coming up with truly innovative research ideas. Claude Fable 5.2 continues that trend. It had the same insight we were impressed with from Fable 5.1 and then came up with a second, entirely new angle. It achieved new best scores on three of the four quant research problems we’ve finished. We’d like to use it for high-impact, long-running research tasks, or for coordinating teams of other models.”

CompanyIMC

AuthorMarquis Wong, Principal AI Engineer

Quote

“In an I-9 compliance review, Claude Fable 5.2 gave the client clearer direction than Fable 5.1. It identified the employees needing immediate attention and explained how to correct each issue and who should act. It’s an exciting improvement in the model’s ability to give practical legal guidance.”

CompanyHarvey

AuthorNiko Grupen, Head of AI Research

Quote

“On one task, Claude Fable 5.2 had to pull a company’s financials out of its 10-K into a forecasting model, and the template didn’t say whether a metric should be the reported figure or calculated. It inferred the author’s intent from the cell formatting, caught that the regional numbers didn’t sum to the reported total, and got every cell right. Better judgment calls like that are the main reason it scored 91% on our eval versus 86% for the next best model.”

CompanyFundamental Research Labs

AuthorJeffrey Liu, Member of Technical Staff

Quote

“In our quantitative research work, Claude Fable 5.2 delivered very strong improvements versus Fable 5.1, especially in the setup with multiple coordinating agents. Its maths research capabilities represent another meaningful advance, too.”

CompanyXTX Markets

AuthorAlex Gerko, Founder and CEO

Quote

“Before putting AI to work across workflows, you need to trust its approach and conclusions. In our testing, Claude Fable 5.2 identified inconsistencies, drew on context across entire document sets, and adjusted recommendations based on relevant evidence. For example, when reviewing files attached to a loan application, it flagged that the salary deposits and the bank statement’s balance didn’t match, so the underwriter could focus on what to check.”

CompanyBox

AuthorYashodha Bhavnani, VP of AI Products

Safety and alignment

No single test can tell us how a highly capable model will behave once it’s deployed, so we rely on many different tests and many different types of evidence before release. For the model underlying Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2, our predeployment safety work included alignment training and testing, newly designed evaluations on the model’s propensity to take unhelpful actions, building stronger safeguards against misuse, and scaling up our behavioral monitoring. The model was also tested before release by external evaluators, including the UK AI Security Institute, Frontier Design, and METR. See the Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 System Card for a summary of their reports⁴ and for a full description of our own safety and capabilities testing.

Alignment testing

We ran a suite of evaluations for how well-aligned Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 are in behavioral terms, testing how often they behave in unintended and potentially unsafe ways. Weighing everything we’ve seen across a range of evaluations, we’ve assessed the risk of these models behaving in unsafe ways in high-stakes situations to be low (as with our other recent models).

We tested Claude Mythos 5.2 (the same underlying model as Fable 5.2 without certain cybersecurity or biology safeguards), on our automated behavioral audit, which tests how a model behaves across approximately 1,900 scenarios. Claude Mythos 5.2 performed as well as, or better than, Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and Claude Mythos 5.1 on most measures. For example, it scored better than all three on most measures that involve misleading users. Hallucinating inputs, falsely claiming to have completed a task, omitting important information, and failing to disclose bad or lazy work were all lower in Claude Mythos 5.2.⁵

Automated behavioral auditOverall misaligned behavior score

  • Mythos 5.1
  • Opus 5.5
  • Sonnet 5.5
  • Mythos 5.2

Overall score from our automated behavioral audit, a composite of many undesirable behaviors including cooperation with human misuse and autonomous actions across a range of scenarios. Lower scores are better. See Section 6.4.1 of the Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 System Card for full details.

We paid particular attention during our testing to behaviors that contributed to recent notable cybersecurity and alignment incidents. For example, we found that Claude Mythos 5.2 has a lower propensity than Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and Mythos 5.1 to engage in biased or motivated reasoning (such reasoning might mean it “explains away” evidence that it isn’t in a simulation and thus takes actions without a realistic understanding of the consequences).

We ran multiple different evaluations to test the model’s tendency to attempt escaping its sandbox. In two evaluations we’d used previously, Claude Mythos 5.2 made substantially fewer attempts at sandbox escape than any other model we’ve tested. In a dedicated evaluation—an adversarial experiment including over 1,800 scenarios, most of which could not be solved without escaping a sandbox, and where the sandbox has a deliberate weakness—Claude Mythos 5.2 made use of credentials or files that we had placed outside its sandbox in 3.1% of scenarios, about as often as Opus 5.5 (3.3%), less often than Sonnet 5.5 (5.1%), and well below previous iterations of Claude Mythos (5 and 5.1, which scored 39% and 21%, respectively). We found that other techniques, such as describing the sandbox and adding tools to report weaknesses, reduced Claude Mythos 5.2’s escape attempts even further. On other measures—one, for example, involving taking harmful actions after erroneously concluding it was in a simulation—Claude Mythos 5.2 scored slightly worse than Opus 5.5, and about level with Claude Mythos 5.1.

The problem of building evaluations that reliably catch every failure before a model is deployed remains unsolved. The complexities of evaluating highly capable models often muddy the picture—for example, Claude Mythos 5.2 and Fable 5.2 each voice suspicion that they are being evaluated more often than any of our recent models, which challenges our ability to assess how they will act in real-world settings. As these settings expand and capabilities increase with future models, we expect this challenge to grow. That is why we do not rely on these evaluations alone to provide a holistic picture of safety: we draw on monitoring during training, reviews of transcripts from internal use, testing by external evaluators, and interpretability techniques for examining what is happening inside the model. We are also working to make our evaluations more realistic and to better understand what they miss.

Safeguards

Cybersecurity and biology safeguards. Consistent with previous Claude Fable models, Fable 5.2 comes with safety classifiers that block high-risk cyber activities, including penetration testing, exploit generation, and binary-based vulnerability, as well as most tasks in research biology. When a query is blocked, users will instead receive a response from Opus 4.8 for cybersecurity and Opus 5 for biology. Since the release of Claude Fable 5.1, we have continued to reduce false positives for our safety classifiers. Based on early testing across claude.ai, Claude Code, and Cowork, we observed about 55% fewer blocks with Fable 5.2 compared with Fable 5.1—about 60% fewer in cybersecurity and 40% fewer in biology. Claude Mythos 5.2 is available to vetted organizations that work in these dual-use areas.

AI research and development. The model that underlies Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 is a step forward in general capabilities. However, during the model’s training, we took steps to limit advances in the specific research capabilities that could most directly accelerate AI development. Thus, in relevant areas, including accelerator kernel optimization and improving large language model architectures, Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 perform at about the level of Opus 5.5. Importantly, we ensured that the training changes did not affect related capabilities like agentic coding, hardware development, and traditional AI or machine learning research (including interpretability research). We do not alter these capabilities as the model is being served to users (that is, at inference time). As described in Section 1.5 of the System Card and similarly to previous models, Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 also include transparent fallbacks to Opus 5 for a small set of topics in this domain, including kernel development on certain nonstandard accelerators.

Anti-distillation. Distillation, where a model is trained on the outputs of a more advanced one to extract the advanced model’s capabilities, occurs illicitly on an industrial scale, often involving thousands of fake Claude accounts. Since distillation allows for advanced capabilities to be released without the safeguards we’ve built into Claude, it creates safety and national security risks (see our September 2026 threat intelligence report for details on illicit distillation activity we’ve detected and disrupted so far). Fable 5.2 has the strongest protections against distillation of any model we’ve released; it uses the techniques we described in a recent report, which have reduced the data harvested by distillers by 90% to 99%.

We are also expanding the rollout of an API feature that helps guard against illicit distillation: preserved thinking now applies to all accounts. Preserved thinking prevents distillers from editing Claude’s prior context in an attempt to extract its reasoning (developers can refer to our preserved thinking docs to learn how to update integrations with new API features).

Data privacy and Enterprise Frontier Safeguards

Some more complex forms of AI model misuse can be detected only when observing patterns across multiple requests. For this reason, powerful models like Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 rely on safeguards that monitor a window of usage data (as opposed to individual responses). With Enterprise Frontier Safeguards, automated safety monitoring is run on prompts and responses that are stored in a customer’s infrastructure, making it compatible with zero data retention (ZDR). Enterprise Frontier Safeguards is now in private beta with customers like Bridgewater, Salesforce, and Stripe.

Enterprise customers can request access to Enterprise Frontier Safeguards by contacting their account team or by completing this form. Eligible customers can continue using Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 with zero data retention before implementing safety monitoring with EFS. For other customers, we have 30-day retention for safety monitoring.

Availability

Claude Fable 5.2 is available today on all platforms, including Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure. Developers can get started with claude-fable-5-2 on the Claude Platform.

This week, we’re giving subscribers on eligible paid plans extra Fable usage. Plans and seats that include Fable models get one to three Fable resets based on how long they’ve subscribed, and Fable is included for up to 50% of weekly usage limits for Pro plans and standard seats on the Team plan. Learn more about the Fable 5.2 launch promotion here.

Cybersecurity professionals can apply for access to Claude Mythos 5.2 through the Cyber Verification Program. Claude Enterprise customers can also use Claude Security, powered by our full family of models, including Claude Mythos 5.2. Life sciences researchers can also apply for access through the Life Sciences Verification Program.

Fast mode for Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 is available on Claude Code, the Claude Platform, Claude Models on Google Cloud (Anthropic managed and Google managed), and Microsoft Foundry (Anthropic hosted). Note that access to Claude Mythos fast mode is available only to organizations who are part of our Verification Programs.

Footnotes

1 CVE refers to Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures, a system that enumerates software vulnerabilities.

2 The counts are raw findings from one tester’s audit, although testers consistently found that Claude Mythos 5.2 identified more vulnerabilities than earlier models. On our own evaluations, vulnerability identification is roughly on par with Opus 5.5 (see the system card).

3 Earlier work on modeling AAV capsids and other large symmetric protein systems includes FoldaVirus, EvoDOCK and its symmetric extension, SymProFold, CapBuild, MoLPC, CombFold, Uni-Fold Symmetry, Apodex Discovery, and the “big bang” initialization (the last of which was referenced in the prompt we gave to Claude Mythos 5.2). These methods typically assemble the full structure from separately predicted chains or small groups of chains. Claude was permitted to use known symmetries but was instructed not to rely on assembly. Note that accuracy is measured by comparing Cα RMSD with the experimental structure: 1.2 Å for OpenFold3-preview2 and 1.4 Å for ESMFold2 on AAV2 (PDB:1LP3). A capsid counts as accurately modeled if either model came within 3 Å. For AAV2, Claude’s method required about 58 minutes of inference on one NVIDIA H200 GPU for OpenFold3-preview2 and about seven minutes for ESMFold2.

4 None of the external organizations reviewed the contents of this blog post or the contents of the System Card. Those organizations do not necessarily agree with any of the claims made in either publication.

5 We ran these tests on Claude Mythos 5.2 because testing the model with reduced safeguards provides the most comprehensive look at model behavior. We expect Fable 5.2 to behave similarly; in some cases, more potential pathways for misuse should be blocked given its stronger safeguards.

item.description: Full title: Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan: A Synthetic Dataset Capturing Japan's Demographics and Financial Context
item.content:encoded:
Back to Articles

Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan: A Synthetic Dataset Capturing Japan's Demographics and Financial Context

Enterprise + Article

Published November 9, 2026

7

Atsunori Fujita

Atsunori

nvidia

Masaya Ogushi

SnowMasaya

nvidia

Vincent Gong

vg1024

nvidia

Kotaro Yamamoto

kyamamoto-nv

nvidia

Yoshi Suhara

suhara

nvidia

Will Jennings

WillJenningsDC

nvidia

Yev Meyer

nv-3mei

nvidia

A compound AI approach to Japanese personas grounded in real-world distributions

Open Data Breaking Down Privacy Barriers to Pave the Way for AI in Finance

In the financial sector, the utilization of real-world data faces significant constraints due to strict privacy regulations, compliance requirements, and the need for advanced domain expertise. In this context, the development of agentic AI in the financial domain requires synthetic data capable of avoiding the risks of using real data while reflecting demographics, household structures, and asset statuses to reproduce diverse, realistic financial scenarios.

To address these challenges, Elith and NVIDIA have released Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan, a financial domain extension of the open-source persona dataset "Nemotron-Personas-Japan." To our knowledge, it is the first open persona dataset at million-record scale that pairs Japan’s official statistics with household finance and financial literacy data. Built upon official government statistics, this dataset was developed using NeMo SDG-PGMs, a probabilistic graphical model framework for synthetic data generation (SDG), and NeMo Data Designer, an enterprise synthetic data generation system. Furthermore, to enhance the practical utility of the dataset in financial use cases, it was designed by incorporating insights and feedback provided by leading domestic financial institutions and industry associations, including Sompo Japan, Tokio Marine Holdings, Bank of Fukuoka, Mizuho Financial Group, Meiji Yasuda Life Insurance, and the Financial Data Utilization Association (FDUA).

This dataset expands the environment where Japanese developers and enterprises can develop and evaluate AI tailored to local and industry requirements, without using real customer data. Released under the CC BY 4.0 license, it is available for commercial use. From building conversational agents to customer simulation and model evaluation, it supports practical financial AI development. The Nemotron-Personas collection, including Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan, is designed to seamlessly integrate with the user simulation framework NeMo User Sim, enabling instant execution of simulations drawn from diverse distributions consistent with the real world.

What’s in the Dataset?

  • 9M personas total (1M records x 9 personas each), written in natural Japanese
  • 50 fields per record: 9 persona fields, 11 persona attributes, and 30 contextual fields based on official demographic and labor statistics
  • ~1.5B tokens total, including ~750M persona tokens
  • ~950k unique names
  • 1600+ occupation categories reflecting Japan's workforce
  • Comprehensive coverage across demographic, regional, asset distribution, and personality trait axes
  • Diverse persona types: Occupations, sports, arts, travel, cooking, finance, financial behavior, and financial concerns
  • Natural language persona attributes: Cultural background, skills and expertise, career goals and aspirations, hobbies and interests, household/parental/financial background, attitudes toward money, and financial planning
  • Available for both commercial and non-commercial use under the CC BY 4.0 license

How We Built It

Data Generation Pipeline

It was built using NVIDIA’s framework for synthetic data generation, NeMo Data Designer. This compound AI system enables complex Jinja templating, Pydantic validation, structured outputs, automated retries, and support for multiple generation backends. This is the essential toolset required for generating such large-scale synthetic datasets. In addition, the following models were utilized:

  • NeMo SDG-PGMs (Apache-2.0): A probabilistic graphical model framework for statistically grounded data generation
  • gemma-4-31B-it (Apache-2.0): For Japanese text generation

Enhanced Cultural Context

Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan was designed to align with Japan's official demographic and labor statistics while taking into account key considerations essential for AI training:

  • Education: Where national statistics broadly aggregate degree levels, we introduced finer granularity to enable the model to reflect diverse educational pathways.
  • Occupation: We incorporated additional categories (such as business owners and specialized professions) to broaden the spectrum of occupations used for training.
  • Life Stages: We modeled scenarios that rarely surface prominently in statistics, such as students, retirees, and periods of unemployment, to represent more realistic personas.
  • Household Finances: In addition to individual income and spending propensity, we incorporated household-level financial and real assets to replicate diverse economic backgrounds.
  • Digital & Financial Literacy: By including internet and smartphone usage along with financial literacy, we enabled the model to precisely capture consumer profiles in financial use cases.

Private By Design

Every persona is fully synthetic. No real individuals are represented, and the dataset is designed to reduce privacy risk. Demographics and household finances follow official statistics and public survey data, and names follow real Japanese naming patterns. Personas are built from these distributions, not from records about real people.

Who This Data Is For

Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan is built first for teams creating financial AI in Japan, at banks and insurers and at the startups and integrators that serve them. Each persona carries household finances and financial literacy alongside demographics. Teams can use them to build customer-service agents, evaluate sales conversations/marketing initiatives, run user simulations in NeMo User Sim, and red-team customer-facing AI.

The release also serves anyone building for Japanese users. It holds 9M personas, 50% more than Nemotron-Personas-Japan, across 50 fields instead of 22. That gives any Japanese-language project finer slices of the population to train and test on.

Practical AI Applications

The synthetic personas in this dataset can be leveraged for:

  • Multi-turn conversation: Using personas as "seeds" to generate human-like dialogue datasets.
  • Domain-specific AI development: Generating datasets to build AI assistants tailored to realistic scenarios in financial use cases.
  • Bias testing and fairness: Evaluating how models and AI agent systems perform across rural and urban divides, various age groups, educational backgrounds, and economic circumstances to check whether AI performs consistently across Japanese society.

Why It Matters

Access to diverse, high-quality training data that reflects real-world populations has long been a challenge in AI development. Enterprise AI development has predominantly relied on private data, creating barriers for researchers, startups, and particularly AI developers in regions with limited available data.

  • Data Diversity: Reflects the full spectrum of Japan's population, which helps reduce biased training and the risk of model collapse.
  • Cultural Authenticity: Reduces reliance on Western-centric datasets and supports the development of Sovereign AI systems.
  • Privacy and Governance: Aligned with Japan’s innovation-first approach to AI governance. Every persona is synthetic, so no customer data is needed to build or test with it.

By releasing Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan under CC BY 4.0, we provide access to enterprise-grade, high-quality synthetic data, empowering anyone to build culturally grounded AI systems with lower cost and less privacy risk.

Pairs with Nemotron-PII-Japan

Nemotron-PII-Japan launches the same day. It holds 100,000 synthetic Japanese business documents with labeled personal information, for training and testing detection and redaction models. Its documents are built on Nemotron-Personas-Japan. Use Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan to simulate customers, and Nemotron-PII-Japan to test how your pipeline protects their data.

Start Building with Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan

You can download this dataset using the command below to help develop AI that genuinely understands Japanese culture and language.

from datasets import load_dataset
ds = load_dataset("nvidia/Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan")

Use cases for building production-ready applications:

  • Using personas as seeds for dialogue generation
  • Fine-tuning models with culturally grounded data
  • Building personalized engines that reflect Japan's overall demographic makeup
  • Developing domain-specific AI agents equipped with Japanese context

From teams building AI in Japan to global developers aiming for broader regional deployment, Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan dataset provides the authentic, privacy-conscious foundation required for your applications.

item.title: [Hugging Face] Your Experts Have Partners. There's HOPE for Keeping Them To…
item.description: Full title: Your Experts Have Partners. There's HOPE for Keeping Them Together
item.content:encoded:
Back to Articles

Your Experts Have Partners. There's HOPE for Keeping Them Together

Enterprise Article

Published November 9, 2026

3

Alex M Tseng

alexmtseng

amazon

Higher-Order Pruning of Experts in Mixture-of-Experts Language Models

Introduction

Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have enabled state-of-the-art LLMs to be scaled to hundreds of billions of parameters, but they come with a fundamental and costly caveat: every expert MLP must occupy memory at inference time, even though the vast majority are idle for any given token. For example, Qwen3.5-122B has 256 experts in each of its 48 MoE layers, and 95% of its ~250 GB parameter memory footprint is taken up entirely by these expert MLPs alone. However, for any given token, only 8 experts in each layer are actually used.

Expert pruning is one of the most direct fixes to this memory bottleneck. That is, permanently delete the least useful experts. Pruning avoids the latency issues which make dynamic loading/off-loading of experts impractical; it does not require any training; and it composes with quantization. Given these attractive benefits and the simplicity of the idea, it's easy to see why expert pruning has become a go-to approach for shrinking MoEs. The difficulty lies in deciding which experts are safest to remove.

Existing pruning methods score each expert independently, assigning every expert a scalar importance score (based on a calibration dataset), and cutting out the least important experts (in each layer independently). These are first-order methods, because they assume each expert's contribution is independent of all others. In reality, experts form cooperative groups. We observe consistent clusters of co-activated experts in our own experiments, and independent work has shown that expert cooperation is a stable property of MoEs and is important for model performance. Ignoring these interactions leads to suboptimal pruning, especially at aggressive rates.

Our newest paper derives HOPE (Higher-Order Pruning of Experts), a second-order method that accounts for pairwise expert interactions. At 50% pruning, HOPE achieves the best average rank of any method, with gains of up to +6.1% on agentic coding tasks over the next-best pruning method.

In this post, we explain how HOPE works, show where it outperforms existing methods, and walk through how to use it for your own models. For readers unfamiliar with MoE architectures, see Mixture of Experts (MoEs) in Transformers.

Experts don't work alone

In a standard MoE, each layer has EE experts, and each input token xx is routed independently to KK such experts ( K=8 K = 8 is a typical choice). Routing is performed by a single layer which produces softmax-normalized gate weights gk(x)g_{k}(x) for each expert kk, wherein the KK experts with the highest gate weights are selected to form the active set of experts, T(x)⊂{1,..,E}T(x) \subset\{1,..,E\}. The output of the layer is then ∑k∈T(x)gk(x)fk(x)\sum\limits_{k\in T(x)}g_{k}(x)f_{k}(x), where fk(x)f_{k}(x) is the output of expert kk for token xx.

Left: typical MoE layer, where each token is routed to the top-K experts. Right: first-order methods rank and delete experts based on a scalar importance score, but the best pruning decisions will also consider the strength of interactions between experts.

Importantly, experts in the selected set T(x)T(x) are not independent. Experts form stable cooperative groups that get consistently co-activated together. This has been observed before in the literature, as well: expert co-selection patterns emerge early in training and stabilize throughout.

This means that when we prune experts from an MoE layer, pruning decisions need to consider the higher-order effects between these experts. Removing expert A might seem fine on its own, but if expert B—which frequently cooperates with and relies on A—is highly important, then removing A would dismantle a cooperative group just through a single deletion. First-order methods miss this entirely, because they score A and B separately.

This effect compounds at high pruning rates. When we remove up to 50% of experts, we risk breaking many cooperative links. This is where second-order pruning is most advantageous.

How HOPE identifies a prune-set

(See Appendix A in our corresponding paper for the full derivation of the HOPE objective)

When we delete a set of PP experts from some MoE layer, the selected set of experts T(x)T(x) (for any token xx) can change. The pruned experts that would have been selected are replaced by the experts with the next-highest gate weights. The resulting change in layer output is the pruning error. Our goal is to find the prune-set PP (of some predefined pruning budget ∣P∣\vert P\vert) that minimizes the resulting pruning error (over tokens xx from our calibration set).

Unfortunately, minimizing the pruning error over PP directly is intractable. The pruning error depends on the identities of the replacement experts, which in turn depend on the prune-set PP itself. HOPE sidesteps this by defining a tractable surrogate ZZ, which strictly upper-bounds the dominant component of the pruning error:

Z=[∑j∈P∩T(x)gj(x)∥fj(x)∥2]2≥true errorZ = \bigl[\sum\limits_{j \in P\cap T(x)} g_{j}(x)\Vert f_j(x)\Vert_{2}\bigr]^{2} \geq \text{true error}

Because ZZ is a squared sum, expanding it naturally produces cross-terms gi(x)gj(x)∥fi(x)∥2∥fj(x)∥2g_{i}(x)g_{j}(x)\Vert f_{i}(x)\Vert_{2}\Vert f_{j}(x)\Vert_{2} between pairs of experts. These are the interaction terms that first-order methods discard.

To find the optimal prune-set, HOPE minimizes E[Z]\mathbb{E}[Z] over the calibration set, which can be reformulated as the following quadratic program:

P∗=arg min⁡p p⊤Fps.t.p∈{0,1}E,∑k=1Epk=∣P∣P^{*} = \argmin_{p}\; p^{\top}Fp \quad \text{s.t.} \quad p \in \{0,1\}^{E}, \sum\limits_{k=1}^{E}p_{k} = \vert P\vert

where F∈RE×EF\in\mathbb{R}^{E\times E} is defined as:

Fi,j=1∣Xi,j∣∑x∈Xi,jgi(x)gj(x)∥fi(x)∥2∥fj(x)∥2whereXi,j={x:i,j∈T(x)}F_{i,j} = \frac{1}{\vert \mathcal{X}_{i,j}\vert} \sum\limits_{x\in\mathcal{X}_{i,j}} g_{i}(x)g_{j}(x)\Vert f_{i}(x)\Vert_{2}\Vert f_{j}(x)\Vert_{2}\quad\text{where}\quad \mathcal{X}_{i,j} = \{x: i,j \in T(x)\}

This F-matrix is collected on the calibration dataset, and the optimal prune-set is obtained by solving the resulting quadratic program (QP) with a continuous relaxation (then rounding to binary solutions). Each entry Fi,jF_{i,j} captures the average gate-weighted output product of experts ii and jj, across tokens where both are co-activated. Whereas the diagonal Fk,kF_{k,k} measures individual expert importance, the off-diagonal entries ( Fi,jF_{i,j} for i≠ji\neq j) measure pairwise cooperative contribution.

What does FF look like in practice? It shows the structure of expert cooperation, which depends on layer:

Visualization of the interaction matrix F for GLM-4.5-Air (128 experts per layer, 106B parameters total) at three representative layers (early, middle, late). Experts have been clustered to reveal block structure. Bright blocks along the diagonal indicate groups of experts with strong pairwise interaction scores.

In terms of practical cost, HOPE requires the same calibration pass as any other expert-pruning method (one forward pass over calibration data). The only addition is solving the quadratic program, which is non-convex, but can be solved efficiently via a standard QP solver (1–2 seconds each layer). The total additional overhead is negligible compared to first-order methods, as the time for calibration dominates.

Connection to REAP

Notably, HOPE has a strong connection to Router-weighted Expert Activation Pruning (REAP), a state-of-the-art first-order expert-pruning method. HOPE's F-matrix encodes individual expert importance scores on the diagonal, and this diagonal effectively recovers the scores used by REAP to independently rank experts for pruning (differing only by the variance of expert contributions). The diagonal of FF recovers REAP's expert rankings almost perfectly (Spearman ρ=0.988\rho = 0.988). Thus, any improvement HOPE achieves over REAP is attributable to the second-order interaction terms in the off-diagonal entries of the FF-matrix.

Results

We evaluated HOPE as an expert pruning method using 3 models (Qwen3.5-122B, Qwen3.5-35B, and GLM-4.5-Air), with 2 calibration datasets (Evol-CodeAlpaca and SWE-Bench Verified trajectories). We used the Tulu3 suite and SWE-Bench Pro (agentic coding) to test the resulting pruned models, comparing HOPE to 4 first-order baselines (REAP, MAN, EAN, and Frequency) across pruning rates spanning from 10% to 50%.

HOPE achieves the best overall rank across conditions and dominates at aggressive pruning rates. Left: average rank (lower = better) across all models, calibration sets, and benchmarks. Right: SWE-Bench Pro performance on Qwen3.5-35B.

Across all conditions, HOPE achieved the best average rank (2.07 out of 5 methods), with the highest rate of top-1 finishes (39% of conditions) and top-2 finishes (67%). In a head-to-head comparison, HOPE beats every other baseline in the majority of conditions.

As expected, HOPE's advantage grows at higher pruning rates. As more experts are removed, more cooperative links are broken, and the off-diagonal terms of FF become more important. At 50% pruning, HOPE's average rank improves to 1.58 (vs. 2.42 for the next-best method, REAP). This is also the most deployment-relevant setting, where memory savings are large enough to accommodate longer contexts, deeper reasoning, and more tool calls.

HOPE's advantage is most pronounced on SWE-Bench Pro, an agentic coding benchmark where models must solve real GitHub issues autonomously. These problems involve compositionally diverse tasks (e.g. coding, tool calls, reasoning, etc.) over many turns and likely exercise diverse expert combinations—exactly the regime where preserving cooperative structure matters most. On Qwen3.5-35B-A3B at 50% pruning, HOPE achieved 42.3 on SWE-Bench Pro, matching the unpruned model's 41.8 (while REAP dropped to 36.2, a 13% regression).

Notably, pruned models can occasionally match or exceed the unpruned baseline, likely because the removal of low-relevance experts reduces noise on the target tasks. This effect is not unique to HOPE and has been observed across pruning methods. Furthermore, our experiments showed that code-focused calibration with any pruning method (including HOPE) did not severely degrade non-coding benchmarks, and HOPE performed well across the Tulu3 suite regardless of calibration set.

HOPE retains more cooperating experts

Average strength of cooperation (measured by F-matrix value) with retained experts, split by experts on which HOPE and REAP disagree.

HOPE's advantage stems from optimizing over the entire interaction matrix FF. To understand how this affects pruning decisions in practice, we examine the experts where HOPE and REAP disagree. For each disputed expert, we compute its cooperative score (i.e. its average F-value with other retained experts). Experts retained only by HOPE consistently have higher cooperative scores than experts retained only by REAP. In other words, as part of the QP optimization, HOPE sacrifices some individually high-scoring experts in favor of preserving cooperative clusters. The gains in benchmark performance (shown above) validate that this trade-off is advantageous.

How to run HOPE

We created a basic package to run HOPE. It has three steps: 1) calibrate; 2) solve; 3) prune. Our package has been tested on Qwen3, Qwen3-Next, Qwen3.5, and GLM-4.5.

Step 1: Calibrate

hope calibrate \
    --model-path Qwen/Qwen3.5-35B-A3B \
    --prompts calibration_prompts.txt \
    --out-path observations.h5

The calibration step runs a single forward pass over calibration data, whether it be agentic rollouts or single-turn traces. This uses HuggingFace transformers to hook into the forward pass of each individual MoE layer. For each token, this records which experts are selected, their gate weights, output norms, and pairwise co-activation statistics. The output of this step is the F-matrix, stored in an HDF5 file.

Step 2: Solve QP

hope solve \
    --obs-path observations.h5 \
    --prune-frac 0.50 \
    --out-path pruneset.json

This command materializes the F-matrix and solves the binary quadratic program via a continuous relaxation. This takes a few seconds per layer, and the output is a JSON file which contains the prune-set. This is technically the final output of the HOPE algorithm.

Step 3: Prune

hope prune \
    --model-path Qwen/Qwen3.5-35B-A3B \
    --pruneset-path pruneset.json \
    --out-path ./Qwen3.5-35B-A3B-pruned-50

To complete the pipeline, we run this command to actually create the smaller model checkpoint from the prune-set. The pruned model is a standard HuggingFace checkpoint which is smaller on disk and in memory (no changes to vLLM or SGLang model definitions needed).

We also released a more compact Python API:

from hope.calibrate import calibrate
from hope.solve import solve
from hope.prune import prune_model

calibrate("Qwen/Qwen3.5-35B-A3B", calibration_prompts, "observations.h5")
solve("observations.h5", prune_frac=0.50, out_path="pruneset.json")
prune_model("Qwen/Qwen3.5-35B-A3B", "pruneset.json", "./Qwen3.5-35B-A3B-pruned-50")

Limitations of HOPE

HOPE's advantage is most pronounced at higher pruning rates (40–50%). At lower pruning rates (10–20%), first-order methods like REAP and MAN are sometimes competitive, and HOPE's advantage shrinks. Additionally, as with most expert-pruning algorithms, HOPE prunes each layer independently and does not account for cross-layer interactions. In our paper, we presented a theoretical framework for cross-layer HOPE, but the results remain preliminary. Finally, HOPE captures pairwise interactions, but even higher-order interactions (triplets and beyond) could provide additional signal, although they are combinatorially difficult to estimate.

More information

For more information, see our corresponding paper and codebase.

Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.18916

Code: https://github.com/awslabs/HOPE

To see how HOPE can be applied to next-generation hybrid architectures, see our corresponding repository.

Citation:

@article{tseng2026hope,
    title={Higher-Order Pruning of Experts in Mixture-of-Experts Language Models},
    author={Tseng, Alex M. and Kaul, Prannay and Zancato, Luca and Xia, Wei and Soatto, Stefano},
    journal={arXiv preprint arXiv:2609.18916},
    year={2026},
}
