item.description: Full title: Professional work deserves professional tools. Meet AWS Quick.
item.content:encoded:
Artificial Intelligence

Professional work deserves professional tools. Meet AWS Quick.

Our first brand campaign celebrates teams who keep business moving and the AI workspace built only for them. Every day, teams at leading enterprises use AWS Quick to research, analyze, and act across the data and applications they already rely on. Today we’re launching our first brand campaign to bring that same experience to millions more knowledge workers around the world. The campaign runs across the United States and the United Kingdom on streaming TV, online video, social media, and leading business publications. AWS Quick is the AI workspace built only for work, where teams use AI agents to research, analyze, and act across the data and applications they already rely on. Across virtually every industry, leading enterprises including 3M, BMW, Mondelez, New York Life, and Southwest Airlines are using Quick to transform how they work. The campaign celebrates the teams who know that the work they do every day deserves tools built for it.

The work you know

Customers tell us their AI assistants make individuals faster, but the gains stay personal. A sales rep still builds territory plans by pulling from the CRM, dashboards, call notes, and email. Because context stays locked inside a single project or one vendor’s suite, productivity never compounds across the team or the company. Most of those tools started as consumer apps and still serve personal and professional use with the same product. AWS Quick took the opposite path: it was built for work from day one, on the same AWS infrastructure that millions of customers use to run their mission-critical applications. These include many of the world’s most complex and security-sensitive workloads.

Built for your business from day one

AWS Quick has no consumer version. Every roadmap decision and every feature we ship starts with one question: does it help individuals, teams, and entire enterprises do their most important work? Quick knows your role, your team, and how your projects, people, and data connect, because it works across the applications and workflows your teams already use. Quick watches for changes, surfaces what matters, and acts on your behalf, which leaves your team free to focus on what moves the business forward. Anyone can build agents, apps, and automations by describing what they need in plain language, without filing an IT ticket. Everything built in a shared space becomes an asset the whole team can use.

Trust built in

Quick is integrated with the security and compliance tools you already use, including Microsoft Purview for data protection, AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM), and Microsoft Active Directory for permission-based controls. Quick reads the sensitivity labels already on your files, enforces existing permissions, and flags potentially sensitive data to administrators. Assets including agents, knowledge bases, and skills reach new teams only through approved sharing, and every approval and denial is recorded with who decided, what they shared, and why. Quick also carries the compliance certifications most organizations require, including HIPAA, FedRAMP, SOC 2, and ISO 27001. Your data is yours, and your conversations are private. No one else can browse your conversations, and IT admins cannot access your chat transcripts. Amazon CloudWatch and AWS CloudTrail are built in, giving your organization a full audit trail of what happened, who did it, and when. Your data never leaves your environment and never trains someone else’s models.

That commitment is also why we’re now AWS Quick, a name that signals the enterprise security and governance that have been part of Quick from the start.

Every decision stays yours

IT leaders, account executives, program managers, and finance leads all work differently, and Quick works the way each of them does, on any device and on their schedule. You bring the judgment, and Quick gives your team the capacity to match its goals.

Ready to transform how your users, teams, and entire enterprise do their best work with an AI built for business? You can download Quick today and get started in minutes, or talk to your AWS account team about options for enterprise pricing plans.

item.title: [Anyscale] Donating KubeRay to the CNCF
item.content:encoded:
HomeBlogBlog Detail

Donating KubeRay to the CNCF

By Andrew Sy Kim (Google), Edward Oakes, Kai-Hsun Chen, Jui-An Huang, Richard Liaw, Robert Nishihara and The KubeRay team | November 9, 2026

The PARK stack (PyTorch, AI models, Ray, and Kubernetes) is emerging as the de facto open source standard for production AI. Within that stack, KubeRay has become the bridge connecting scalable AI applications built on Ray with the compute orchestration of Kubernetes.

Nearly every core piece of the PARK stack already lives under the Linux Foundation: PyTorch and Ray through the PyTorch Foundation, and Kubernetes through the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF). KubeRay was the missing piece.

Today, we’re announcing that KubeRay is joining the CNCF, bringing the entire PARK stack under Linux Foundation governance and giving teams full confidence in its neutrality and openness.

Kuberay

LinkScaling Ray clusters on Kubernetes

KubeRay is a powerful, open source toolkit and Kubernetes operator designed to run distributed AI, machine learning, and Python workloads powered by Ray seamlessly on cloud-native infrastructure. As distributed AI workloads become a core cloud native construct, KubeRay bridges the gap between Python-first AI frameworks and Kubernetes-native infrastructure.

Kubernetes-native infrastructure

KubeRay provides three Kubernetes Custom Resource Definitions (CRDs) for scaling and operating Ray workloads in production:

  • RayCluster: The foundational building block for running Ray on Kubernetes. RayCluster manages the full lifecycle of a Ray cluster, automating head and worker pod provisioning, health checks, Global Control Service (GCS) fault tolerance, and dynamic autoscaling in coordination with the Ray Autoscaler.
  • RayJob: Purpose-built for batch processing, distributed training, and reinforcement learning (RL) workloads. RayJob automatically provisions an ephemeral RayCluster, submits a Ray job once the cluster is ready, and tears down the cluster upon completion to maximize compute and accelerator utilization.
  • RayService: Designed for long-lived, high-availability online inference with Ray Serve. RayService manages both the underlying RayCluster and the Ray Serve deployment graph, enabling zero-downtime rolling upgrades, automated failover, and seamless traffic routing for production AI services.

Together, these custom resources provide the foundation for enterprises to build modern machine learning platforms on top of Ray and Kubernetes. For example, end users like Hark use KubeRay to scale their AI agent workflows.

“Running multimodal AI workloads at scale requires a platform with tight integration between Python-first AI and Kubernetes. KubeRay is that bridge, helping us scale reliably and manage complex agentic workflows At Hark, that is why we use it, and why I contribute: I want to help more builders scale production AI with confidence.”Kai-Hsun Chen, AI Infrastructure Lead, Hark

LinkGrowing the KubeRay ecosystem

Beyond core cluster lifecycle management, KubeRay has seen widespread adoption because of how deeply it integrates with other CNCF projects and the broader cloud-native ecosystem. Rather than reinventing infrastructure primitives, KubeRay plugs directly into the tools platform teams already rely on:

  • Observability with OpenTelemetry, Prometheus and Fluent Bit: Ray uses OpenTelemetry within its metrics pipeline and exposes metrics in Prometheus format, enabling platform teams running KubeRay to monitor cluster utilization, task execution, and Ray Serve latency alongside their existing Kubernetes infrastructure. Paired with Fluent Bit for lightweight log collection and forwarding, operators can easily aggregate distributed worker and job logs across ephemeral and long-lived Ray clusters.
  • Batch Scheduling and Quota Management with Kueue, Volcano, and KAI: As organizations scale distributed training across scarce GPU and TPU resources, KubeRay integrates natively with different schedulers to bring Kubernetes-native job queueing to RayJob and RayCluster. This enables gang scheduling (all-or-nothing pod placement), multi-tenant resource quotas, priority preemption, and topology-aware scheduling.
  • Workload Security and Isolation: As AI workloads scale, robust security and multi-tenancy are critical. KubeRay provides the foundation to secure Ray clusters using automated mTLS and Kubernetes network policies.

LinkWhat’s Next?

KubeRay’s success so far has been due to its fast-growing community members -- we want to give thanks to everyone who has contributed to KubeRay so far.

Becoming a CNCF sandbox project is just the beginning of KubeRay’s next chapter under open, vendor-neutral governance, and we’d love for you to be part of it.

If you’re at KubeCon NA 2026, come meet the KubeRay maintainers at our Birds of a Feather (BoF) session to discuss the roadmap, share production use cases, and help shape the future of Ray on Kubernetes. Hark will also be giving a talk about how they use KubeRay for multimodal AI use cases as well.

You can also connect with the community in the #kuberay channel on the CNCF or Ray Slack workspaces and attend our biweekly community meetings.

Table of contents

  • Scaling Ray clusters on Kubernetes
  • Growing the KubeRay ecosystem
  • What’s Next?

item.title: [Meta Llama] Design the Muse App, Just for You
item.content:encoded:
Back to Newsroom

Meta

November 6, 2026November 6, 2026

0.25× 0.5× 1× 1.25× 1.5× 2×

https://about.fb.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Design-the-Muse-App_Just-for-You_Header.mp4

Takeaways

  • Today we’re introducing spaces, a custom experience you design inside the Muse app.
  • Build a space to organize your day, keep up with what you love, or bring a creative idea to life.
  • Organize the app the way you want it — add spaces to your sidebar or main tabs and change them out whenever so your Muse app fits your routine.

Today, we’re introducing spaces, an interactive way to build a more personalized Muse. A space is a custom experience you create inside Muse by describing your idea, like a holiday gift tracker, a daily word game, or a planning board for your next DIY project. It’s shaped around your routines, goals, and interests, and can be as practical or entertaining as you want. Every space you create becomes part of Muse, so you can keep it where you want and come back to it any time.

From An Idea to Something Real

Have an idea you’ve been meaning to try? Tell Muse about it, and it builds it for you. Your initial idea is just the starting point. As you use your space, you can keep adjusting it with Muse, whether that’s adding what’s missing, trying a new look, or changing how it works.

You can also choose where your spaces live in Muse. Add them to your sidebar, move them into your main tabs, hide the ones you don’t need right now, and schedule when they appear. For example, keep your weekly planner up front during the workweek, then swap it for your weekend plans on Saturday.

https://about.fb.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/01_Design-the-Muse-App_Just-for-You.mp4

What You Can Build

Spaces can help you get things done, have a little fun, or give your creative projects a home. Here are a few ideas:

  • A shopping hub that brings holiday and birthday gift ideas, wishlists from Instagram saves, and your Marketplace listings and buyer messages into one view
  • A school dashboard that finds the events relevant to your kids in school emails and adds them to your calendar
  • A music tracker for the artists you love, with new releases and upcoming shows
  • A wedding planner with your RSVP list, vendor invoices, and to-dos
  • A trivia game that quizzes you on your favorite movies, music, or sports team
  • A podcast studio to keep your episode ideas, research, and scripts together
  • An order tracker for your small business, with new orders, customer messages and what needs to ship today
  • A client hub for your freelance work, with projects, deadlines, and invoices
  • A trip planner with your flights, hotel, reservations and a day-by-day itinerary.

Got a half-finished idea sitting in your notes app, a spreadsheet you keep meaning to clean up, or a hobby you want to dive into? Chances are you can turn it into a space.

A Space That Keeps Up With You

Your spaces are personal from the start. Connect the apps you use, and your spaces keep themselves up to date in the background, so new concert dates, price changes, or savings progress show up without you having to ask. You can check things off, add notes, and make edits right in your space, and everything will be there when you return.

Looking Ahead

Starting today, spaces are available everywhere Muse is available. We’re also exploring ways for you to share your spaces with others to build a more collaborative experience in Muse.

We’re also rolling out specialized versions of our models to Muse, trained with learnings from Muse Wonder, to make your overall experience even better.

item.title: [Hugging Face] ToyBlocks: A controlled world for robot learning and evaluat…
item.description: Full title: ToyBlocks: A controlled world for robot learning and evaluation
item.content:encoded:
Back to Articles

ToyBlocks: A controlled world for robot learning and evaluation

Enterprise Article

Published November 6, 2026

5

Kyle Wiggers

Ai2Comms

allenai

💻 Code | 📊 Data | 🤖 Models | 📖 Documentation

Robots are learning to fold laundry, sort parts, and handle unfamiliar objects. But those demonstrations are often rather narrow and don't explain what a robot has learned or why it fails.

To study a complex system, scientists often begin with a small, controlled environment, such as a petri dish or terrarium, where they can vary conditions and observe the effects. Robotics needs environments that make this kind of investigation possible—researchers should be able to change the training data or model design, repeat a test, and trace the cause of a failure.

Today we're introducing a framework for creating these environments; we call them FoundationWorlds. Each pairs a controlled, simulated world targeted at studying robotics in a specific environment with tools for automatically generating tasks and training demonstrations, as well as metrics for measuring a robot's behavior over time. Together, they provide a setting for studying questions such as how models improve as more training data becomes available, and how to best combine high-level reasoning with precise physical control.

Our first foundation world is ToyBlocks: an open simulation framework built around a robot arm and blocks on a tabletop. The setting is deliberately simple, but the robot must still reason about how the blocks interact and how to arrange them while pushing, flipping, and stacking.

ToyBlocks automatically generates demonstrations, which are recordings of a robot completing tasks in simulation, without requiring time-consuming teleoperation, in which a person remotely controls the robot. Researchers can easily vary these training experiences. For example, a team could generate more pushing or flipping demonstrations, then evaluate performance on tasks kept out of training.

Starting with ToyBlocks as our first FoundationWorld, we aim to extend the approach to increasingly complex environments.

How ToyBlocks works

Building on our earlier work in open robot learning, including MolmoAct 2, MolmoBot, and MolmoSpaces, ToyBlocks gives researchers a way to study robotics questions in a deliberately constrained domain.

As a FoundationWorld, ToyBlocks is designed around four requirements: (1) realistic physics and appearance, (2) automatic generation of tasks and demonstrations at scale, (3) challenges that combine reasoning with dexterity, and (4) broad coverage of the tasks possible within a domain.

Open-ended domains require modeling a wide range of objects and interactions, making it infeasible to fulfill all these requirements. ToyBlocks’ narrow scope, on the other hand, makes it possible to fulfill them all.

Within ToyBlocks' smaller setting, researchers can work toward investigating how a robot can learn to perform any reasonable task while being confident that the simulated arm and blocks behave very similarly to their physical counterparts.

A physical robot gripper above wooden blocks in the ToyBlocks setup.

ToyBlocks is not just about picking and stacking blocks: pictures and letters on the blocks' faces allow for searching, sorting, and arranging tasks. A robot may need to turn a block to see a hidden face before deciding where it belongs. Domain randomization – varying block size, table height, and other physical properties from scene to scene – tests how well models generalize as the geometry changes.

ToyBlocks automatically generates skills (behaviors for short tasks) and task demonstrations that can be used to train models or adapt previously trained models through additional training (fine-tuning). High-level reasoning models decide what to do; low-level action models control the robot’s movements. The framework can also be used to easily design experiments and validate hypotheses.

ToyBlocks uses reinforcement learning (RL) and motion planning, which computes how the robot should move, to generate skills for short-horizon tasks, which involve brief sequences of actions. Skill training takes place in Isaac Lab, Nvidia's open-source framework for robot learning in simulation. Through trial and error, these policies – models that choose the robot’s actions – learn non-prehensile skills such as pushing a block across the table or flipping it onto another face without picking it up. Skill generation can draw on privileged information – values the simulator can supply directly but a real robot cannot, such as a block's exact position and orientation – instead of estimating it from camera images. This enables the automatic generation of skills that would require teleoperation in the real world.

To generate demonstration data, a task-and-motion planner (TAMP) automatically selects and sequences the skills needed to solve a task and plans the robot’s movements between them. Running each plan in simulation produces a dataset of recorded demonstrations along with labels describing which task or skill the robot performs. ToyBlocks scales data generation through generating and executing hundreds of such plans in parallel on a single graphics processing unit (GPU), reaching up to 24 times real-time performance.

Acting from sensor observations adds a perception problem: a model has to estimate a block’s pose – its position and orientation – which the simulator could supply directly. To reflect real-world conditions, ToyBlocks trains models that map raw sensor observations to actions.

Execution of Molmo 2 (a high-level model) and ManiFlow (a low-level model) trained in ToyBlocks. Molmo 2 selects skills such as rotation and flipping, indicating the relevant block via a pointing interface, while ManiFlow controls the simulated arm to execute the commanded skills.

ToyBlocks' controllable data generator lets users create training mixtures that emphasize particular skills or fill gaps in existing datasets. Researchers can study how much data a model needs and which experiences help it generalize to unseen tasks. For example, they could test whether adding rotation and pick-and-place demonstrations improves flipping, or vary the balance of examples inside and outside a defined workspace region—evaluating their choices on tasks kept out of training. Importantly, evaluation of trained models generates metrics beyond success rates; it provides information such as execution speeds, forces exerted on objects, and task progress measured via the same specifications used by the planning module.

A webpage interface lets users connect Claude – or another frontier model – and use natural language to instruct the robot or try tasks, offering a way to explore how a model plans and acts without needing robotics expertise.

Research building on ToyBlocks

The evaluations below use ToyBlocks to study how training data and methods affect performance, spatial reasoning, generalization to new letters and block appearances, multi-step planning, transfer to physical robots, and frontier models that act through tools. Users can easily design their own tasks and measures to investigate other questions—for example, whether a model performs better when it selects objects by pointing or by issuing text commands such as "pick the yellow block."

Low-level action models: VLA spatial generalization

Low-level action models, such as vision-language-action models (VLAs), map language instructions and visual observations to robot actions.

The premise of VLAs is that, by pretraining on large-scale datasets, they can rapidly generalize to different scenarios or a specific workspace. However, evidence on how well these action models generalize remains conflicting. Some studies report that these action models are brittle to changes in inputs, such as different object layouts and lighting, whereas others show that VLAs generalize well. We argue that these studies often rely on real-world datasets with limited flexibility in spatial variations. ToyBlocks enables us to test how well action models generalize in a simple, easily reproducible setting with meaningful task-space diversity.

We design generalization tests that vary the skill sequences needed to complete an instruction, the letters or colors on the blocks, and the number of blocks in a scene. A stacking study can withhold four-block stacks from training, then test whether a model can combine familiar movements to build them. Workspace studies distinguish performance at new positions within a training region from performance beyond its boundaries, where the model has to extrapolate. We illustrate the study setup and findings below.

We consider four tasks: Stack, Unstack, Flip, and Rotate. For these tasks, we study interpolation (new configurations within the training range) and extrapolation (configurations beyond that range). For example, we evaluate generalization by training on scenarios where objects spawn only in the left region (green) and testing on the right region (orange), or by training on stack heights of 2 and 5 blocks and testing on heights 3 and 4.

Spatial generalization studies for VLA models (results based on ManiFlow, π0.5, and MolmoAct 2). Despite large-scale pretraining, these popular action models generalize poorly in the initial results. We improve generalization and analyze the contribution of each technique. The chart’s LoRA label stands for low-rank adaptation, a method for fine-tuning a model with a small set of trainable weight updates. We believe action model generalization remains far from solved; ToyBlocks provides a valuable testbed for systematically exploring generalization techniques.

High-level reasoning: vision-language models

Long-horizon tasks, which require many steps, allow us to measure how well models can plan a sequence of actions to solve them. Our framework enables us to create such long-horizon tasks, and create oracles – reference components that provide correct plans or actions – at both the high and low levels. This allows us to isolate whether the high-level planning or low-level execution failed when a model fails at a task. An example long-horizon task might be to spell “Ai2” with a block stack; because the letters may not be immediately visible, the agent must first choose actions that reveal information, and then plan and execute a sequence of actions to build the stack.

We evaluate hierarchical models with explicit high-level planning and low-level execution models. In this instance, we choose Molmo 2, a vision-language model (VLM), as the high-level planner, and ManiFlow as the low-level policy. Molmo 2 chooses the skill to execute and the block to execute it on, while the low-level model executes the instruction. We train low-level models such as ManiFlow to pause after completing the execution and query the high-level model for the next instruction. We evaluate the model’s planning abilities on three scenarios of increasing difficulty. The easiest scenario initializes with each character upright and facing the camera. The medium scenario has characters that may not be upright, and the hardest scenario contains characters that are not visible at the start of the episode.

Success rates on three-letter block-spelling tasks using Molmo 2 as the high-level reasoning model and either ManiFlow or a motion planner for low-level manipulation. An example task is “Stack Ai2”. Molmo 2 and ManiFlow are trained on ToyBlocks and evaluated across three difficulty settings and two generalization conditions.

High-level reasoning: agentic systems

Our experiments with agentic systems test how frontier models plan and act through tool calls. We study three settings using Claude Opus 5.5. In the search-and-spell setting, we expose ToyBlocks skills through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), a standard for connecting AI applications to tools. The agent sees the scene through camera images, calls skills such as pick, flip, or rotate by pointing at a pixel, and decides when to search, build, or declare the task complete or impossible. The same MCP tools can execute either the scripted skills that generate ToyBlocks demonstrations (motion-planned pick and place, plus RL-based rotate and flip) or learned ManiFlow skills. ToyBlocks includes the framework behind these experiments, which also powers the natural-language web interface described earlier.

A frontier model (Claude Fable 5.1) controls a robot in a ToyBlocks world to search for and stack blocks into a tower spelling “Ai2.” During the episode, the agent muses, “I need to figure out whether pick-and-place naturally straightens orientation or if I need to correct it manually… I have 63 calls left, plenty to run a controlled test” (0:06). The agent later hypothesizes: “…maybe the gripper’s yaw is radial—pointing from the robot base toward the block” (0:15) and eventually confirms this hypothesis (0:26) before constructing the three-block tower, but the ‘A’ is sideways (1:11). Surprisingly, current frontier models often make similar perceptual errors (see the next figure), despite their impressive planning, spatial reasoning, and search capabilities.

For classical planning, the agent (our system using Claude Opus 5.5 to plan and choose actions) solves all 30 of a group of block-stacking tasks similar to ones that frontier models struggled with a few years ago, using text descriptions. It also solves 30 out of 30 while repeatedly observing camera images and choosing its next action in a closed loop.

In the search-and-spell setting, the agent had to generate stacks spelling out three-letter words. It had to find the blocks with the corresponding letters among up to eight blocks in the scene. Importantly, 50% of the scenes did not have blocks with all the required letters, rendering the task infeasible. In this case, we required the agent to state that the task is infeasible. We found that in this experiment, the agent was able to successfully solve or correctly declare infeasible 63% of the tasks. Errors were mostly caused by the agent confusing letters with look-alike letters (13%) or choosing an incorrect orientation for a letter in a stack (15%).

Our results also show that the agent was able to solve the task more efficiently when the blocks had semantic regularities, or patterns, taking advantage of such patterns to reason about occluded faces. For instance, in most of the infeasible scenes, when the blocks had no patterns, the agent correctly looked at all the blocks’ faces before declaring infeasibility, whereas it was able to declare infeasibility significantly faster when the blocks had semantic patterns.

Our third experimental setting asks whether an agent can learn how its skills behave, using experiments as a scientist would. When a skill behaves unexpectedly, the agent forms a hypothesis, designs a small test, and revises its understanding from the result. We expand on this idea by having an agent run its own experiments and write its own skill descriptions based on what it finds. These learned descriptions raise success rates from 24% with the default descriptions to 63%, outperforming the 36% achieved with descriptions written by a human expert.

Share of letter-block faces the agent had exposed by the end of each “search and spell” episode (bars averaged over 20 episodes; one marker per episode, styled by outcome). In a feasible task every letter of the three-letter target word is present; in an infeasible task, one letter is missing and the agent should say so. Each patterned block carries uppercase and lowercase instances of a letter, plus images that begin with the letter (e.g., A-block: apple, ant, A, 1, airplane, a); an unpatterned block’s six faces are randomized and unrelated. Correct: the tower spelled the word, or for infeasible tasks, the agent correctly declared the task impossible. Letter rotated or look-alike: the agent built the tower, but a letter was turned or a look-alike substituted, including five infeasible tasks declared solved with a look-alike in the missing letter’s place. Block fell out of reach; reported: a needed block was pushed out of the arm’s reach, so the agent reported that its task had become impossible. No report: the agent used up its motor-skill budget and stopped without claiming either outcome. With patterned blocks, the agent finishes having seen fewer faces, because it can infer what hidden faces must depict rather than checking every one.

Action-conditioned world models as simulators

Action-conditioned world models are trained to predict how a scene changes in response to a robot’s actions. Using them as an alternative to model-based simulators for training and evaluating robot policies is an active area of research. How well they serve this purpose depends on how accurately they predict physical interactions, which is hard to measure without knowing the true state of the scene. ToyBlocks provides this ground truth – the actual simulated scene state – enabling highly controlled tests of how recently developed world models perform in low-level object manipulation. Here, the arm’s end effector is its gripper.

Specifically, we tested whether action-conditioned world models are capable of predicting the motions of blocks or the outcomes of skill executions after being trained on example executions. To do so, we chose four different skills (pick-and-place, flip, rotate, and a mixed task) and generated 900 trajectories – sequences of robot states and actions over time – for each skill. 50% of these trajectories were successful demonstrations of the skill, and 50% were unsuccessful because of small changes to spatial configurations. With equal numbers of successful and unsuccessful executions, a model that always predicts success would be correct only half the time. The models were fine-tuned on these demonstrations and then tested on their ability to predict the outcome of action sequences of the same skills.

We find that Wan 2.2 predicts block motion and task outcomes most accurately. Astra tracks the gripper well but struggles to simulate contact. LeWM is fast and more accurate over short interaction segments, though it drifts over full trajectories. In additional experiments, we also showed that models that score higher on pose and success prediction also produce better training data: adding 100 model-generated trajectories (rollouts) from the best video-generation model raises a policy’s success in an unseen region from 19% to 78%.

We tested three types of models: a video prediction model with 5 billion parameters (Wan 2.2), an agentic model that created its own physics simulator tuned to match the demonstration data (Astra), and a latent world model (LeWM). During testing, each trained model has to predict future images, simulator states, or latent states (learned internal representations), respectively, based on an initial image and a sequence of actions. For full trajectories, models use the initial image as the only observed image, along with the action sequence. For short interaction segments – a single pick, place, flip, or rotate – models start from the real image immediately before that interaction. Full trajectories show how errors accumulate over long horizons, while interaction segments isolate a single interaction, such as the gripper making contact with a block, and show how well the model predicts it. To compare models fairly, we probe each model’s predictions, reading out where it expects the blocks and gripper to be at different points in the trajectory and whether it expects the task to succeed at the end.

Real-world experiments with high- and low-level models

Sim-to-real evaluations test policies trained in simulation on physical robots performing block manipulation tasks. By comparing simulation and real-world execution, we assess whether behaviors and failure patterns observed in simulation provide meaningful indications of real-world performance. For example, researchers can evaluate individual skills and their composition in longer-horizon tasks to identify where failures arise and whether these patterns carry over to physical deployments.

We test whether the models trained entirely on ToyBlocks simulation datasets can be deployed in the real world zero-shot, without training on real-world examples. We evaluate ManiFlow and each low-level skill (pick, place, flip, and rotate) individually. We test whether the hierarchical system (Molmo 2 + ManiFlow) can complete long-horizon three-block spelling tasks requiring sequences of these actions. Real-world experiments use a Franka FR3 arm with a Robotiq gripper across thirty scene configurations. Each scene contains 4–10 blocks seen during training. An episode is successful only if the relevant blocks are moved to target poses without collisions. If the operator intervenes to stop the robot due to an unsafe motion during an episode, it is marked as a failure.

ManiFlow’s atomic-skill success rates were similar in simulation and the real world (80.0% and 81.1%). The hierarchical Molmo 2 + ManiFlow system succeeded in 55.5% of simulated episodes (111/200) and 50.0% of real-world episodes (15/30); further trials are needed to establish statistical confidence across tasks.

Success rates of the ManiFlow low-level model and the hierarchical Molmo 2–ManiFlow system in simulation and the real world. For ManiFlow, the total count represents individual skill executions (pick, place, flip, and rotate), whereas for Molmo 2–ManiFlow, it represents block-spelling task episodes. The Molmo 2–ManiFlow evaluations use the easiest scene configuration defined in the simulation evaluation, with block characters visible and upright.

Side-by-side real-world and simulated block-stacking executions using the same high-level planner. Pink rings mark the planner’s target point for each skill. The scenes use different block labels, and simulation playback is retimed to align grasps and releases with the real robot.

To transfer Molmo 2 and ManiFlow – both trained exclusively on ToyBlocks data – to a physical robot, we address the differences between simulation and reality in three stages.

Before data generation, we perform system identification by tuning simulated robot parameters, including joint friction and armature (the motor and gearbox inertia reflected at the joint), to match real-robot trajectories. During data generation, we randomize physical properties (object size, friction, and table height) and visual properties (lighting, backgrounds, materials, and camera parameters). At inference time, observations are captured using a front-facing ZED camera and a wrist-mounted ZED Mini. For policies that use depth images, we generate clean depth maps, which estimate distance at each pixel, from paired red-green-blue (RGB) camera images using FastFoundationStereo, rather than relying on noisy depth sensor measurements.

The physical ToyBlocks setup: a robot arm, wooden blocks, and a camera.

Opening the tools for further research

ToyBlocks connects data generation, training, and evaluation in one controlled setting, so researchers can investigate how robots learn over time and test how changes to a model or its training data affect robot behavior. We’re releasing simulation assets, procedural task and demonstration generators, automatically generated demonstrations, two trained models showcasing what the framework can do (one based on Molmo 2 and one based on ManiFlow), training code, and evaluation code and validation sets. This allows other teams to build their own training mixtures and investigate failure modes beyond those covered in our initial experiments.

Our initial data release is a proof point with 85,336 long-horizon demonstrations, each comprising about 6–12 skill demonstrations, depending on the set. The initial datasets cover nearly 1,600 hours of robot execution data and 144 million frames. In a few weeks, we're targeting a second release with a larger-scale dataset, more skills, and more comprehensive benchmarking. We’ll also add fully integrated RL training capability that is not contained in the current package.

Other directions for ToyBlocks include bimanual (two-arm) manipulation and dexterous robot hands, equipped with force and touch sensors for studying motion and tasks that involve frequent physical contact. We're also exploring play with unstructured piles of blocks as a way to collect data and study how new behaviors and tasks might emerge through interaction.

Future direction: RL-based pile manipulation.

Future direction: bimanual block manipulation.

With ToyBlocks, we want to advance the science of robot learning toward a future where robots can reliably apply what they've learned to unfamiliar tasks and environments. We encourage the research community to explore ToyBlocks for their own investigations and even as a basis to build their own FoundationWorlds.

item.title: [Hugging Face] Egyptian and Nigerian English join the Open ASR Leaderboard
item.content:encoded:
Back to Articles

Egyptian and Nigerian English join the Open ASR Leaderboard

Published November 6, 2026

Update on GitHub

5

Eric Bezzam

bezzam

Ashley Mo

ashleymo2025

liva-ai

Aoi Otani

aonorii

liva-ai

A few months ago, we added private data to the Open ASR Leaderboard: 11 splits from Appen and DataOceanAI covering scripted and conversational speech from five accents (blog). The community response was great, with many highlighting the importance of held-out sets for trustworthy evaluations. Since then, we added one more private split for Indian-accented English with Voice Arena (blog).

We’re excited to announce a new collaboration with Liva AI to add even more private data with two new accents: Egyptian 🇪🇬 and Nigerian 🇳🇬.

DatasetAccentDuration [h]StyleTranscription
Liva AI Conversational EGEgyptian1.34Conversational, spontaneousPunctuated, cased, with disfluencies.
Liva AI Conversational NGNigerian1.55Conversational, spontaneousPunctuated, cased, with disfluencies.

This is part of our continued effort to improve representation in ASR evals (more accents and more languages) and to improve trust (new private data to minimize benchmaxxing, and new data providers). We’re excited to see the community continuing to push ASR performance for the world 🤗

Richer accent breakdown in the Private tab

With these new accents, we can now present a richer breakdown of accents, based on Kachru’s Three Circles (kudos to Hume AI for this idea in their leaderboard). The Open ASR Leaderboard will now report:

  • US vs. non-US (UK, Australia, Canada, India, Nigeria, Egypt)
  • Inner Circle (US, UK, Australia, Canada) vs. Outer & Expanding Circles (India, Nigeria, Egypt)

As more accents join, we’ll split the Outer and Expanding Circles.

About Liva AI

Liva AI collects multimodal interaction data through consumer products used by real people. Because Liva owns both the collection environment and distribution, it can design products around specific model gaps across domains, industries, languages, modalities, and interaction types. This gives it access to natural, high-context behavior that emerges through real product use, rather than artificially elicited or task-based interactions.

item.title: [OpenRouter] Introducing the New Auto and Auto Code Routers
item.content:encoded:
Introducing the New Auto and Auto Code Routers

Brian Thomas ·11/6/2026

Today we’re launching the next generation of Auto Router. Taking all we’ve learned from running Auto Router for the past 3 years, we rebuilt it from the ground up on an entirely new technical foundation that outperforms the old router by up to 4× depending on the benchmark, with a routing step that is 3× faster at the p90 in our live test (0.65s against 1.96s).

It’s easier for a router to score well on benchmarks than to perform well in practice. Auto Router sees over 2.5T tokens from over 100k people every month, so it has to hold up in the real world.

This launch includes a brand new router specialized for coding work, Auto Code (openrouter/auto-code), alongside our flagship general purpose Auto Router (openrouter/auto).

Try it now by setting model to openrouter/auto or openrouter/auto-code in any request, or open Auto Router in the chatroom. Check out the Auto Router docs for all the details.

What’s new in this generation

The previous Auto Router relied on a couple of imprecise signals, such as task type, to drive model selection, a limit required to keep latency low and judgments consistent. The new Auto Router and Auto Code choose models by weighing eleven factors about each request and combining them with live pricing, provider health, and cache status.

This new process lets Auto Router work with any set of models. You can apply any governance policies, including guardrails, zero data retention requirements, provider restrictions, allowed model lists, and BYOK keys. Auto Router makes efficient choices from the models available to you.

We introduced the new Auto Code router based on feedback about what it was like to use a general purpose router in a coding harness. This router is tuned from the ground up for coding performance by including a higher tier of coding models and optimizing for latency. Across the five benchmarks below, Auto Code scores in line with Claude Opus 5.5 while costing 74% less per task.

In the previous generation, we also observed that the remarkable efficiency of the lowest cost models had caused Auto router to drift lower on cost per task, leaving out many exceptional models. We made a decision with this release to return to pricing closer to where Auto was a few months ago in order to introduce a greater variety of models. If you preferred the previous behavior, you can set the cost_tier to low to get similar cost performance.

See the reasoning behind routing decisions in the chatroom

The easiest way to start learning how these new routers work is to pick Auto Router or Auto Code in the chatroom. A routing insights panel appears beside each reply showing why the router picked that model. The same analysis is available via the API when you enable router metadata.

Watch the live routing mix on each model page

The Auto Router and Auto Code model pages now show which models each router picks most often, split by session type, and how the mix shifts as difficulty rises.

Compare performance against other routers and single models

Auto Router and Auto Code benchmark results are published on the model routing benchmarks page alongside the other routers on OpenRouter and single-model baselines. We rerun them periodically, so you can track how each router keeps up as new models are released.

Built upon years of lessons from running Auto Router

Auto Router is coming up on its third birthday. If you set openrouter/auto in an agent years ago, you’re still getting the latest cost-optimal choice today. We’ve learned a lot about where automatic model selection goes wrong, and built the new generation to avoid those problems. Some examples:

We separated out Auto Code to optimize for harnesses. The most common complaint about previous versions of Auto Router was how it performed in coding harnesses. Auto Code favors a slightly more expensive tier of models whose strengths match coding work. It weighs speed more heavily because responsiveness matters while you build. It also penalizes failures more harshly, so it course corrects faster on work where success and failure are clear cut.

It’s restrained about switching to protect caching benefits. Switching models costs extra while the new model rebuilds the input token cache. Auto Router favors a change in reasoning effort when that’s enough, and switches only when the gain is worth the cache it gives up. In our beta period it stayed on the same model for nearly nine of every ten agent turns.

It adapts to failures. When a session is going wrong in ways that point at the model, such as the same error coming back or tests failing after an edit, those signals raise the odds of a switch. That makes it much less likely a session stays stuck with a model that was the wrong pick early on.

It’s tuned based on both real usage as well as benchmarks. Auto Router gets better with every benchmark run and every real routing decision it sees. Through typesafe/jev-router and openrouter/auto-beta we have already verified it on production workloads, while respecting zero data retention throughout. In our beta, against the previous router, invalid tool calls were 4× lower and agentic responses were cut off half as often.

Model Routing built upon the leading Provider Routing foundation

Model routers like Auto Router and Auto Code pick which model will process the request. Provider routing picks who will serve that model. OpenRouter has done this for every request since the beginning: once the model is picked, the provider router chooses among the providers hosting it using your provider preferences, live uptime and latency, price, and whether a provider already holds your prompt cache.

A model router can only be as good as the underlying provider router. We built Auto Router to be aware of our entire catalog, so it adapts to governance restrictions, benchmark results, and market signal from new model releases as they happen. Every one of the 600+ models on OpenRouter enters the consideration set the day it’s added, and benchmarks and popularity signals decide whether it earns a place in the cost-optimal set.

How a request moves through Auto Router

  • Auto Router narrows the model pool. Guardrails, zero data retention, model capabilities, provider restrictions, BYOK keys, and any allowed or excluded model lists decide which models are considered.
  • A fast decision model processes the request. In one call it rates eleven things, such as what kind of task this is, whether the task just changed, how hard it is, whether speed matters, whether it needs vision or knowledge of a codebase, and whether a bigger model, more thinking, or a cheaper model would serve it better.
  • The routing policy chooses the model. It weighs live prices, cache status, and benchmark performance to pick both the model and the reasoning effort.
  • The request goes through the same provider routing a direct request to that model would, so it lands on the best provider for that model.
  • The results of each turn inform the next turn’s model selection. The router carries signals like whether the model is struggling and what’s already cached into the next decision.

Routers versus single models

Benchmarks consistently show that no router on the market beats the single best frontier model at every point on the cost and quality curve. The new Auto Router is no exception, and we publish its benchmarks to show its strengths and weaknesses plainly.

Routers earn their place when the work is varied, when an organization needs to hold costs steady, and for people who don’t have the time or interest to keep up with the constant stream of model releases. Choosing Auto Router or Auto Code over a single model trades a little peak performance for consistent, cost efficient performance over time.

If you know the model that works best for your specific work, keep using it. If you’d rather choose once and stay focused on the work itself, a router is the way to do that.

Get started

Auto Router and Auto Code work wherever you’d put a model string:

curl https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $OPENROUTER_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "model": "openrouter/auto-code",
    "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Add a retry with backoff to fetchUser in api/users.ts"}]
  }'

Read the Auto Router docs for the full settings, or open Auto Router in the chatroom and send it the prompt you’d normally hand-pick a model for. Tell us what it gets right and wrong in #feedback on Discord.

Frequently asked questions

What do I need to change to switch from the old Auto Router?

Nothing at all. The slug is still openrouter/auto and the auto-router plugin settings cost_tier, allowed_models, and excluded_models still work.

What is the difference between Auto Router and Auto Code?

Both run on the same routing engine. Auto Router is the general purpose router for mixed traffic and general agents, and favors a cost-efficient tier of models. Auto Code is specialized for coding agents and harnesses, starts in a higher cost tier, and weighs measured pass rate, speed, and cost per solved task across models and reasoning efforts.

Is model routing the same as provider routing?

No. Model routing picks which model handles a request; provider routing picks which provider serves that model. Auto Router and Auto Code do the first, then OpenRouter’s provider routing does the second with your provider preferences, uptime data, and prompt cache state.

Do the routers respect my guardrails and data policies?

Yes. Guardrail policies, zero data retention requirements, provider restrictions, allowed and excluded model lists, and BYOK keys define the model pool, and the router picks the cost optimal model inside it.

Does a router cost extra?

No. You pay the standard price of whichever model serves the request, and the response’s model field tells you which one it was.

What is openrouter/auto-beta?

Auto Router Beta is the release channel for the next version of Auto Router. New routing changes ship to openrouter/auto-beta first and graduate to openrouter/auto once they prove out, so use it to see what is coming in advance. If you try it, tell us what it gets right and wrong in #feedback on Discord.

item.title: [Amazon Bedrock] SageMaker Inference now supports Multi-Instance GPU to maxim…
item.description: Full title: SageMaker Inference now supports Multi-Instance GPU to maximize GPU utilization for model endpoints
item.content:encoded:
Artificial Intelligence

SageMaker Inference now supports Multi-Instance GPU to maximize GPU utilization for model endpoints

When you deploy a model to a GPU endpoint, the smallest unit of GPU you can request is one whole accelerator.

This constraint can cost you twice. First, you can’t host more models on an instance than it has accelerators. An ml.p4d.24xlarge has eight A100s, so it holds eight models, whether each one needs 40 GB or 14 GB. Second, and less obvious, it makes every deployment come down to a choice of which full GPU to deploy to. As your concurrency and prompt lengths grow, a full GPU on an older instance stops being enough, but a full GPU on a newer one is more than your model can use. You end up either under-served or paying for capability you never reach.

Today, Amazon SageMaker Inference supports GPU partitioning, which uses NVIDIA Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) to divide a physical GPU into independent partitions. Each partition receives a fixed share of the GPU’s compute units and a dedicated block of its memory, with isolation enforced in hardware. That changes both constraints: you can place a different model in each partition, and you can choose a fraction of a newer accelerator instead of a whole one of either generation.

This post covers both. The first part is the direct benefit: deploy more models than you have GPUs, with isolation between them. The second is the one customers ask about when the question turns to cost: how the granularity of partitioning helps you pick the right-sized unit, and what we measured when we did.

One thing to know before you read further: GPU partitioning works on endpoints that use inference components, the construct you use to deploy several models to one endpoint and set the compute each model gets. Partitioning builds directly on it. A partition is a resource a component asks for, in the same place it already asks for CPU and memory. If you haven’t used inference components, this post introduces them. Single-model endpoints, serverless endpoints, and heterogeneous instance pools cannot be partitioned.

What customers do today, and why each option falls short

If you have more models than accelerators, you have had three choices.

Run fewer, larger endpoints and batch harder – This raises utilization, but only when the models are interchangeable. A portfolio of fine-tuned variants or per-tenant models is not.

Use multi-model endpoints – These load and unload models from a shared GPU on demand, which fits sparse, bursty traffic. But models share the device without isolation, so a heavy request for one model affects the others. A model that isn’t loaded also pays a load penalty on first use.

Move to self-managed Kubernetes – This is where customers who need real GPU partitioning have gone. MIG works there, but you take on driver versioning, partition configuration, a device plugin, scheduling, and keeping it all consistent across a fleet. That’s a lot of work for a hardware capability your instances already have.

Why MIG

NVIDIA Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) splits one GPU into as many as seven instances, depending on the GPU. Each instance has its own compute, cache, memory and memory bandwidth. Because the split is in hardware rather than software, you get guarantees that other sharing methods can’t give:

  • Predictable latency – Each partition has dedicated memory bandwidth, so one model’s traffic spike doesn’t show up in another model’s p99.
  • Fault isolation – A crash or memory error stays inside its partition instead of taking down every model on the GPU.
  • Right-sized capacity – Small and mid-sized models get a slice that fits them instead of a whole GPU. You can mix slice sizes on one device.
  • No cold starts – Every model keeps its own partition and stays loaded, with no load penalty and no eviction.
  • Tenant isolation – Memory protection between partitions is enforced in hardware, which makes security and compliance reviews simpler.
  • Reliable planning and chargeback – A partition performs the same way regardless of its neighbors, so load tests predict production. GPU cost also maps cleanly to a model, team or tenant.

Partitioning has boundaries worth knowing up front. The maximum number of partitions depends on the accelerator and never exceeds seven. MIG itself only allows a layout to change while its partitions are idle, and on SageMaker AI that means choosing a layout when you create the endpoint. A model that needs more than one GPU still needs whole devices. Within those boundaries, you get the isolation of separate GPUs without dedicating one to each model.

Partitioning without the platform work

Until now, getting MIG meant running the Kubernetes stack yourself. GPU partitioning on Amazon SageMaker AI removes that step: you pick a partition profile for your model, and SageMaker AI handles GPU configuration, placement and scaling. You get hardware-isolated GPU sharing on a managed endpoint, without having to run the platform underneath it.

Salesforce has been part of this work from the start, helping define the requirements and validating the initial implementation.

“NVIDIA MIG partitions a single GPU into multiple isolated instances, each with dedicated compute and memory resources. Salesforce sees this as an important capability because many inference workloads do not require an entire GPU. MIG would allow us to consolidate workloads safely, significantly improve GPU utilization, reduce inference costs, and maintain predictable performance and strong isolation.
This capability would help us scale AI Inference more efficiently across different use cases. Salesforce has helped define requirements, validated the initial solution. We are now preparing to validate the solution with representative production workload and demonstrate strong customer demand with AWS. We believe MIG support would deliver meaningful technical and business value for enterprise customers.”
— Richard Chang, Software Engineering Architect, Salesforce

How it works

GPU partitioning adds two optional fields to API calls you already make. There are no new API operations, no new resource types, and no new AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) actions, and an endpoint that omits both fields behaves exactly as it does today.

AcceleratorPartitionLayouts goes on a production variant in CreateEndpointConfig and declares how each accelerator is divided:

{
  "EndpointConfigName": "multi-model-partitioned",
  "ExecutionRoleArn": "<execution-role-arn>",
  "ProductionVariants": [
    {
      "VariantName": "AllTraffic",
      "InstanceType": "ml.p4d.24xlarge",
      "InitialInstanceCount": 1,
      "AcceleratorPartitionLayouts": [
        { "AcceleratorPartitionTypes": ["mig-4g.20gb", "mig-2g.10gb", "mig-1g.5gb"] }
      ]
    }
  ]
}

An A100 has seven compute slices to divide. The preceding layout uses all seven, so each of the eight A100s on the p4d instance carries three partitions and the endpoint provides 24, eight of each type.

The carve applies uniformly. One layout entry describes how one accelerator is divided, and every accelerator on every instance in the variant is divided the same way. The list isn’t positional, so an entry doesn’t map to a specific GPU.

AcceleratorPartitionType goes on an inference component and selects which partition the model runs on:

{
  "InferenceComponentName": "summarizer",
  "EndpointName": "multi-model-partitioned",
  "VariantName": "AllTraffic",
  "Specification": {
    "ModelName": "summarizer-model",
    "ComputeResourceRequirements": {
      "AcceleratorPartitionType": "mig-4g.20gb",
      "NumberOfAcceleratorDevicesRequired": 1,
      "NumberOfCpuCoresRequired": 1,
      "MinMemoryRequiredInMb": 2048
    }
  },
  "RuntimeConfig": { "CopyCount": 1 }
}

Each component copy occupies one partition of the requested type. With eight partitions of each type on the instance, raising CopyCount places additional copies on free partitions. This is useful for a small model serving high concurrency, where a single process leaves the GPU waiting on requests.

NumberOfAcceleratorDevicesRequired is always 1 here. With a partition type set it means one partition rather than one accelerator. NumberOfCpuCoresRequired and MinMemoryRequiredInMb still describe host CPU and host memory, because GPU memory comes from the partition type.

Invocation doesn’t change. InvokeEndpoint addresses a model by inference component name, and the partition it occupies never appears in the request.

Partitioning happens while the endpoint is provisioned. When it reaches InService every accelerator is carved and the partitions are empty, which is a valid state as components land on them afterward. In our testing, carving accelerators added roughly 17 seconds to provisioning. The rest of the time is the usual instance launch and container pull.

Partition profiles by GPU

The profiles available to you are a property of the GPU, so start by finding out which GPU your instance type carries and look it up in NVIDIA’s supported MIG profiles, which is the authority on the full profile set and the combinations valid on one device.

Instance familyAcceleratorGPU memoryGranularity (compute / memory)Available partition profilesMax partitions per GPU
P4dNVIDIA A10040 GB7 / 8mig-1g.5gb, mig-1g.10gb (see driver note), mig-2g.10gb, mig-3g.20gb, mig-4g.20gb, mig-7g.40gb7
P5NVIDIA H10080 GB7 / 8mig-1g.10gb, mig-1g.20gb, mig-2g.20gb, mig-3g.40gb, mig-4g.40gb, mig-7g.80gb7
G7NVIDIA RTX PRO 4500 Blackwell32 GB2 / 2mig-1g.16gb, mig-2g.32gb2
G7eNVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition96 GB4 / 4mig-1g.24gb, mig-2g.48gb, mig-4g.96gb4

Read the profile name as compute units followed by GPU memory: mig-3g.40gb takes three compute units and 40 GB. The granularity column is what limits a layout. An A100 and an H100 divide into sevenths on compute and eighths on memory, while G7 divides into halves and G7e into quarters. Profile names differ between GPUs even where the slice counts match, so don’t carry a layout from one instance family to another without checking it against this table.

Within those limits you have real choice. On a P4d or P5 you can carve seven of the smallest profile, or two 3g partitions, or the 4g plus 2g plus 1g layout used in the earlier example, or take the whole device as one. On a G7e you can take four of the smallest, or two 1g beside a 2g, or two 2g, or one whole device. On a G7, either two partitions or one.

The 3g profile is the one to know, because its two dimensions don’t match: it takes three of the seven compute units but four of the eight memory units. Two of them fill the GPU and nothing else will fit beside them.

The high-level rule: Every profile in your layout must be one your GPU offers, and the compute and memory units your profiles add up to must not exceed what one device provides. Both are checked when you create the endpoint configuration, and either one failing is a rejection rather than a fallback to a whole accelerator.

Driver note for P4d: mig-1g.10gb requires an R525 or newer NVIDIA driver, and the default P4d image ships 470.256.02. Request it on the default image and the carve fails without an error naming the profile. Set InferenceAmiVersion to al2023-ami-sagemaker-inference-gpu-4-1 on the production variant to get an image on the 580 driver line, which offers it.

Choosing a layout for your workload

Choosing well is a separate question from choosing a layout that is merely accepted. A partition hands you compute and memory in fixed proportions, and the two do different jobs during inference.

Compute units are what you need for prefill. Prefill reads the prompt and builds its representation. This is the compute-heavy phase, and it scales with the streaming multiprocessors, and so the TFLOPs, your partition holds. The longer your inputs and the more prompts arriving at once, the more it governs how quickly you return a first token.

Memory units are what you need for decode and for capacity. Generating tokens re-reads the model weights on every step, so decode is bounded by memory bandwidth rather than by math, and memory also caps how much KV cache you can hold. That cap in turn sets the context length you can serve and how many sequences you can serve concurrently.

Almost no real workload exercises only one of these, so the goal isn’t to pick a dimension but to choose a combination that supports your use case. Choose a profile whose proportions cover your heaviest phase while leaving the other adequately served. On the compute side, what matters is how long your prompts are and how many arrive at once. On the memory side, it’s your output length, your context window, and your concurrency.

Memory is the easier of the two to underestimate, because a partition has to hold three things and not just the model: the weights, which for an 8B model at FP16 are about 16 GB. The KV cache, sized for the context length and the number of concurrent sequences you intend to allow, which is the term people leave out and the one that grows with traffic. And 1–2 GB of runtime overhead for the CUDA context and the serving process. Add those up before choosing a profile, because a partition sized to the weights alone will load the model and then fail under load, or quietly serve a much shorter context than you configured. For a concrete reference point, that same 8B model at FP16 comfortably serves an 8,000-token context on a 40 GB partition.

Where MIG adds the most value

A portfolio of small and mid-size models – The direct case. Fine-tuned variants, embedding models, rerankers, and classifiers that each leave most of an accelerator unused now share one.

Multi-tenant model serving – When you host a model per customer, MIG gives you a hardware boundary between them: a process in one partition can’t read another partition’s memory or take its throughput. Scope the claim accurately, though. Models on the same instance still share host CPU, system memory, storage, networking, and endpoint routing, so partitioning is an isolation mechanism for the GPU and not a complete tenancy boundary.

Multi-stage pipelines on one instance – A transcription model, a diarization model, and a language model, or an embedder, a reranker, and a generator. Each stage is a separately addressable component on its own partition, and a network hop between stages disappears.

A small model in the request path – A safety classifier or guardrail model that has to run on every request but cannot justify an accelerator, with predictable latency because it isn’t time-slicing against the main model.

Challengers and canaries – Run a candidate model on a small partition beside the model serving production traffic instead of standing up a second endpoint.

Performance: A slice of a newer GPU against a whole older one

In addition to bin-packing, the other benefit you get is granularity on high-end GPUs: more GPU options to deploy a model onto, and the choice of which one is yours. Every supported accelerator becomes several sizes rather than one, so the practical way to think about it is that each profile is a GPU option in its own right, sitting alongside the whole accelerators you already choose between. That matters most when you are considering a larger or newer instance type, because moving up stops being all-or-nothing: you can take as much or as little of that bigger GPU as your workload needs, at any of the sizes it publishes, instead of paying for the whole accelerator.

To see whether that pays off, we compared one mig-3g.40gb partition of an H100 against one whole, uncarved A100-40GB. The two have comparable GPU memory, which makes it a clean way to see how powerful a slice of a more advanced instance can be.

We used genai-bench to generate load, driving both endpoints from the same client so the GPU is the only variable. Both sides ran Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on production SageMaker real-time endpoints, one model replica each, with an identical container image, tokenizer, and client configuration. Both were invoked through the SageMaker AI native OpenAI-compatible route. We swept five traffic shapes, written D(input tokens, output tokens) and ranging from short prompts to long-context summarization, each across a concurrency ladder from 2 to 512.

Figure 1: Aggregate output tokens per second for one mig-3g.40gb partition of an H100 against one full A100-40GB, across five traffic shapes and a concurrency ladder from 2 to 512

Figure 2: Partition cost benefit per million output tokens against concurrency for the same five traffic shapes

Four things stand out.

  • The partition is faster everywhere – It delivered more output tokens per second in every scenario at every concurrency, by 53 percent to 89 percent at the load where each scenario’s cost benefit is largest, and lower inter-token latency in every one too, by 8.9 percent to 42.1 percent. The gap widens with load.
  • Time to first token is lower in every case, by 5.6 percent to 47.5 percent.
  • On cost it’s 18–34 percent cheaper per million output tokens, above a crossover that moves earlier as prompts lengthen. Concurrency 64 for 100-token prompts, 4 for 8,000-token prompts. Below the crossover the whole A100 is the cheaper unit. These prices are all on-demand, which at the time of analysis were measured as $25.251286 per hour for an ml.p4d.24xlarge and $63.296000 per hour for an ml.p5.48xlarge in the US West (Oregon) AWS Region. Purely for our own analysis, we derived the unit cost by dividing the whole-instance cost by the number of units on it: 8 on the p4d, and 16 on the p5, where our partition is half of a GPU.
  • At the top of the ladder on long-context traffic, the A100 stopped serving. On both the 6,000- and 8,000-token workloads it failed a third to a half of its requests against a serving-path deadline, while the partition failed none. That is why those two panels end earlier than the rest.

Treat this as a case-by-case comparison, not a verdict. The useful mental model is to regard the available GPU fractions as GPU types in their own right. List them alongside whole accelerators, work out what your traffic actually demands of compute and of memory, and compare them on your own workload. For high-concurrency, long-input traffic the partition won on both performance and cost here. For short-input or low-concurrency workloads the whole A100 remained cheaper. Partitioning isn’t a one-size-fits-all answer. It gives you more sizes to choose from, so you can pick the one that fits your workload.

What to know before you commit to a layout

Partitioning changes the shape of an endpoint, and a few properties are worth understanding before you design one.

A component’s partition type is fixed for the life of that component. Moving a model to a different profile means creating a new component. Changing the endpoint’s carve means a new endpoint and a traffic migration, because updating an endpoint configuration doesn’t re-carve hosts that are already running. This makes partitioning a good fit for a stable portfolio and a poor one for a mix you reshuffle daily.

A requested profile has to exist in the endpoint’s layout. There is no fallback to a whole accelerator, so a component asking for a profile the variant didn’t declare is rejected.

Partitioning applies to real-time inference on inference component endpoints. Serverless endpoints and heterogeneous instance pools aren’t supported, and asynchronous invocation cannot address an inference component, so async workloads are out of scope.

You’re billed for the full GPU instance, as you are today. Partitioning raises how much of that instance you can use. It doesn’t change its hourly price.

Finally, a model that genuinely needs a full accelerator, or more than one, should keep having one. No partition spans accelerators.

Supported instances and Regions

GPU partitioning is available on the P4d, P5, G7, and G7e instance families. Support is at the family level, so smaller sizes within a family are covered.

It’s available in the following AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), US West (Oregon), Asia Pacific (Singapore), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), Europe (Frankfurt), and Europe (Ireland).

Instance availability varies by Region, so confirm that your chosen instance type is offered in your Region and that you have endpoint usage quota for it.

Getting started

To partition a GPU endpoint, work out the memory and compute each of your model’s needs, pick the profiles that fit, declare a layout on your endpoint configuration, and deploy each model as an inference component that requests a profile from that layout. Nothing about how you invoke your models changes.

For the API reference, the full profile tables for each instance family, and a step-by-step walkthrough, see GPU partitioning in the Amazon SageMaker AI Developer Guide.

To try it yourself, run the GPU partitioning sample notebook, which deploys several models onto partitions of a single GPU endpoint.

The broader change is worth keeping in mind as you plan capacity. Every supported accelerator is now several sizes rather than one. Whether a partition of a newer GPU or a whole accelerator of an older one is the right unit for a given model is no longer a question you need to answer by rounding up. It’s one you can measure.

About the authors

item.title: [Amazon Bedrock] Taxonomy of agentic primitives in AWS Quick
item.content:encoded:
Artificial Intelligence

Taxonomy of agentic primitives in Amazon Quick

Over the past year, as we built Amazon Quick, our agents went from answering questions to taking actions: scheduling meetings, running research, generating reports. As the system evolved, one problem kept resurfacing: there was no shared definition of the primitives that agentic work is built from. The same few ideas kept getting rebuilt under different names: an actor that does the work, a signal that starts it, a packaged procedure, and a memory that carries lessons forward. This repetition leaked into product design and onto the user.

Take the user who says “monitor my Slack channel and send me a daily digest”. Is that a new agent, a scheduled instruction to an existing one, a workflow, or a skill? These are different questions, but without a shared vocabulary they collapse into one confusing choice.

This post shares the taxonomy we converged on: one set of primitives found by decomposing agentic work into four plain questions: When?, What?, Who?, and How? Most of the framework stays invisible to end users by design, but a shared vocabulary makes the system easier to reason about for anyone building beneath it.

The framework at a glance

Figure 1: How triggers, agents, and capabilities relate, with learning feeding back from the session runtime

A trigger starts the work and carries the task (When and What), an agent takes it on (Who) and uses its capabilities (tools, skills, and workflows) to perform the task (How). This post describes these primitives and how they relate to one another. It’s the first post in a series, and upcoming posts cover our agentic operating system, background learning, proactive feeds, and much more.

Triggers: What causes work to begin

Triggers are the activation mechanism for getting work done, but they also carry instructions: a human message is both the moment of activation and the description of what to do. They are both the When? and the What? of a task.

  • Human-initiated: A person opens a conversation and asks the agent to do something. Interactive, synchronous, conversational.
  • Agent-delegated: One agent, mid-task, invokes another to handle a sub-problem. Programmatic, composable, potentially recursive.
  • Scheduled: Time-based activation, like “run financial research every Monday at 9am.” Deterministic, with the same standing instructions applied across runs.
  • Event-driven: A signal from an external system, such as a new email, a Slack mention, a file change, or a webhook.

The type of trigger conditions the execution: a scheduled background task might stay conservative (for example, do nothing if uncertain), while a human-initiated one would be responsive (for example, ask rather than stop).

Agents

We define an agent as a persistent, learning actor. It’s the Who? in any execution, and the anchor against which learning accrues. Two agents given identical input can differ, because they carry different instructions, capabilities, and histories. The agent isn’t the instructions it follows. It’s the entity that interprets them. It consists of three things:

  • Instructions: Standing guidance defining persona, role, context files, and operating principles. A Finance Agent behaves differently from a general assistant primarily because of this.
  • Capabilities: The tools, skills, workflows, and sub-agents available for use, updated dynamically. A charting library can be added in one session and removed the next.
  • Learned context: Memory that accumulates through use: the queries that work for a tool, the formatting users prefer, the edge cases they care about. This is how the tenth execution beats the first without anyone changing the instructions.

Everything else is extrinsic: the large language model (LLM) underlying the agent is a swappable model parameter, conversation history is per-session state, and triggers belong to the platform.

A consequence of this definition is that a user request “I want an agent that monitors my Slack and sends a digest every morning” is usually a trigger added to an existing agent, not a new agent or workflow. With this framing, we can merge chat, scheduled, and “autonomous” agents into one actor that you can converse with, schedule, and that can orchestrate and inspect its own past work.

Capabilities

Capabilities are How an agent acts, spanning a spectrum from fully agentic to fully deterministic. That axis is really a confidence contract: how much latitude the agent keeps versus how much the user fixes in advance.

Tools are atomic operations with a typed schema: send an email, query a database, read a file. Whether a local function, a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, or another agent behind a protocol boundary, the caller sees the same interface: name, description, parameters, result.

Skills are structured guidance with room for judgment: instructions bundled with resources (templates, scripts, examples) that describe an approach rather than a rigid sequence. They load through progressive disclosure, so the agent sees only names and short descriptions until one becomes relevant, then reads the full instructions in. A skill can therefore bundle arbitrary depth of expertise without a constant cost.

Workflows are deterministic coordination: declared steps, control flow, branching, and error handling that execute in fixed order, with decision logic in code rather than model inference. Think of a purchase-approval route: budget check, manager sign-off, then finance, each recorded. The route is fixed, but the judgment inside a step is still the agent’s.

Figure 2: Skills versus workflows, which differ in whether the agent or the code decides the step order

Why skills and workflows outlast model improvements

A natural question arises: if models keep improving, won’t skills and workflows become unnecessary? We don’t think so, because each holds value independent of model capability. Skills are the unit for capturing, versioning, and sharing institutional expertise, while workflows deliver auditability, step-wise visibility, and deterministic multi-service coordination. Nor are they fixed: a well-understood skill can tighten into a workflow (crystallization), a workflow that keeps hitting edge cases can loosen back into a skill (dissolution). This is done in Quick through our continuous learning framework, which we will describe in a future post.

What this means in practice

Return to “monitor my Slack channel and send me a daily digest”. Because these primitives compose, the same request can be met several valid ways:

  • A scheduled task with a one-line instruction, leaving the agent to figure out the rest.
  • The same task backed by a skill with explicit formatting rules and channel priorities.
