item.title: [AI21 Labs] Introducing Teel – Turbo-Efficient Execution Library for Age…
item.description: Full title: Introducing Teel – Turbo-Efficient Execution Library for Agents (but not only)
item.content:encoded:
In Brief

Teel is an open source Python runtime that overlaps independent IO-bound calls in code you wrote sequentially. No *async**, no await**, no futures, no gather**. Mark expensive functions with @cacheable**, mark orchestration with @jit**, and a magic shadow interpreter reads ahead through your bytecode, finds calls whose arguments are already known, and dispatches them on background threads before the main thread arrives. On Princeton’s Tree of Thoughts, unmodified: 83% less runtime on average, and 8.07x on the longest run. 19% faster on average than LLM-generated async JavaScript inside a Deep Agents coding agent. Check the repo: github.com/AI21Labs/teel*

Figure 1: Same code, different schedule. In plain Python, each search waits for the one before it. With Teel, the three independent searches run at once, and summarize and check start as soon as their inputs are ready.

Why this matters for agents

Agent quality right now comes mostly from spending more compute at inference. Run an ensemble. Generate five candidate patches instead of one. Split a task across N subagents and merge what they come back with. Different techniques, one execution shape underneath: fan out a lot of independent, IO-bound work, then join it back.

Our recent results on BrowseComp-Plus, SWE-rebench and DeepResearch Bench II came from three unrelated techniques and drew the same picture at the compute level: many independent rollouts, retrievals, tool calls or whole agent runs, overlapping, then merged.

And more and more, the agent writes that orchestration itself. In LangChain’s Deep Agents, the model writes a short script that dispatches its own subagents, instead of calling them one tool call at a time. Whoever writes it, all that fan-out comes with a price. Agent swarms take it furthest: Moonshot’s Kimi Agent Swarm runs up to 300 sub-agents in parallel and reports finishing tasks about 4.5x faster than a single agent.

The problem

When we profiled our agents’ runs, most of the wall clock was a thread sitting on a socket: model calls, retrievals, tool calls, a shell exec in a sandbox. Shaving the main agent code barely moved the total. The leverage is in the waits that do not depend on each other.

In Python, overlapping those waits means rewriting your code first. To run two calls at once you make them async. Then every function that calls them has to become async too, and so does every function that calls those. A change you wanted in one place climbs the whole call chain, until orchestration logic and concurrency plumbing are the same lines of code. Every new fan-out means doing it again. And when a model writes that code, it has to get all of it right on every run.

Here’s a small code-review agent three ways: as written, rewritten with asyncio, and as written plus Teel’s decorators. It asks a model for the worst bug in each changed file, asks whether those findings should block the merge, then either requests changes or approves.

Figure 2: One code-review agent written three ways: plain Python (7.1s), rewritten with asyncio (3.0s), and the original code with Teel’s decorators (2.9s). The asyncio version needs three tasks, two cancellations and a finally block to match what Teel does on its own.

Versions 2 and 3 finish in about the same time, 3.0s and 2.9s against 7.1s sequential. Both get there the same way: they start both possible follow-ups before the verdict is in, and keep whichever one it picks. Teel does that on its own, by following both branches of the if while the verdict is still pending. The asyncio version does it by hand, with three tasks, two cancellations, a finally block, and an async twin of every function it calls. The difference isn’t the concurrency. It’s who has to find it and manage it.

That’s why we built Teel. Concurrency shouldn’t have to be part of the code a developer, or an agent, writes. It can be the runtime’s job. You write the sequential version. Teel reads your function’s bytecode ahead of the line currently running, spots calls that aren’t waiting on anything, and starts them early on background threads. By the time your code reaches them, the results are already there or on their way.

Results

WorkloadBaselineWith TeelSpeedup
Tree-of-thoughts-llm (longest run)307s38s8.07x
RLM in LangChain Deep Agents (sync Python)150s58s2.58x
RLM in LangChain Deep Agents (async JS)71s58s1.22x

Tree of Thoughts, unmodified. We ran Princeton’s tree-of-thoughts-llm on Game of 24 samples with GPT-4 without editing the repo: @jit, @cacheable and @inline were applied from the outside. It is a textbook fan-out written as textbook sequential code (generate candidates, evaluate, keep the best, recurse), and the original walks independent siblings one at a time. Average runtime reduction was 83%, from 148s down to 24s at the low end and 307s down to 38s at the high end.

Code the model writes at runtime. LangChain’s Deep Agents ships a dcode agent with a js_eval tool: the model solves a task by emitting a snippet that runs in a QuickJS sandbox. The snippet can call tools.web_search() and spawn subagents via task(), so the model is authoring a fan-out on the fly. But it authors it in async JavaScript, which hands the concurrency model to the model itself, and models are inconsistent at reaching for Promise.all.

We forked Deep Agents and swapped the snippet language for synchronous Python under Teel, expecting simpler generated code at some cost in speed. It came out faster instead: across ten mixed web-search-and-LLM prompts, 58s average against 71s for the async JS and 150s for the same Python run sequentially. Teel parallelizes the independent calls the model forgot to overlap, and speculatively runs fallback branches ahead of the decision that needs them. (The same prompt yields different code each time, so this compares distributions of generated programs, not two implementations of one.) Our fork is at github.com/AI21Labs/deepagents.

The API

There are three decorators and a context manager. Teel currently needs Python 3.12.13 exactly; Known limits explains why.

1from teel import cacheable, jit, Teel
2
3@cacheable                     # a discrete, expensive, parallelizable step:
4def fetch(url): ...            # an LLM call, an HTTP request, a retrieval
5
6@cacheable
7def summarize(text): ...
8
9@jit                           # orchestration Teel is allowed to analyze
10def research(a, b):
11    pa = fetch(a)              # no dependency between these two
12    pb = fetch(b)              # Teel runs them at the same time
13    return summarize(pa + pb)  # waits only for what it truly needs
14
15with Teel():                             # inside this context, independent
16    answer = research("a.txt", "b.txt")  # calls overlap - no async in sight

@cacheable marks the heavy functions worth dispatching early. Results are memoized on a key built from json.dumps of the arguments, so keep those arguments JSON-serializable and boring.

@jit marks the functions Teel is allowed to look inside. This is your orchestration layer.

@inline is optional. It marks cheap helpers (string formatting, dict digging) that Teel may actually execute during lookahead, which usually uncovers more @cacheable calls to dispatch ahead of time.

with Teel(): turns it on. Outside the context every decorated function runs as plain Python, untouched.

How it works

Why bytecode? Teel’s implementation is strange enough that the path there is worth 30 seconds, because each step explains the next. Every step kept the same execution idea, independent calls running in parallel, and changed only the interface you wrote orchestration in.

The first version ran orchestration on Celery. Canvas signatures gave us a real DAG the cluster could schedule: utilization up, runs resumable, orchestration finally separate from computation. It was also miserable to write, because orchestration is business logic and Celery makes you write business logic in a pipe-and-signature dialect that is not quite Python.

So we brought it back into Python, or into a restricted subset of Python. We parsed that subset with ast, compiled it into an execution graph and wrote our own executor. The graph paid off on its own terms: independent functions ran in parallel, if bodies could be entered speculatively before the test resolved, and a call like func(x, y) could push into its subcalls while x and y were still pending. All of it available only for the slice of the language we were willing to parse.

Giving up the restriction meant giving up ast. Bytecode is the level at which every Python program looks the same.

How does a runtime know what you are about to call? When a @jit function runs, Teel duplicates the execution state into a limited shadow interpreter and steps through the bytecode your main thread hasn’t reached yet. It works on its own copy, so your program’s state is left alone.

Does Teel build a dependency graph? No. The ast version did. Teel never needs the whole graph, only one answer per call: are this call’s arguments ready yet? Any value it can’t compute yet, like the result of a @cacheable call still in flight, is marked pending, and anything computed from a pending value is pending too:

1pa  = fetch(a)        # arguments known: dispatched now, pa is pending
2pb  = fetch(b)        # arguments known: dispatched now, pb is pending
3s   = pa + pb         # built from pending values: pending
4out = summarize(s)    # pending argument: not dispatched yet

When lookahead reaches a @cacheable call with no pending arguments, Teel dispatches it to a ThreadPoolExecutor and memoizes the result. When your code reaches that line for real, the answer is already there or on its way. Two calls that don’t consume each other’s results never wait on each other, which is why fan-out needs no special support: [answer(q) for q in sub_questions] dispatches every answer(q) whose question is already known. Parallelism is the default, and you opt out by creating a real data dependency.

How does it get at your program’s state? Teel grabs the frame stack with sys._getframe(), uses a small C extension (frameinspect) to pull each frame’s full value stack out of CPython, and reads f_lasti to find the last instruction that was actually executed. That’s where the shadow interpreter starts stepping forward.

Getting to that state is a cursed operation. Reading a live frame’s value stack is not something CPython offers you, which is why frameinspect compiles against CPython’s internal headers and the whole thing is pinned to one exact interpreter version. The full walkthrough, opcode by opcode, is in the README’s Under the hood section.

The contract

What you promise. Teel does three things a normal interpreter never does: it runs a function earlier than your code would, sometimes runs one your code would never reach, and hands back a saved result instead of running it again. Each is only legal if the function does not care when it runs or how often. Picture a @cacheable function that sends an email or charges a card: Teel might run it for a branch your program never takes, and nothing unsends the email. That is the @cacheable contract, and it is on you: no database writes, no reading the clock, no hidden state, and JSON-serializable arguments, because json.dumps of them is the memo key. @jit promises nothing. It is permission to read your bytecode, not a claim about what the function does.

What Teel promises. The same call runs once: pending and finished tasks are keyed by function plus arguments, so a second lookahead that discovers the same fetch(url) attaches to the first instead of firing another request. Failed calls are dropped rather than cached, on the assumption the failure was transient.

And a wrong guess costs time and tokens, not correctness. The shadow interpreter never produces your answer. CPython still executes your function to completion, instruction for instruction, exactly as it would without Teel, and the only difference is that some calls find their result already in the cache. Guess wrong and you burned a background call, plus its tokens if it was an LLM call. Guess nothing and you pay full sequential price. Break the purity contract, though, and you own the result. That is the one failure mode Teel cannot protect you from.

Observability: where the wall clock actually went

When the runtime decides what runs early, you need a way to see what it decided. Give the context a path and Teel records the run:

1with Teel(trace_path="teel-trace.json"):
2    research("a.txt", "b.txt")
3
4# open teel-trace.json at https://ui.perfetto.dev/

The output is a Chrome trace-event file, so Perfetto renders it as a timeline: one bar per @cacheable call, on the thread that ran it, with start time and duration, and overlapping work showing up as bars side by side.

Per-call is the granularity that starts to matter once you dial test-time compute up and down. A result on a hard agentic benchmark is rarely a single number anymore: our BrowseComp-Plus work reported a frontier of accuracy against cost and latency, so a team can read off the quality it can afford. You cannot chart a latency frontier you can only measure end to end.

To measure the speedup, run the same code twice. A @cacheable function runs untouched with no active context, so the baseline is not a separate sequential implementation, it is the identical program.

1# timed(label) runs research("a.txt", "b.txt") and prints its wall clock
2
3baseline = timed("sequential")       # no context, plain Python
4
5with Teel():
6    optimized = timed("with Teel")   # same code, now overlapped
7
8assert baseline == optimized         # same answer, different clock

Where this goes

Parallelism and observability both follow from one decision: the run is a set of calls keyed by their arguments. Take that one step further and an agent run stops being a disposable process and becomes reusable data. Persist the results and a later run can be served from them: unchanged calls are hits, and any call an edited input flows into gets a new key and re-runs. That gives you crash resume, debugging against pinned outputs, and iterating on orchestration without re-paying for every tool call. It also gives you human-in-the-loop: an agent freezes its state at a decision point, a person reviews, and the run resumes hours later on a different host.

Known limits

This is a proof of concept with two sharp edges. It’s pinned to Python 3.12.13 exactly, because frameinspect compiles against CPython’s internal headers. And the GIL still applies: background calls run on a ThreadPoolExecutor, so IO, network calls and GIL-free work like NumPy overlap fine, but for CPU-bound, GIL-constrained work, no dice.

Clone it, decorate your own functions, wrap your entry point, and start with the README: github.com/AI21Labs/teel

item.title: [Anyscale] How Lila Sciences and Anyscale Scaled GLM-5.3-Flash Training…
item.description: Full title: How Lila Sciences and Anyscale Scaled GLM-5.3-Flash Training to 1M tokens
item.content:encoded:
HomeBlogBlog Detail

How Lila Sciences and Anyscale Scaled GLM-5.3-Flash Training to 1M tokens

By SkyRL Team and Lila Sciences' AI Research Team | November 5, 2026

Lila Sciences and Anyscale trained GLM-5.3-Flash, an open model, on 1 million tokens per sequence using 64 B200 GPUs. That's 64x longer than the training stack could handle when we started, and every change is open source in SkyRL. Our team for SkyRL at Anyscale worked closely with Lila Science researchers on their infrastructure on an open source stack to explore the research path on increasing context length for this particular model.

Scientific data is long by nature. A genome, a family of related protein or RNA sequences, or the record of an experiment run over several days loses the structure that matters when it is cut into a few thousand tokens. AI that runs science in a closed loop with an autonomous lab has the same need: across rounds of hypotheses, protocols and instrument readouts, its context grows to hundreds of thousands of tokens.

Many open models now support 1M-token context, but they may not have out of the box performance for the target task at large context values. Closing that gap means training on the task's own data at its full length, without cutting or heavily compacting the context. This work set out to do it with an open model and an open training stack.

The result, at a glance:

  • 1M tokens per sequence fits in 144.5 GiB per GPU, under the B200's 178 GiB.
  • 13.7k tokens/s at 1M, and a peak of 24.9k tokens/s at 256k, on 64 B200s.
  • The model uses the context: fine-tuned on the human genome, its loss improves most on tokens with hundreds of thousands of tokens of context before them.
  • Open source: the recipe is in SkyRL, and several fixes are going upstream to Megatron-LM.

LinkHow do we reach 1M tokens context on GLM 5.3 Flash?

GLM-5.3-Flash is a hybrid model: 34 of its 45 layers use linear attention (Kimi Delta Attention), and 11 use DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA). It also uses a residual stream that's 4x wider than usual, and mixture-of-experts (MoE) layers. Each of these needed its own work. Memory grows with sequence length in every layer, and in attention it grows with the square of the length, so each optimization only pushes the limit out until the next one is hit. We did several optimizations all which are covered in detail with their own experiments and PRs in the original post.

Every optimization is load-bearing

Most of what we ran into is not specific to GLM and can be applied to models sharing the same type of components:

  • Check that each layer runs the kernel you think it does: GLM's sparse attention layers were silently falling back to dense attention, because the fused kernels only accepted DeepSeek's exact tensor shapes. Nothing raised an error; the run simply used 114 GiB per GPU at 16k and ran out of memory at 32k. Padding the tensors to fit the sparse kernel halved memory.
  • Sparse attention moves the quadratic cost; it doesn't remove it. DSA attends to only 2,048 tokens per query, but choosing those tokens means scoring every query against the whole sequence. Computing that score matrix a few hundred queries at a time keeps it under 2 GiB, and splitting the scoring across GPUs instead of repeating it on each one made the full training step 2.1x faster at 256k.
  • Every memory fix costs throughput, so use only what the length needs. Full recompute, CPU offloading and context parallelism each buy more context for some speed. Offloading, for example, cuts peak memory at 256k from 142 to 98 GiB but adds 21% to step time. We turn each one on only at the length where training wouldn't fit without it.
  • Benchmarks on random tokens underestimate memory for MoE models. Real text distribution routes unevenly across experts: on a real long context dataset, the busiest GPU received about 4x the average number of tokens, and 512k ran out of memory where random-token runs fit easily. Processing the MoE layer over the sequence in chunks fixed it. Test memory on real data before sizing a cluster.
  • Plan host memory, not just GPU memory. At 1M tokens, the layer inputs offloaded to CPU come to about 180 GB per GPU before context parallelism, over 1 TB per 8-GPU node, and they share host RAM with the optimizer state. Use pinned memory for the copies (they were 22% faster than pageable memory) and release it every step.
  • Verify correctness separately from speed. Speed and memory numbers can come from random weights, but correctness can't. In RL runs with the real weights, the trainer's log-probabilities matched vLLM's to within 0.04 -- 0.07 (mean absolute difference) from 128k to 1M tokens, and an overfit test drove loss from 1.65 to 0.17 in 20 steps.

With combination of these ideas we were able to maintain a good throughput across different context lengths

Training throughput, 16k -> 1M tokens

LinkTraining Results

We post-trained on the human genome at 512k tokens per sequence, the model's held-out loss fell 4.8% in 80 steps, and the gain was largest on tokens with the most context before them. That last part is the evidence that it learned to use long context, not just local patterns.

We trained on chromosomes 1 and 2 of the human reference genome (hg38) and evaluated on chromosome 22, which the model never saw. DNA is a good test because it has structure at every scale, from short motifs to patterns spanning very long stretches.

To separate long-range learning from local learning, we split the held-out loss by token position, in 32k-token buckets, and compared it before and after fine-tuning:

  • Early tokens have little context before them, so any improvement there comes from local patterns such as short motifs and base composition.
  • Late tokens have up to 500k tokens of context before them.
  • Local learning helps every position equally, so a larger improvement at late positions has to come from the long context that only they have.

Loss before and after fine-tuning

LinkRunning on Anyscale

Every experiment in this post ran on Ray, managed by the Anyscale platform, on a 64-GPU B200 cluster in Lila's cloud. SkyRL uses Ray to place and coordinate its training and inference workers, so the same setup ran memory benchmarks on random tokens, fine-tuning on real data, and RL runs that check the trainer against vLLM.

For a more in-depth look at the specific techniques used to support long-context see this detailed blog post.

Table of contents

  • How do we reach 1M tokens context on GLM 5.3 Flash?
  • Training Results
  • Running on Anyscale

item.content:encoded:
We’ve added new agents and products to Claude Marketplace, where teams find partner tools and services to help them get more from Claude. The additions cover security, developer infrastructure, creative, and productivity.

Eligible enterprise customers can apply a portion of their committed Anthropic spend toward these solutions. This lets them use one commitment across Claude and partner products, whether they’re buying something new or expanding with a platform they already use.

There are now over 25 partner agents and products on the marketplace. Here are the latest additions and what teams can do with them.

Products and agents for securing code and systems

Chainguard: Chainguard Harness builds applications from source in an isolated microVM and probes the live app for exploitable vulnerabilities. It helps teams fix what Claude finds, with custom remediation recommendations for reproducible vulnerabilities.

Checkmarx: Checkmarx One pairs rules-based analysis with AI reasoning to find vulnerabilities in code. It helps teams prioritize findings and fix them before code ships.

Cyera: Cyera Agent Guardian inventories Claude deployments, governs permissions before Claude runs, and enforces policy on prompts, files, and tool calls. It helps teams test those controls through red teaming.

Rubrik: Rubrik Code Guardian uses frontier AI models from Anthropic to review a secure copy of GitHub or Azure DevOps repositories for multi-step attack paths. It helps security and engineering teams rank issues by severity and turn confirmed critical ones into tracked tickets.

Tanium: Tanium Cloud gives teams real-time visibility and control across their endpoints. It helps IT and security teams find and fix vulnerabilities, misconfigurations, and missing patches.

Development infrastructure for engineering teams

Datadog: Datadog Agent Observability traces agent execution through tools and services. It helps teams improve agent quality, performance, and cost efficiency by surfacing production patterns and recommending fixes.

Netlify: Netlify Enterprise deploys apps, sites, and agents to a global edge network, with preview URLs on every change. It helps teams take what they build with Claude from prototype to production with no infrastructure to configure, and includes SSO, role-based access, and audit logs.

Tools for marketing and creative work

AirOps: AirOps provides an agentic platform for AI search strategy, content, and multichannel execution. It helps marketing teams analyze brand performance in AI search and tie results to pipeline and revenue.

Runway: Runway generates and edits video, images, and audio. It helps creative and marketing teams turn a brief into finished assets and edit footage with natural language.

Webflow: Webflow provides built-in tools to build, manage, and optimize websites. It helps marketers, designers, developers, and agents make changes, with controls and governance built in.

Productivity apps for every team

Asana: Asana AI Teammates are prebuilt agents that use context from the Asana Work Graph, each with its own identity, scoped permissions, and audit trail. They help teams handle multi-step work, routing decisions that need judgment to the owner.

Glean: Glean connects company knowledge and workflows across systems. It helps employees find answers and complete multi-step tasks across connected apps.

monday: monday agents work inside projects, boards, docs, and meetings, using their owners and deadlines as context. They help PMO, IT, marketing, finance, and operations teams control what AI can access, approve, and spend.

Zoom: Zoom Agentic Search answers questions inside Claude using the latest meeting summaries, work conversations, documents, and connected third-party sources. Teams get permission-aware results without analyzing raw transcripts or chaining tools together.

Get started

You can browse all agents and products on Claude Marketplace and request to buy from any listing. If you’re building on Claude and want to join the marketplace, see the ways to join.

item.title: [Cohere] Embed 5 and Rerank 5 now on OpenRouterAccess Cohere’s state-…
item.description: Full title: Embed 5 and Rerank 5 now on OpenRouterAccess Cohere’s state-of-the-art retrieval models through a single API, with unified billing and no additional SDKs.
item.content:encoded:
Nov 04, 2026

6 minute read

Embed 5 and Rerank 5 now on OpenRouter

Access Cohere’s state-of-the-art retrieval models through a single API, with unified billing and no additional SDKs.

Embed 5 and Rerank 5 are now live on OpenRouter. Here’s how to turn them into a working RAG pipeline in a few dozen lines of Python code through a single API.

There are Cohere’s most powerful retrieval models yet, delivering leading performance on enterprise documents and complex retrieval tasks. If you’re already using OpenRouter, you can get started immediately - using the same API key and credits as your existing models, with no additional setup.

RAG grounds an LLM's answer in your own data by fetching relevant chunks before it writes. Embedding search provides a fast and effective first-stage approximation. A reranker then reads the query and each candidate together, adding precision to what’s been retrieved.

Two features of the Cohere models shape this design:

  • Embed 5 Pro and Fast share one embedding space. Index with embed-5-pro for quality, then query with embed-5-fast for latency.
  • Rerank 5 scores are calibrated. A score means the same thing across queries and domains, so one relevance threshold can filter out weak context before it reaches the LLM.

By the end you'll have a short Python script that answers questions over your docs with scored citations. This same approach can be applied to virtually any retrieval use case, from enterprise search and customer support to knowledge management and document discovery.

A RAG pipeline has two halves: an offline job that builds a searchable index, and an online path that runs for every question. Knowing which calls happen once and which happen per request help explain most of the pipeline's cost and latency. Indexing runs once per corpus. Each question then costs one Embed 5 Fast call, one Rerank 5 call and one chat call, all through OpenRouter's API.

Setup

You’ll need Python 3.10 or newer, an OpenRouter API key, the OpenRouter Python SDK, and NumPy for an in-memory vector store.

pip install openrouter numpy
export OPENROUTER_API_KEY="sk-or-..."
import os
import numpy as np
from openrouter import OpenRouter

client = OpenRouter(api_key=os.environ["OPENROUTER_API_KEY"])

EMBED_INDEX_MODEL = "cohere/embed-5-pro"   # indexing: highest quality
EMBED_QUERY_MODEL = "cohere/embed-5-fast"  # queries: lowest latency
RERANK_MODEL      = "cohere/rerank-5-pro"  # or cohere/rerank-5-fast
CHAT_MODEL        = "deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash-1017"       # any chat model on OpenRouter
DIMS = 1024                                    # 256 | 512 | 768 | 1024 | 1536 | 2048

Embed 5 returns Matryoshka vectors at six sizes, 2048 by default. We suggest 1,024-dim int8 vectors as the best quality-to-cost point; OpenRouter's embeddings API returns floats, so this post uses 1,024-dim floats.

The NumPy store keeps this demo simple. For production, replace it with your preferred vector database, such as pgvector, Qdrant, Pinecone, or Weaviate.

Indexing

Indexing turns each chunk of text into a vector, a list of numbers where similar meanings sit close together. It runs once per corpus, so it's the step where the highest-quality model pays off.

Split each document into chunks, embed them with Embed 5 Pro as search_document, and normalize the vectors so a dot product equals cosine similarity.

The sample corpus is a fictional API's docs, with a few near-misses on purpose:

docs = [
    {"title": "Rotating API keys",
     "text": "To rotate a key without downtime, create a second key, deploy it to every service, "
             "confirm traffic on the new key in the usage dashboard, then revoke the old key."},
    {"title": "Creating API keys",
     "text": "Create keys under Settings > API Keys. Each key can be scoped to read or write and to one project."},
    {"title": "Revoking API keys",
     "text": "Revoking a key takes effect immediately. Requests with a revoked key return 401 Unauthorized."},
    {"title": "Webhook signing secrets",
     "text": "Rotate your webhook signing secret from the Webhooks page. The old secret stays valid "
             "for 24 hours so you can update your verifier."},
    {"title": "Log rotation",
     "text": "Request logs rotate daily and are kept for 30 days. Export them to S3 for longer retention."},
    {"title": "Rate limits",
     "text": "Each API key is limited to 600 requests per minute. Going over returns 429 Too Many Requests."},
]
def chunk(doc, max_chars=1500):
    """Split on blank lines, packing paragraphs up to ~max_chars."""
    out, buf = [], ""
    for para in doc["text"].split("\n\n"):
        if buf and len(buf) + len(para) > max_chars:
            out.append({"title": doc["title"], "text": buf.strip()})
            buf = ""
        buf += para + "\n\n"
    if buf.strip():
        out.append({"title": doc["title"], "text": buf.strip()})
    return out

def embed(texts, model, input_type, batch=96):
    vecs = []
    for i in range(0, len(texts), batch):
        res = client.embeddings.generate(
            model=model,
            input=texts[i:i + batch],   # one request per batch
            input_type=input_type,      # "search_document" | "search_query"
            dimensions=DIMS,
        )
        vecs += [d.embedding for d in res.data]
    v = np.array(vecs, dtype=np.float32)
    return v / np.linalg.norm(v, axis=1, keepdims=True)

chunks = [c for d in docs for c in chunk(d)]
doc_vecs = embed([c["text"] for c in chunks], EMBED_INDEX_MODEL, "search_document")

Three key details to point out:

  • input_type: tells Embed 5 which side of the search a text is on. OpenRouter passes it through to Cohere.
  • Batching: sends many chunks per request, which cuts round trips and speeds up indexing. It doesn't change the cost, since embeddings are priced per token.
  • Chunk size: packing whole paragraphs follows the by-paragraph strategy in OpenRouter's guide, and 1,500 characters is roughly 300–400 tokens of English. Embed 5 accepts up to 128k tokens, but every chunk also goes through Rerank 5, which reads up to 32k tokens of query and chunk combined and splits anything longer into several passes.

Retrieval

Retrieval finds the chunks whose vectors sit closest to the question's vector. This acts as a representation of semantic similarity between the two pieces of content.

Embed the question with Embed 5 Fast as search_query, then pull a wide candidate set of 20 chunks by cosine similarity.

def retrieve(query, k=20):
    q = embed([query], EMBED_QUERY_MODEL, "search_query")[0]
    scores = doc_vecs @ q                 # cosine, since both sides are normalized
    top = np.argsort(-scores)[:k]
    return [(chunks[i], float(scores[i])) for i in top]

Querying a Pro-built index with Fast works because the two models share an embedding space, as long as both sides use the same dimensions. It's the split we recommend: in Cohere's tests across 40 datasets, Fast queries on a Pro index kept 98.4% of all-Pro retrieval quality, against 96.6% for Fast on both sides. With any other model family, you’d have to use the same model on both sides.

Let’s cast a wide net at this stage: recall is the retriever's job, precision is Rerank’s. OpenRouter's guide suggests 10–20 candidates feeding a top 3–5 rerank.

Reranking

Reranking re-scores the shortlist by reading the question and each chunk together. That's too slow to run over a whole index but more accurate than vector similarity, so it runs only on the top candidates. Rerank doesn’t require Embed - or any embedding model. It works as a simple second stage with your existing semantic, keyword, or hybrid search system.

Send the query and the 20 candidates to Rerank 5, keep the top 5, and drop anything under a relevance threshold.

MIN_SCORE = 0.3

def rerank(query, candidates, top_n=5):
    res = client.rerank.rerank(
        model=RERANK_MODEL,
        query=query,
        documents=[c["text"] for c, _ in candidates],
        top_n=top_n,
    )
    return [
        (candidates[r.index][0], r.relevance_score)
        for r in res.results          # sorted by relevance, highest first
        if r.relevance_score >= MIN_SCORE
    ]

Each result carries the candidate's position in your list (index) and a relevance_score, per the rerank response schema.

What Rerank 5 adds at this step:

  • Calibrated scores. Scores stay consistent across queries and domains, so a single MIN_SCORE decides what reaches the LLM.
  • 32k-token context. Long chunks are scored whole.
  • Semi-structured data. JSON records and tables rerank well when formatted as YAML strings.
  • No re-indexing to upgrade. Rerank reads raw text at query time, so switching models is a one-line change.

Use rerank-5-pro for reasoning-heavy queries and long or domain-specific documents. Use rerank-5-fast for high-volume search and agents that search many times per task. One thing to note: Rerank 5 is text-only, but will work for parsed pdfs.

Generation

Generation hands the best chunks to an LLM as numbered sources and asks it to answer from those alone. That keeps answers grounded in your docs and gives readers citations they can check. If nothing clears the threshold, skip the LLM call entirely.

SYSTEM = (
    "Answer using only the numbered sources. "
    "Cite them inline like [1]. "
    "If the sources don't contain the answer, say you don't know."
)

def answer(query):
    hits = rerank(query, retrieve(query))
    if not hits:
        return "I couldn't find that in the docs."

    sources = "\n\n".join(
        f"[{i}] {c['title']}\n{c['text']}" for i, (c, _) in enumerate(hits, 1)
    )
    res = client.chat.send(
        model=CHAT_MODEL,
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM},
            {"role": "user", "content": f"Sources:\n\n{sources}\n\nQuestion: {query}"},
        ],
    )
    return res.choices[0].message.content

print(answer("How do I rotate an API key without downtime?"))

Sending each chunk's title with its text lets the model cite something readable; add URLs too if your docs have them. OpenRouter's guide uses the Responses API for this step instead. To follow it, call client.responses.send with the system prompt as instructions and the sources and question as input, then read the answer from the message item in res.output rather than from choices.

Results

Here we’ll validate whether the steps we implemented improved our responses.

Reranking earns its extra call when it confidently picks the right chunk and drops near-misses that embedding search ranks just below it.

q = "How do I rotate an API key without downtime?"

cands = retrieve(q)
hits = rerank(q, cands)

print("Embedding only (top 3):")
for c, s in cands[:3]:
    print(f"  {s:.3f}  {c['title']}")

print("After Rerank 5:")
for c, s in hits:
    print(f"  {s:.3f}  {c['title']}")
RankEmbed 5 onlyEmbed 5 + Rerank 5
1Rotating API keys · 0.522Rotating API keys · 0.808
2Webhook signing secrets · 0.337below 0.3 cutoff
3Creating API keys · 0.316below 0.3 cutoff

Wrap-up

Everything in this pipeline ran through one API key and one client. Embed 5 Pro built the index, Embed 5 Fast and Rerank 5 handled each question, and a chat model wrote the answer, with no separate SDKs, accounts or bills to juggle.

That single surface is also what makes the pipeline easy to evolve. Every model is just a string, so trying rerank-5-fast instead of rerank-5-pro, or a different chat model, is a one-line change.

Start with the sample corpus, swap in your own docs, and see what Rerank 5 moves to the top.

Where to take it next:

  • Hybrid search. Add keyword (BM25) hits beside the vector hits. Rerank reads raw text, so it scores both lists in one call.
  • A smaller index. Drop to 512 or 256 dimensions, or use int8 or binary vectors through Cohere's own API.
  • Images and PDFs. Embed 5 embeds images and mixed text-and-image inputs such as PDF pages, and OpenRouter's embeddings API accepts image_url content parts. Rerank 5 is text-only, so rerank those results on their text, such as parsed page text or captions, or skip reranking for them.
  • Evaluation. Label a small set of real queries, compare hit rate at 5 with and without rerank, and tune MIN_SCORE on the same set.
  • Explore Compass. Cohere’s enterprise search and retrieval platform brings Embed and Rerank together in a single solution, making it easier to build powerful search and AI applications across enterprise data. Now available to cloud customers.

Useful links

  • OpenRouter embeddings API
  • OpenRouter Python SDK rerank
  • Embed 5 announcement blog
  • Rerank 5 announcement blog
  • Embed 5 benchmark results
  • Rerank 5 benchmark results

item.description: Full title: Dharma Field Extractor: Any Document In, Structured Fields in JSON Out
item.content:encoded:
Back to Articles

Dharma Field Extractor: Any Document In, Structured Fields in JSON Out

Team Article

Published November 4, 2026

15

Gabriel Pimenta de Freitas Cardoso

GabrielPimenta99

Dharma-AI

Paulo Henrique de Medeiros Araujo

Paulo-DharmaAI

Dharma-AI

Bruno Duarte

brunoduarte01

Dharma-AI

Francisco de Almeida Rocha Alves

falves9101

Dharma-AI

A 2-billion-parameter model that extracts exactly the fields you ask for, from any document type, outperforming every frontier LLM we tested, at a fraction of the cost.

In April, we released DharmaOCR-LITE, a model specialized for OCR across a wide range of documents, from contracts and court filings to invoices, IDs and forms. The paper behind it made a narrow, well-measured case for domain specialization: a smaller model trained closer to its task beating general-purpose frontier APIs on that task.

OCR gives you the text on a page, faithful to the original formatting. That's exactly what you want when the job is the whole document, like a contract you'll read end to end or a manuscript you're digitizing.

However, there's a different use case: you don't want the page, you want specific fields out of it, in a shape a system downstream can consume. Every line item on an invoice, as a list. The patient name, exam type and date from a medical requisition, ready to schedule. The fields off an ID, mapped to the columns of an employee record.

Run that document through OCR and you get back everything printed on it, line by line, with no indication of which string is the exam type, which is the date or which number is the total. Someone still has to write the code that maps each value to the right field before it reaches the database.

A general-purpose LLM can do this work today, with careful prompting. At frontier API pricing and latency, on a task many businesses need to run at high volume, that quickly becomes the expensive way to solve a well-defined problem.

So we built a model for it instead. The Field Extractor takes a document image and either a request for everything it can find, or an exact schema to fill, and returns structured JSON: typed, field by field, nested where the document nests. An invoice comes back with every line item as an ordered list, each with its own quantity and value, alongside the totals. An ID comes back as the fields you'll store, under the names your system already uses for them. The same checkpoint handles all of it, with no per-type fine-tuning.

You can try it yourself here.

What the Model Does

Say a batch of supplier invoices lands every morning, and you need four things off each one to push into your system: the supplier, the invoice number, the due date, the total. Same story for medical requisitions going into a scheduler, or contracts feeding a compliance system, where what matters is the parties, the term, the penalties and the fine amounts. You don't need the page, you need certain fields. With the Field Extractor there are two ways to ask for them:

  • Open: no schema supplied. The model reads the page and works out which parts of it are structured fields (a label followed by a value, a table with a header row over its columns) from context and layout, not from a fixed list of field names, and returns everything it finds as key-value pairs.
  • Schema-directed: you specify the exact shape wanted, field by field, with a type for each one (string, number, or boolean), under the key names your system already uses. Ask for "service_provider" and "client_company", and those are the exact keys that come back. Ask for a table and it fills it row by row, column by column, matching each cell to the key it belongs under. Ask for a field that isn't on the document, and it returns null instead of inventing a value.

The choice comes down to what you already know. Send an open request when you don't know what the document holds. Send a schema when the output has to match a shape that already exists somewhere else.

Either way, what comes back is JSON: the fields as keys, the values typed as requested, and null where the document didn't have what you asked for. When you send a schema, the output follows it exactly, with the same keys and no extra fields, so it can go straight into the next system.

How It Was Trained

The base model is DharmaOCR-LITE v1.1, a new 2-billion-parameter version optimized from the one in the paper and already specialized for OCR through supervised fine-tuning and DPO. On top of that checkpoint we trained a LoRA adapter on 43,384 training examples covering both request modes.

The data is organized into three streams:

  • English multi-domain data: diverse documents collected from the public web, spanning many document types.
  • Brazilian domain data: real Brazilian documents sourced internally, in Portuguese.
  • Multilingual data: a smaller share covering other European and Asian languages, for broader generalization beyond English and Portuguese.

All three streams are annotated at the field level. The mix is deliberately multi-domain: receipts, commercial invoices, forms, bank statements, ID documents and synthetic documents, rather than one filing type.

Where the Benchmark Draws the Line

The full benchmark covers 546 documents across three request scenarios, for 1,638 total cases: extracting every field with no schema, a partial schema naming only real fields, and a schema that also includes deliberately nonexistent fields. The score is field-level F1 (matched by path, including position inside a table), multiplied by the Levenshtein similarity on the values that matched and by the share of outputs that come back as valid JSON.

We ran the same benchmark against four general-purpose frontier configurations.

Against general-purpose LLMs, the quality gap runs from 1.8 points (Claude Opus 5, the closest) to 9.3 points (GPT-5.6 Luna, the widest).

Cost runs from roughly 6 times lower (GPT-5.6 Luna) to roughly 147 times lower (GPT-5.6 Sol). The two sides are priced differently. The frontier figures come from measured average input and output tokens per page, reasoning tokens included, against each provider's published list pricing. Every frontier model ran with reasoning set to low; Claude Opus 5 used adaptive effort, which can skip reasoning on simpler pages while staying at the low level. Ours isn't billed per token: the model runs self-hosted, so the figure is GPU time on a single L40S at $2.24 per hour.

This is not a sales price. Self-hosted cost depends on the hardware, the volume and the latency each deployment needs. The comparison is here to show that a sovereign SSLM, deployed on your own infrastructure, is a real alternative to frontier APIs.

A Test of Generalization

SROIE and FUNSD are two public datasets in our benchmark, not used in training. Below is one example from each.

On a SROIE receipt, we asked for all 18 fields printed on it, with no phantom fields this time, and every one comes back correct: the multi-line, unlabeled billing address captured as a single field, the two blank fields (salesperson and ref) correctly returned as null, and every number on the receipt matching to the cent.

On a FUNSD photocopying variance form, a checklist of twelve boolean fields with one nested group of five sub-options, the model marks exactly the one box that's checked (poor quality original, with a handwritten "faded" note beside it) as true, and the other eleven as false, matching the form exactly. It also reads the handwritten Bates ID off the page correctly, and returns null for the two fields left blank.

Quality and Cost, at the Same Time

A 2-billion-parameter model scored 0.834, above every frontier configuration we tested, from Claude Opus 5 at 0.816 to GPT-5.6 Luna at 0.741, while running on a single L40S at a lower cost per extraction than every API in the comparison. Higher quality and lower cost, measured on the same benchmark, in the same run.

This isn't the first time we've measured it. Our OCR paper put the first DharmaOCR-LITE, a 3-billion-parameter model, above every commercial frontier API tested on Brazilian Portuguese; three months later, newer and better-resourced models arrived, and the gap held. Now a 2-billion-parameter model does it on field extraction. Each result adds evidence for the thesis we started Dharma-AI with: on a bounded task, a small model trained close to that task beats a frontier model asked to do the same thing in general. In this benchmark, it also cost 6 to 147 times less to run.

Parameter count sets the ceiling; training decides how much of it a model reaches on your task. Your business doesn't need the biggest model available. It needs one trained for your problem.

Try it on your own documents here. To learn more about Dharma-AI and the specialized models we build, visit dharma-ai.com.

Sources

  • BID. Brazilian Identity Document Dataset. Soares, Neves Jr., Bezerra (2020), "BID Dataset: a challenge dataset for document processing tasks," Anais Estendidos XXXIII SIBGRAPI. github.com/ricardobnjunior/Brazilian-Identity-Document-Dataset
  • CORD. Park et al., NAVER CLOVA (2019). huggingface.co/datasets/naver-clova-ix/cord-v2
  • DocVQA. Mathew et al., WACV 2021 (ICDAR 2019). huggingface.co/datasets/lmms-lab/DocVQA
  • WildReceipt. Sun et al., IJCAI 2021. huggingface.co/datasets/Theivaprakasham/wildreceipt
  • SROIE (ICDAR 2019). Held out from training, evaluation only. huggingface.co/datasets/darentang/sroie (mirror); upstream rrc.cvc.uab.es/?ch=13
  • FUNSD. Jaume et al. Held out from training, evaluation only. huggingface.co/datasets/nielsr/funsd (mirror); guillaumejaume.github.io/FUNSD
  • Zenodo Invoices (PT). Cruz & Castelli, NOVA IMS (2022). zenodo.org/records/6371710
  • line_items. Sagarjha456, Hugging Face. huggingface.co/datasets/Sagarjha456/line_items
  • Katanaml Invoices (Donut). Kozłowski & Weichbroth (2021), Mendeley Data doi:10.17632/tnj49gpmtz.2. huggingface.co/datasets/katanaml-org/invoices-donut-data-v1
  • HumynLabs Brazilian Bills and Invoices. huggingface.co/datasets/HumynLabs/Brazilian_Bills_and_Invoices_Dataset
  • Tech4Humans BR-Doc Extraction. huggingface.co/datasets/tech4humans/br-doc-extraction
  • Cardoso, Gabriel Pimenta de Freitas, et al. "DharmaOCR: Specialized Small Language Models for Structured OCR that outperform Open-Source and Commercial Baselines." arXiv preprint arXiv:2604.14314 (2026).

Further Reading

  • Direct Preference Optimization Beyond Chatbots
