item.description: Full title: How Indegene is modernizing and scaling enterprise data quality in life sciences
item.content:encoded:
Artificial Intelligence

How Indegene is modernizing and scaling enterprise data quality in life sciences

This post is co-written with Shravan K S from Indegene Limited.

Enterprise AI is creating new opportunities for life sciences organizations to improve decision-making across commercial, medical, market access, and other business functions. But the quality of every AI model, dashboard, and business insight depends on one thing: trusted data. As enterprise data grows across multiple platforms, pipelines, and business domains, maintaining consistent data quality has become increasingly difficult. Manual data quality rule creation, fragmented governance, and evolving business definitions make it challenging to scale data quality across the enterprise.

This post explores how Indegene built a production-grade, large language model (LLM) powered Data Quality Agent within its NEXT Unified Data Platform (NEXT UDP) on AWS. The agent generates context-aware data quality rules, validates them, and produces ready-to-run SQL and Python code under centralized, human-in-the-loop governance. Together, these capabilities help organizations improve data quality at enterprise scale while reducing the effort required to build and maintain data quality programs.

About Indegene

Indegene Limited (BSE: 544172, NSE: INDGN) is the strategic operating partner to the life sciences industry, orchestrating commercial, medical, R&D, and safety operations across the product lifecycle. Trusted by the world’s top 20 biopharma companies, Indegene helps run complex, highly regulated workflows at global scale. Indegene combines deep life sciences expertise with AI-embedded platforms and governed operating models to improve speed, consistency, and compliance across mission-critical operations. By integrating technology into how work is executed and scaled, Indegene helps life sciences organizations deliver measurable outcomes in regulated environments.

Why conventional data quality programs break down

Most organizations have established data quality processes but keeping them effective is becoming increasingly difficult as enterprise data ecosystems evolve.

One of the biggest challenges is the divide between technical and business rule ownership. Data engineers typically define technical rules that confirm whether data is structurally correct. For example, verifying that an HCP ID (Healthcare Professional ID) isn’t null, follows the required format, is unique, and maps to a valid reference record. Business teams define rules that determine whether the data makes sense in its operational context. For example, confirming that product market share totals 100 percent within a territory or that an HCP’s prescription activity aligns with their specialty and eligibility criteria. Because technical rules are often maintained in code while business rules reside in glossaries, SOPs, and subject-matter expertise, keeping them aligned and consistently governed across datasets and platforms becomes difficult.

Traditional validation techniques also have inherent limitations. Checks for null values, data types, uniqueness, or referential integrity remain essential, but they can’t capture business-specific context. Validating product hierarchies, customer segmentation, territory alignment, or commercial business rules requires domain knowledge that static validation logic can’t easily represent.

Creating and maintaining data quality rules is equally demanding. Every new dataset requires data profiling, rule definition, SQL development, validation, and ongoing maintenance. These rules are often spread across SQL scripts, pipeline code, spreadsheets, data catalogs, and tool-specific configurations. As schemas, business definitions, or validation thresholds change, the effort required to update and govern these rules grows significantly.

Additionally, the operational impact is significant. Onboarding new datasets becomes slower because many activities are repeated manually. Maintaining quality rules across hundreds of datasets consumes valuable engineering effort. Business users lose confidence when validation rules are difficult to understand, trace, or relate to business context.

As a result, data quality often becomes a periodic governance activity rather than a continuous, scalable capability.

Rethinking data quality with generative AI

Traditional data quality tools often operate as standalone capabilities, disconnected from the broader enterprise data ecosystem. As organizations scale AI and analytics, data quality needs to be embedded within the data platform itself, where governance, metadata, lineage, and analytics work together.

Indegene addresses this through the NEXT Unified Data Platform (NEXT UDP), a modern, AI-driven data platform built specifically for life sciences. NEXT UDP brings together fragmented commercial, medical, clinical, and enterprise data into a single, governed environment so organizations can manage the complete data lifecycle from ingestion to analytics. NEXT UDP provides several standalone AI agents, such as the Data Ingestion agent, Data Quality agent, Orchestration agent, Data Catalog agent, and SQL Bot Generator agent. You can use them standalone within your data pipelines or customize them further for agent-to-agent communication.

By integrating data ingestion, transformation, data quality, governance, metadata management, and analytics within a unified platform, NEXT UDP helps organizations:

  • Consolidate fragmented enterprise data into a trusted source of truth.
  • Standardize data quality and governance across business domains.
  • Improve metadata visibility, lineage, and traceability.
  • Reduce manual effort across data engineering workflows.
  • Deliver trusted, AI-ready data for enterprise analytics and decision-making.

Figure 1: NEXT Unified Data Platform dashboard with use cases and AI agents

Figure 2: NEXT UDP technical architecture on AWS

Indegene’s life sciences clients needed an agent that could run reliably in production and meet strict governance requirements, while giving the team flexibility in how they build it. Within NEXT UDP, Generative AI powers an intelligent Data Quality Agent that augments existing data quality processes. The agent boosts data engineer and data steward productivity by accelerating rule creation, simplifying validation, and helping maintain consistent governance at enterprise scale.

Indegene built the Data Quality Agent on a set of AWS services, with Amazon Bedrock, Strands Agents and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore at its core. Amazon Bedrock, provides a choice of foundation models (FMs), built on a foundation of security, privacy, and responsible AI controls. For life sciences organizations, this matters because their data often includes sensitive healthcare professional and patient information. Strands Agents streamlines building and updating the agent, and its evaluation tools help Indegene test rule accuracy, which is critical in regulated life sciences environments. The agent runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. The solution also inherits existing AWS security and audit controls, so Indegene can focus on data quality logic instead of agent infrastructure.

What makes the Data Quality Agent unique? Two knowledge bases that power context-aware data quality

Any data quality tool can check for null values, duplicates, or invalid data types. Services such as AWS Glue Data Quality, a capability of AWS Glue, already recommend rules like these from data statistics, and they remain a strong foundation. The harder problem is determining whether the data makes sense for its business purpose. To address this, the Data Quality Agent uses two complementary knowledge bases that combine curated domain knowledge with experience gained from governed usage.

The first is an Internal Enterprise knowledge base: It combines internal business glossaries, data dictionaries, SOPs, regulatory guidance, approved data quality rules, validated scripts, profiling results, historical anomalies, and subject matter expert (SME) feedback. Content is ingested, vectorized, and retrieved through Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) to generate data quality rules grounded in enterprise standards and proven outcomes.

The second is an External Reference knowledge base: It’s built and periodically updated using approved standardized data quality frameworks, web search, and controlled web-scraping. When a dataset is selected, the agent analyzes table and column metadata and retrieves relevant data quality standards, reference values, and validation best practices from trusted sources. For example, for an NPI (National Provider Identifier) column, it can identify applicable quality standards, recommend format (the required 10-digit numeric format) and perform reference-validation checks.

How it works

Figure 3: Data Quality Agent process flow

The Data Quality Agent takes users from data profiling to rule creation and governance in a single workflow:

  • Select source: Connect to a supported source such as Amazon Redshift or Snowflake.
  • Select database and schema: Browse the available tables, with the rule count and active rule status for each.
  • Profile data: The solution computes quality metrics and column patterns for the table, which users review.
  • Detect anomalies: The solution flags anomalies against historical baselines, and users review the total, critical, and warning issues and the affected records.
  • Manage rules: Review a table’s existing rules or start creating new ones.
  • Choose rule mode: Pick Column Level, Table Level, or Custom Query.
  • Generate rule suggestions: The agent uses metadata, profiling results, anomalies, existing rules, and knowledge base context to recommend technical and business rules, each with a severity.
  • Review, refine and apply: Users edit or approve each recommendation.
  • Generate and validate code: The agent produces SQL and Python for approved rules, and a validation step checks them.
  • Store in the central rule repository: Approved rules become available for execution, monitoring, and audit.

Solution architecture of the generative AI-powered Data Quality Agent on AWS

The following diagram shows the end-to-end architecture of the Data Quality Agent on the NEXT UDP platform, from the data steward request to rule execution.

Figure 4: Solution architecture of the Data Quality Agent on NEXT UDP

Data stewards and data quality analysts call the solution from the Indegene application. The following table provides a walkthrough of the solution pipeline and lists the AWS services used for each layer. It also captures other options the solution supports, so you can adapt it to your data volumes, existing tools, and operational preferences.

LayerAWS / platform servicesAlso supportedRole
API and accessAWS WAF, Amazon API Gateway, Amazon Cognito–Data stewards and data quality analysts call the solution through Amazon API Gateway. AWS WAF filters requests before they reach the API, and Amazon Cognito authenticates users with OAuth 2.0 and validates the JWT on each request.
Data source layerAmazon RedshiftSnowflake connector, Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), JDBC/ODBC sourcesProvides structured and semi-structured data for data quality profiling and rule execution.
Metadata catalog layerAWS Glue Data CatalogAWS Glue crawlers for automatic schema discoveryCaptures databases, schemas, tables, columns, data types, and rule coverage.
Profiling and anomaly detection layerAWS Lambda (Python), with results stored in Amazon DynamoDBAWS Glue jobs, Amazon Athena, Amazon Redshift SQLColumn statistics, such as null rates, distinct counts, data type conformance, patterns, value ranges and table-level signals are computed by a Python-based profiling process on AWS Lambda, The same Lambda performs anomaly detection using statistical comparison against historical baselines to flag unexpected shifts, such as a null-rate spike or a cardinality change.
Knowledge/RAG layerAmazon Bedrock Knowledge Base with Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL (pgvector) and S3 for storing knowledge documents exposed as tools through AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCoreAmazon OpenSearch Serverless for vector store, Amazon S3 Vectors, a capability of Amazon S3Retrieves from the Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases (external reference standards and internal enterprise knowledge). AgentCore Gateway connects the agent to its knowledge bases as tools.
LLM intelligence layerStrands Agents on AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, Claude Sonnet 4.5 on Amazon Bedrock, Amazon Bedrock Guardrails, AgentCore memoryOther foundation models available in Amazon BedrockGenerates data quality rules and uses the assembled context and few-shot prompting to recommend both technical checks (completeness, format, uniqueness) and pharma-specific business rules. Amazon Bedrock provides a choice of FMs to generate rules. AgentCore runtime provides a managed, session-isolated environment, AgentCore memory retains reviewer feedback to improve future recommendations.
Orchestration and human review layerAWS Step Functions, AWS Lambda, Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS), Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS), Amazon EventBridge–Coordinates profiling, LLM calls, rule generation, rule execution, status updates, and human review.
Rule metadata repositoryAmazon DynamoDBAmazon Aurora / Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS)Stores rule ID, name, type, column, status, author, created date, severity, and version details.
Code generation, validation and storageAmazon Bedrock – Claude Sonnet 4.5 and AgentCore Code Interpreter, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, with approved scripts store in Amazon S3–Generates Python / SQL code and checks before storage
Execution layerAWS LambdaAWS Glue jobs, Amazon Athena, Amazon Redshift SQLRuns data quality checks and writes violation counts and detailed anomalies.
Monitoring and dashboard layerAmazon CloudWatch, AgentCore Observability, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore or application UIAmazon Quick, Amazon OpenSearch DashboardsData quality dashboard displays the rules applied and their status, along with total anomalies, critical anomalies, checks run, and issue details.
Security and governanceAWS Identity and Access Management (AWS IAM), AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS), AWS Secrets Manager, AWS CloudTrail, AWS Config, Amazon GuardDuty, AWS Security Hub, Amazon Inspector, virtual private cloud (VPC) endpoints–Authentication, encryption, secrets, audit, and threat detection

How the Data Quality Agent builds context

Before recommending any validation rule, the Data Quality Agent assembles context from six distinct sources, each answering a different question about the data:

Context SourceWhat it providesQuestion it answers
Table/Column Metadata (Catalog)Schema, data types from the Data CatalogWhat is this data?
Data ProfileColumn-level statistics computed from the actual data, such as null rates, distinct counts, value ranges, frequent values and detected patternsWhat does the data look like right now?
Anomaly Detection ResultsUnexpected changes flagged by comparing the latest profile with historical baselines, such as a sudden rise in nulls, a change in distinct values, or out-of-range valuesWhat has changed or looks wrong?
Existing Active Data Quality RulesRules already applied at the table or column level, retrieved from the rule repositoryWhat rules already exist, so we don’t duplicate or conflict?
External Reference Knowledge BaseUniversal, publicly established data quality standards and validation best practices (for example, format and structural rules for identifiers like the National Provider Identifier)What are the industry standards for this field?
Internal Enterprise Knowledge BaseOrganization-specific data quality rule patterns, prior reviewer feedback, and curated business/technical rule librariesHow does this organization define quality?

Together, these sources let the agent reason like an experienced data steward. Grounding every recommendation in what the data is, what the standards require, how the enterprise defines quality, and what has already been implemented.

What the solution does

The Data Quality Agent generates several categories of checks and keeps data stewards in control of the results.

Anomaly checks generation

The solution generates anomaly checks that catch values which are technically valid but don’t match how a pharmaceutical market behaves. These include negative switch percentages, market shares that don’t add up to 100 percent within a market, inconsistent drug rankings (for example, a drug ranked first with a lower share than the drug ranked second), rating values outside the defined scale, and panel sizes that are too small or don’t match the number of respondents.

Context-aware rule generation with RAG

The Data Quality Agent generates rule recommendations in three modes:

Rule TypeDescription
Column LevelGenerates data quality rules for a specific, individual column selected by the user. The agent reads that column’s metadata and profiling signals to suggest checks such as data type validation, null and mandatory-field checks, length and range validation, pattern/format validation, and uniqueness.
Table LevelGenerates data quality rules for the table as a whole, driven by the table’s metadata and relationships across its columns. This covers record consistency, duplicate detection, cross-column validation, referential integrity checks, and table-wide business consistency.
Custom QueryGenerates SQL-based rules from natural language input. The user describes the business validation in plain English and the agent produces the corresponding SQL, which can then be refined conversationally or edited directly to support complex validations that fall outside standard column and table checks.

The Create New Quality Rule interface provides dedicated Column Level, Table Level, and Custom Query modes.

The platform supports both technical validation and business-specific quality checks.

For technical rules, the agent generates checks that confirm the data is structurally sound. These include null checks for mandatory fields, data type validation, range validation for numeric and date values, pattern validation for formatted fields such as identifiers and codes, duplicate detection, and referential integrity checks between related tables.

For business rules, the agent generates life sciences checks that confirm the data is consistent with how the business operates. These include account affiliation consistency (for example, a healthcare provider linked to the correct organization), segmentation logic, eligibility criteria, and market share and product share validation (for example, shares within a territory not exceeding 100%).

Real use-case example

Consider an HCP Product Performance table with the columns HCP_ID, Specialty, Territory_ID, Product_ID, Prescription_Volume, Market_Share_Pct, Switch_Pct, Rating_Scale, and Reporting_Month. Using the table profile and the two Knowledge Bases, this is how the Data Quality Agent generates and performs the following checks:

  • Anomaly checks performed. Negative switch percentage. Market share total mismatch. Sudden increase or decrease in prescription volume. Inconsistent product rankings. Invalid rating-scale values.
  • Technical rules generated. HCP_ID must not be null or duplicated. Prescription_Volume must be numeric and non-negative. Market_Share_Pct and Switch_Pct must be between 0 and 100. Reporting_Month must follow the required date format. Territory_ID and Product_ID must match their reference tables.
  • Business rules generated. Market share across all products must total 100 percent for each territory and reporting month. The HCP’s product eligibility must align with their specialty. Only eligible HCPs can be included in the target segment.

AI-assisted severity recommendation

The solution recommends severity based on dataset context, rule type, and business impact. Severity categories help distinguish between:

  • Critical issues, such as invalid commercial metrics, incorrect identifiers, or business rule violations.
  • Basic validations, including schema conformance, null checks, and length validation.
  • Complex validations involving advanced SQL logic, multi-column rules, or domain-specific business checks.
  • Information: Validation conducted for awareness and transparency purposes only. No action is required unless concerns are identified.

SQL/Python code generation and ETL integration

After a rule is approved, the LLM generates the equivalent SQL, Python, and PySpark code. Before it’s stored, the code is validated automatically with syntax checks, a check against the target schema, and a test run on sample data where the language supports it. This means existing extract, transform, and load (ETL) and orchestration tools can run them as part of the current data pipelines.

AI-assisted validation

Using an LLM as a Validation Agent to review data quality (DQ) rules/scripts generated by another LLM for reducing hallucinations and improving governance. Further, Amazon Bedrock provides security, privacy, and responsible AI controls. Prompts and outputs aren’t used to train the models or shared with model providers. Amazon Bedrock is HIPAA eligible and in scope for compliance programs such as SOC, ISO and GDPR, which helps Indegene meet the requirements of its life sciences clients. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails adds configurable safeguards on model inputs and outputs. It detects and masks personally identifiable information (PII), blocks harmful content and prompt injection attacks, and uses contextual grounding checks to flag responses that aren’t supported by the retrieved knowledge.

Human oversight remains central

The Data Quality Agent is designed to augment existing data quality processes. Each generated rule receives a confidence score. Only high-confidence, low-risk rules are approved automatically, while critical and business rules always go to an SME for review. Every decision is recorded in the rule repository, so rule management stays governed, traceable, and aligned with enterprise standards.

Delivering operational impact and business value

In production, across Indegene’s deployments of NEXT UDP for life sciences clients, the Data Quality Agent has reduced the effort to define and implement data quality rules from about 30 hours to about 4 hours per dataset. That’s roughly 85 percent less effort, or about 7x higher productivity. Onboarding a new table now takes 2–4 hours instead of 2–5 working days. Data engineers and data stewards now spend their time reviewing and approving rules rather than writing them from scratch.

Key outcomes include:

  • Less manual effort through AI-generated rules, SQL, and Python.
  • Faster onboarding of new tables, schemas, and business domains.
  • More consistent rules, grounded in approved standards, enterprise knowledge, and existing rules.
  • Better collaboration between business and technical teams through the review, refine, and approve workflow.
  • Earlier detection of data quality issues through automated profiling and anomaly detection.

Table 1: Performance and Scale

MetricImpact*
Enterprise profiling25–50 schemas; 500–2,000 tables; 10,000–50,000 columns
Table profiling45–90 sec (~1M rows); 2–5 min (~10M rows)
AI rule generation20–45 sec per table
SQL generation3–8 sec per rule; 20–60 sec for 10–15 rules
Rule execution20–30 sec (standard); 1–3 min (complex SQL)
Central rule repository1,000–10,000 rules
DQ checks per execution100–500 per domain. Scalable to 1,000+

*Estimated from Indegene’s production deployments

Table 2: Rule quality and validation

MetricImpact*What does it mean
Rule suggestion accuracy80–90%Suggestions that are technically valid and apply correctly to the column or table
Rule acceptance rate60–75%Suggestions approved without any changes
Rule refinement rate / Human Override Rate20–35%Suggestions approved after the reviewer edited logic or thresholds
SQL validity90–97% (schema-grounded); 80–90% (custom SQL)Generated SQL that passes validation on the first attempt
Severity recommendation accuracy75–85%Recommended severity matching the reviewer’s final severity
Business relevance (SME rating)4.0–4.5 / 5SME rating of how useful the recommended rules are to the business
Hallucination rate<5–8%Suggestions that reference non-existent columns or incorrect business logic

*Estimated from Indegene’s production deployments

Table 3: Operational efficiency

MetricImpact*
Manual SQL rule authoring60–80% reduction in end-to-end effort, including review and refinement
New table onboarding2–5 working days → 2–4 hours
Rule reuse40–60% of new rules adapted from existing approved rules
LLM cost optimizationUp to 90% lower input-token cost on cached context with Amazon Bedrock prompt caching
Compute optimization~45–51% reduction with metadata-first profiling

*Estimated from Indegene’s production deployments

Table 4: Manual compared to agent-assisted data quality

ActivityTraditional DQ ApproachGenerative AI-powered DQ approachImpact*
Rule DiscoveryManual review of schemas, profiling reports, sample data, and documentation. Existing tools can generate basic profiling checks but often miss domain-specific business logicAgent uses metadata, profiling results, table context, existing rule patterns, and optional business descriptions to recommend technical and life sciences-specific data quality rules80-85% faster
Technical Rule GenerationManual creation of null, data type, range, uniqueness, and integrity rulesAutomated rule generation with human review80-85% faster
Business Rule DefinitionValidation is often based on technical metadata with limited understanding of product, segment, customer, or eligibility logic. Business context depends heavily on SME discussions and manual translation into validation logicUses RAG to retrieve business glossaries, data dictionaries, existing rules, and historical anomaly patterns to generate context-aware recommendations.70-75% faster
Rules authoring and SQL/Python DevelopmentEngineers manually define validation rules and perform coding, debugging, and testing for each dataset or business requirement.Auto-generated rules at the Column Level, Table Level, and Custom Query levels, and generate SQL/Python for the selected DQ checks. Users can review, refine, and apply the recommendations.80-85% faster to first working code
Rule ValidationRules are validated manually, involving multiple iterations of executing the queries and refiningAgent scores, refines, and optimizes rules automatically80-85% faster
Rule ReuseManual copy, modify, and reuseApproved rules and feedback added to the agent’s knowledge50% faster onboarding for new datasets in an existing domain
Anomaly DetectionManual analysis of profiling outputs and recordsAutomated anomaly detection with business-context explanations80-85% faster
Severity classificationRule severity and business impact are determined manually, which can lead to inconsistent prioritization.Recommends severity based on rule type, dataset context, and business impact.Consistent, context-based severity
Governance & TraceabilityRules are often distributed across tools, scripts, spreadsheets, or catalogs, making governance and traceability difficult. Approval and review workflows vary across teams.Central, versioned rule repository with ownership85% reduction in maintenance effort
Human EffortSMEs and engineers drive every stepSMEs focus on review and approval. The agent handles discovery and generationHigher productivity & scalability, ~7x productivity

*Estimated from Indegene’s production deployments

Looking ahead

As enterprise data ecosystems continue to grow, maintaining consistent and scalable data quality becomes increasingly difficult using manual rule creation and fragmented governance processes. Generative AI provides an opportunity to augment these workflows by accelerating rule generation, incorporating business context, and supporting governed decision-making.

The generative AI-powered Data Quality Agent within the NEXT Unified Data Platform demonstrates how large language models, RAG, and centralized rule governance can work together to simplify data quality management while keeping humans in control of review and approval. Future enhancements will continue to build on this foundation, including:

  • AI-assisted remediation recommendations to help users resolve failed data quality checks.
  • Root cause analysis to identify recurring anomaly patterns and support faster investigation of repeated data quality issues.

As these capabilities evolve, the focus remains the same: helping organizations improve data quality through AI-assisted automation while maintaining governance, transparency, and business oversight.

To learn more, refer to the following resources:

  • Indegene in the life sciences space
  • Generative AI in Healthcare & Life Sciences
  • AWS Skill Builder course: Building Generative AI Applications Using Amazon Bedrock
  • GitHub repo: Sample Healthcare and Life Sciences Agents on AWS

About the authors

item.title: [Amazon Bedrock] How U Mobile built agentic telco operations with Amazon Bedr…
item.description: Full title: How U Mobile built agentic telco operations with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
item.content:encoded:
Artificial Intelligence

How U Mobile built agentic telco operations with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore

U Mobile, Malaysia’s newest 5G network provider, has always run its telco operations lean, doing more with less through continuous automation. When new AI capabilities became available, U Mobile explored how to enhance operational efficiency beyond basic productivity gains. The real opportunity was further upstream, in how operations teams diagnose and resolve problems in the first place. The same lean operating discipline shaped the foundation for AiDaH: not a one-off technology initiative, but the next step in a long-running journey to simplify operations and scale capability without adding complexity.

When a subscriber can’t purchase a data add-on, resolving it isn’t a single problem. It’s a coordination problem. A customer service agent needs to pull interface logs for error codes. The same agent must then query business support system APIs for subscriber eligibility, and cross-reference internal knowledge bases for applicable business policies. All of that happens across multiple systems, before drafting a single word of response. And when that fails, the ticket escalates to backend IT teams and the subscriber waits even longer.

Traditional automation tools can help agents write better responses. What they can’t do is navigate multiple systems, analyze the results, and propose corrective action. Closing that gap takes an agentic architecture built on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore.

U Mobile’s Information Systems Division (ISD) built exactly that. Working with AWS and AWS Partner Axrail, they created AiDaH, the AI-Driven Agentic Helpdesk, on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. Two capabilities decided the choice. The managed agent runtime meant there was no agent infrastructure to operate. Built-in memory carried conversational context across turns without standing up a separate state store. Within a year of starting the journey, AiDaH handles over 150 documented operational scenarios across six business divisions. U Mobile’s internal measurements show trouble ticket volumes falling by up to 84.5 percent in key categories.

In this post, we walk through the six-layer architecture behind AiDaH. We then describe the security foundation beneath the platform, and close with a brief note on the spec-driven method the team used to build it.

The problem: Too many systems, too much friction

U Mobile’s IT landscape reflects the complexity typical of modern telecommunications: business support and customer relationship management systems, mobile number portability platforms, big data analytics, and infrastructure monitoring tools, running hybrid across on-premises and cloud.

Before AiDaH, this fragmentation meant that even routine diagnoses required manually checking logs, querying subscriber eligibility, and consulting knowledge bases for business policies, across separate systems and portals. Each lookup was a context switch, each context switch was time lost, and each unresolved query became an escalation to a backend IT team. Expanding coverage to additional operational domains compounded the problem, because every new system typically required a bespoke integration.

The ISD team’s strategy rested on three pillars.

  • Reach: agents that coordinate across backend systems in real time.
  • Depth: chain-of-thought reasoning for multi-step root cause analysis.
  • Community: a secure multi-tenant framework with role-based access control and built-in guardrails, available to every division.

The journey: From knowledge base to agentic platform

AiDaH started with a principle: think big, start small. U Mobile began conceptualization in late 2025 with two pilot agents and Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases, a fully managed Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) capability. A Q1 2026 pilot brought the internal IT helpdesk online with 4 agents and 20 operational scenarios. Through 2026 the platform hardened and expanded, adding three-tier routing and reaching 6 agents by mid-year. AiDaH went live to 50 L2 call center and branch users in Q3 2026 with 8 agents, and now covers more than 150 documented operational scenarios.

What agentic means in practice

The difference between traditional AI assistance and agentic AI is best illustrated through a real example.

With a traditional AI assistant, a support agent handling “mobile data not working overseas” gets help drafting a response and some suggested troubleshooting steps, but still manually checks roaming status, verifies eligibility, raises tickets, and sends the final reply.

With AiDaH, the system independently checks the subscriber’s roaming configuration, verifies international data eligibility, and identifies the specific point of failure. It then assembles a remediation plan: which services to reset, what configuration to push, and whether a network ticket is warranted. The support agent reviews and confirms, and the actions execute. The investigation that used to consume the agent’s time now happens before they read the first line. The human decision point is preserved where it matters: at the moment something changes on a live subscriber account.

In one production case, a subscriber reported being unable to purchase an add-on. AiDaH traced the failure to an error code, “Subscriber has pending order.” It also revealed that the customer had attempted the same purchase more than 30 times across multiple channels over three days, every attempt blocked by the same underlying pending order. AiDaH surfaced the root cause and the remediation steps in a single response. Previously that would have required manual investigation across several systems.

Architecture: Six layers, one interface

AiDaH runs on a layered architecture built on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, deployed in the Asia Pacific (Singapore) Region. Staff interact through Microsoft Teams, a deliberate choice to meet most users where they already work, with no new application to learn and no portal switching.

The following diagram shows how the layers fit together.

Figure 1: AiDaH’s layered architecture

As shown in Figure 1, the platform is organized into six layers.

Layer 1: Staff interface

Staff reach AiDaH through Microsoft Teams and a web portal served by Amazon CloudFront and protected by AWS WAF, with an AWS Lambda backend and a REST API for programmatic triggers.

Layer 2: Orchestration

The routing brain on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. Every request passes a pre-flight security check covering role-based access control, identity validation, and guardrails, then enters a cost-optimized routing tier. Roughly 70 percent of requests resolve through deterministic keyword matching with no model invocation, 20 percent are classified by a lightweight model, and only 10 percent require the full orchestrator. The cheapest path that can confidently handle the request is the one that runs.

Layer 3: Specialist agents

Eight experts spanning customer relationship management, customer problem management, number portability, order and SIM operations, infrastructure monitoring, big data analytics, cloud cost management, and finance operations. They communicate over the Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol, which lets them delegate subtasks and complete cross-system workflows no single agent could handle alone.

Layer 4: Gateways and backend APIs

AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, exposes U Mobile’s backends to agents through a unified Model Context Protocol (MCP) interface. Behind each gateway sit AWS Lambda functions and MCP servers that translate agent intent into calls against a specific system.

Layer 5: Data and knowledge

Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases, the fully managed RAG capability, grounds agent responses in governed content, using an Amazon OpenSearch Serverless vector store. Content spans a shared enterprise knowledge base and a separate finance corpus. AgentCore memory, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, maintains conversational context across turns, and Amazon DynamoDB holds the six-tier role-based access control model and session metadata.

Layer 6: Operational systems

U Mobile’s on-premises and cloud operational systems are reached over AWS Transit Gateway and AWS Site-to-Site VPN, an IPsec-encrypted tunnel with no public internet exposure.

How a request flows through the layers

Tracing a single request makes the interaction between the layers concrete. Consider a support agent who types a port-in status question into the AiDaH channel in Microsoft Teams.

  • Interface: The Teams message reaches an AWS Lambda function, which forwards the request and the caller’s federated identity to the orchestrator.
  • Pre-flight check: The orchestrator resolves the caller against the six-tier role-based access control model held in Amazon DynamoDB, validates the token issued by AgentCore Identity, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and applies Amazon Bedrock Guardrails to the incoming prompt. A request that fails any of these checks stops here.
  • Routing: The orchestrator selects the cheapest tier that can handle the request. A recognized phrase such as “port-in status” matches deterministically and skips model invocation entirely. An ambiguous phrasing goes to the lightweight classifier. A novel or multi-part question goes to the full orchestrator.
  • Agent instantiation: The selected specialist agent runs as a session in AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. AgentCore memory rehydrates the conversation so the agent inherits the subscriber number and any prior findings from earlier turns, instead of asking the user to repeat them.
  • Tool discovery and invocation: The agent queries AgentCore Gateway for the tools it is entitled to use. Each gateway publishes its backend as MCP tools with typed inputs and outputs, so the agent picks a tool by name and schema rather than by hand-coded integration logic. Amazon Cognito brokers the OAuth authorization for the call.
  • Backend call: The gateway’s Lambda function or MCP server translates the tool call into a request against the target system, traversing AWS Transit Gateway and the Site-to-Site VPN tunnel to reach the on-premises number portability platform. Sensitive fields are masked on the way back, before the response reaches the model.
  • Reasoning and collaboration: If the answer spans domains, the agent delegates over the Agent2Agent protocol. A port-in query that turns out to be a billing block, for example, hands off to the business support systems agent, and the results are merged into one narrative.
  • Response and audit: The agent grounds its explanation against Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases, then returns the finding and proposed remediation to Teams for human confirmation. AgentCore Observability, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, writes the full trace of prompts, tool calls, token counts, and latencies to Amazon CloudWatch, and AWS CloudTrail records the corresponding API activity.

Onboarding a new operational domain adds a gateway and its MCP tool definitions at step 5. Steps 1–4, and steps 7 and 8, are unchanged. The stable core is what keeps the marginal cost of each new domain low.

Amazon Bedrock AgentCore capabilities in production

The following table maps each AgentCore capability to the job it does in AiDaH.

CapabilityRole in AiDaH
RuntimeHosts AiDaH and its sub-agents as managed containers that scale automatically, with no servers to provision
MemoryMaintains conversational context such as subscriber number, order IDs, and prior findings across turns
IdentityIssues short-lived access tokens so only authorized users can invoke agents
GatewayConnects agents to U Mobile backends through a unified, secure MCP interface
ObservabilityStreams every prompt, tool call, token count, and latency measurement to Amazon CloudWatch

Securing the foundation

Deploying an agentic AI platform that reaches subscriber data, billing systems and network infrastructure demands more than application-level security. It requires a secure cloud foundation. U Mobile took a two-pronged approach: validating and enhancing the underlying AWS Landing Zone, and building on the security capabilities in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore.

Landing Zone security – Before scaling AiDaH to production, U Mobile engaged AWS to run a Well-Architected Security Review of the Landing Zone hosting the platform. The review validated the environment against AWS security best practices. Infrastructure protection came first, through AWS Control Tower guardrails and AWS Organizations service control policies. The review then examined centralized identity federation and network security controls for ingress and egress. Consolidated security findings in AWS Security Hub and encryption standards across every architecture tier completed the assessment. The outcome was twofold: confidence that every AiDaH component operates on an independently validated foundation, and a prioritized roadmap for continuous improvement.

Application-layer security – Every agent action traces to a specific authenticated user. Staff federate through Microsoft Entra ID, and AgentCore Identity issues the short-lived token that authorizes agent invocation. Amazon Cognito brokers OAuth authorization at the gateway. An agent can therefore reach only the systems its invoking user is entitled to see. A six-tier role-based access control model enforces permissions per agent, per tool, and per data source. Sensitive subscriber data is masked at the gateway before it reaches the model, with Amazon Bedrock Guardrails enforcing content policies.

Every prompt, tool invocation and response is streamed to Amazon CloudWatch Logs through AgentCore Observability, and AWS CloudTrail records the underlying API activity. That audit trail matters: AiDaH is now written into U Mobile’s L2 support standard operating procedures and is subject to operational audit. All compute runs in private VPC subnets, on-premises connectivity is exclusively over encrypted VPN, and AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) manages encryption keys for data at rest and in transit.

Over 150 documented operational scenarios

The scenarios AiDaH covers currently span six domains. The following table summarizes the coverage in each.

DomainCoverage
Customer managementAccount details, billing history, payment status, active plans and contracts, SIM information, service status
Order operations and logisticsOrder and delivery status, pending orders, resource allocation, tracing workflows, delivery tracking, shipment history
Customer problem managementRoot-cause diagnosis for failed add-on purchases, plan changes and top-up failures. Number portability port-in and port-out checks. Service disruption diagnosis across SMS, calls and data
IT infrastructure operationsServer and device status monitoring, IP and hostname lookups, network device inventory
Business intelligence and analyticsSubscriber trend analysis, device take-up trends, revenue trending, anomaly detection, individual subscriber analytics. The analytics agent converts plain-language questions into SQL queries, so no technical skills are required
Knowledge retrievalEnterprise-wide retrieval with context-aware, grounded responses and citations back to source evidence

Measuring progress: An AI competency model

To track progress and establish a shared vocabulary across the organization, the team adopted an eight-level AI competency model, from basic digital access to autonomous self-healing operations. It draws on industry thinking, including the TM Forum Autonomous Networks maturity levels, adapted to U Mobile’s operational context. The following table lists the eight levels.

LevelNameDescription
1Digital accessSelf-service portals, online tools and dashboards
2Scripted automationRules-based workflow triggers and auto-routing
3Basic AI assistanceSimple chatbots, FAQ look-ups, intent classification
4Contextual intelligenceContext-aware suggestions, basic natural language understanding with memory
5Proactive AIPredictive alerts, anomaly detection, recommendation engines
6Autonomous task executionAI completes defined tasks end to end with guardrails
7Collaborative multi-agentSpecialist agents collaborate, use tools, retrieve governed knowledge
8Self-healing and adaptiveAutonomous systems that detect, diagnose, remediate, and learn continuously

AiDaH reached Level 7 within nine months of the first pilot: specialist agents collaborate, use tools, retrieve governed knowledge, and support operational decision-making across domains. Level 8, where problems are detected, diagnosed, and resolved without human involvement, is the current target.

Driving adoption: From tool to teammate

Deploying AiDaH was one challenge. Getting people to trust and use it was another.

ISD recognized early that adoption isn’t a technology problem but a behavior change challenge. Staff were accustomed to established workflows, trusted tools, and familiar escalation paths. Introducing AiDaH meant asking them to change deeply embedded habits. It also meant trusting an AI to retrieve information, diagnose problems, and propose next steps on their behalf.

The team leaned on directed prompting. Rather than expecting open-ended exploration, ISD provided structured prompt templates for common scenarios. Those templates turned “ask AiDaH anything” into “here is exactly how to ask for a billing check or a port-in status.” That reduced hesitation and produced immediate, tangible results. When responses proved fast, accurate, and actionable, word spread. An internal survey rated the platform 4.6 out of 5 for ease of use, and daily use is now routine among frontline teams.

The clearest signal came when AiDaH was formally incorporated into U Mobile’s L2 support standard operating procedures. Moving from optional tool to auditable SOP is what marked the shift from experimentation to operations.

ISD’s approach was never about buying a finished solution. It was about owning the journey: building internal AI capability, encouraging responsible experimentation, and embedding practical AI fluency into the daily operating rhythm. Beyond AiDaH itself, ISD maintains a dedicated internal AI channel where teams share use cases, techniques, and early experiments. The goal isn’t to concentrate AI expertise in one team but to distribute it, so every division can use AI confidently within governed guardrails. Progress was not linear. The path involved setbacks and recalibrations, and each one made the platform and the team stronger.

Results

According to U Mobile’s internal measurements, monthly trouble ticket volumes declined across three major categories between January and September 2026:

  • Provisioning and network tickets fell 84.5 percent.
  • General inquiries dropped 81.6 percent.
  • Billing and charging reduced by 48.7 percent.

How the team built it: Spec-driven development with Kiro

U Mobile accelerated AiDaH’s development using Kiro, the AWS agentic IDE built around spec-driven development. In Kiro, a new capability begins as a spec rather than a prompt: requirements, design, and task breakdown are written down and reviewed first, and code generation works against that agreed artifact. For AiDaH, this mattered most at the agent and tool boundary. Each new operational domain means a new gateway, a set of MCP tool definitions, and the role-based access control entries that decide who might call them. Writing those down first made each new domain a repeatable unit of work rather than a fresh design exercise.

The supporting toolchain is conventional. The team used Kiro IDE for local development, with agent hooks and MCP integrations, alongside Kiro CLI for pipeline automation. Source control runs on GitLab, with AWS CodePipeline and AWS CodeBuild driving continuous integration, container images published to Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR), and SonarQube providing continuous code quality scanning. Specifications drove the code generation. The discipline let a small team grow from a two-use-case proof of concept to over 150 documented use cases on a 12-week sprint cadence.

Key architectural decisions

Several choices shaped how AiDaH scaled from proof of concept to production platform. Four stand out, each one reducing the cost of adding the next operational domain or keeping the platform governable as it grew.

AgentCore as managed infrastructure – Rather than building a custom agent framework, the team used the built-in scaling, identity, memory, and observability capabilities in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. AWS manages the underlying provisioning, scaling, and patching, which removed an entire layer of infrastructure engineering.

MCP for universal tool connectivity – Standardizing on the Model Context Protocol means AiDaH can onboard new backend systems without rebuilding agent logic. Each new operational domain needs a new gateway, not a new integration architecture.

A2A for specialist collaboration – The Agent2Agent protocol lets domain specialists delegate subtasks to each other. A query spanning customer records, interface logs and billing data routes naturally across the relevant agents.

Secure foundation first – Running the Well-Architected Security Review on the Landing Zone before scaling to production means security controls are inherited by every new agent and gateway, rather than bolted on afterwards.

What’s next

U Mobile’s roadmap focuses on expanding both breadth and depth: onboarding additional operational domains and backend integrations, while evolving the platform’s capabilities from single-system queries toward multi-system correlated diagnosis. The longer-term goal, Level 8 on the competency model, is to move from informing support agents to autonomously resolving issues.

Security governance matures in parallel. The team is aligning practices with NIST SP 800-53, the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications, the CSA AI Trust Framework, and MITRE ATLAS. Compliance with Malaysia’s Personal Data Protection Act and Malaysian Communications and Multimedia Commission regulations continues alongside it.

Conclusion

AiDaH shows what changes when AI stops assisting and starts acting. In under a year, U Mobile went from a two-agent proof of concept to eight specialist agents serving over 150 documented operational scenarios. According to U Mobile’s internal measurements, trouble tickets fell by up to 84.5 percent in key categories, and U Mobile has now written the platform into its formal L2 support procedures.

We walked through the six layers, followed a request from Teams to an on-premises system and back, and described the Well-Architected Security Review that preceded the production scale up. The technical foundation mattered, but so did the less glamorous work. That meant validating the Landing Zone before scaling, writing structured prompts so staff knew how to start, and treating adoption as a behavior change problem rather than a deployment milestone. Teams facing similar system fragmentation might find the same pattern useful. Start with a managed agent runtime, add a standard tool protocol at the integration boundary, and run a security review before the scale up rather than after it.

The direction remains clear: expand securely, automate responsibly, and move steadily toward autonomous, self-healing operations, one deliberate and governed step at a time.

To learn more, visit Amazon Bedrock AgentCore and the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Developer Guide. To explore spec-driven development, see Kiro.

About the authors

item.title: [Fireworks AI] Kimi K3.1 Pro is live on Fireworks
item.content:encoded:
Kimi K3.1 Pro from Moonshot AI is available on Fireworks at launch. You can use it on serverless with pay-per-token pricing, or run it on a dedicated deployment for reserved capacity.

What’s new in K3.1 Pro

In our Specialized Intelligence Index evaluations, K3.1 Pro was the fastest model on Legacy Bench and CorporateBench, and second-fastest on ORCA. Moonshot post-trained K3.1 Pro from K3 and swapped K3’s full-attention layers for sparse attention, which makes long contexts more efficient to serve. Key specifications:

Spec

Kimi K3.1 Pro

Modalities

Text and vision

Total parameters

2.78T

Active parameters

104B

Input context length

1040k tokens

Experts

896 (16 active per token)

Attention

Kimi Delta Attention + Gated DeepSeek Sparse Attention

How it performs on the Specialized Intelligence Index

We evaluated K3.1 Pro on the Fireworks Specialized Intelligence Index (SII): benchmarks built by companies like Sierra, Harvey and Rogo to choose the models they run in production.

K3.1 Pro sits on the quality-for-cost frontier on five of these benchmarks: no model scores higher without costing more.

Figure 1: Kimi K3.1 Pro on Sierra’s τ³-Banking, score vs. cost per trial, from Fireworks’ Specialized Intelligence Index.

  • Customer support (Sierra’s τ³-Banking): agents resolve banking requests using database tools while following bank policy. K3.1 Pro ranks first of 19 at 64.7%, 8.7 percentage points ahead of Claude Opus 5.5.
  • Legacy code (Factory’s Legacy Bench): maintaining COBOL, Fortran and Java 7 codebases. K3.1 Pro scores 61.0%, third of 14 and the highest-scoring open model.
  • Legal (Harvey’s LAB): work typically handled by a first-year associate. K3.1 Pro ranks second of 13 at 15.4%, behind Grok 4.6.
  • Finance (Rogo’s Big Finance Benchmark): 928 questions drawn from financial research workflows. K3.1 Pro ties Claude Opus 5.5 at 48.2%.
  • Incident response (Traversal’s ORCA): finding the root cause of production incidents from traces, logs and metrics. K3.1 Pro scores 32.9%, third of 13 and the top open model, at less than one-fifth the cost per task of either model ahead of it.
  • Corporate legal (Epiq’s CorporateBench): K3.1 Pro scores 76.9, fourth of 12 and the top open model.

Here’s how K3.1 Pro compares with Kimi K3 on five benchmarks:

How Kimi K3.1 Pro scores on Moonshot’s evaluations

Moonshot reports the following results at maximum reasoning effort:

  • Long-horizon coding: 51.7 on SWE Marathon v1.1, ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 (46.3), Claude Fable 5.1 (45.6) and GPT-6 Astra (42.5).
  • Agentic research: 70.0 on Humanity’s Last Exam with tools and 92.1 on BrowseComp, the top scores in Moonshot’s comparison on both.
  • Office work: 64.4 on OfficeQA Pro v2 and 73.3 on Artificial Analysis’ Automation Bench, ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 on both (62.2 and 69.5).

Moonshot evaluated K3.1 Pro using harnesses including Claude Code for coding, and sourced most competitor scores from published reports and leaderboards.

Pricing

Standard serverless pricing per million tokens: $2.00 uncached input, $0.20 cached input and $10.00 output.

Get started

Try Kimi K3.1 Pro in the Fireworks playground, or call it with model ID accounts/fireworks/models/kimi-k3p1-pro.

item.title: [Together AI] Together Compiler: Continual Compilation for AI inference
item.content:encoded:
All blog posts

Published 11/4/2026

Together Compiler: Continual Compilation for AI inference

  • AuthorsReyna Abhyankar, Dylan Lim, and Simran Arora
  • Table of contents40+ Models Chosen for Production...40+ Models Chosen for Production...40+ Models Chosen for Production...
  • Links in this articlePolymorphic InferencePaper

AI inference workloads are dynamic. There are thousands of regimes spanning new models, hardware platforms, customers, use cases, and traffic shapes. It’s no longer scalable to optimize each of these regimes by hand.

  • Architectures are highly variable: it’s been ~11 years since the Transformer. We might have thought there would be more consolidation, but none of the top-10 open-source LLMs on OpenRouter use the same architecture!
  • Workloads are highly variable: Together serves many trillions of tokens per day across thousands of customers, each with a different traffic shape (batch size, sequence length, MoE expert imbalance, attention sparsity, session duration, domain).
  • Hardware is highly variable: H100s, B200s, B300s, NVL72, VR, Groq, and more each require distinct strategies.

Agents are a great fit for this problem, in theory. They can adapt to new workloads and search over the space of possible optimizations without relying on fixed rules or heuristics that plague human experts and traditional machine learning compilers. However, today’s agentic systems are bottlenecked by the speed of experimentation.

**We introduce Together Compiler (TKCC), the first truly continual optimization loop that leverages high-throughput agents to optimize to diverse inference workloads**

In less than 24 hours, TKCC achieves up to 2.6x higher TPS across frontier open source models (Kimi K3, GLM 5.3, MiniMax M3.1-Flash, DeepSeek v4.1-Flash), sets the state-of-the-art on SemiAnalysis’ InferenceX benchmark for low-latency with 1111 TPS on MiniMax M3.1-Flash and 1205 TPS on DeepSeek v4.1-Flash, and outperforms available open-source megakernels by 1.7x on their workhorse Llama 1B batch size 1 setting. Furthermore, TKCC generalizes to domains beyond language model inference (weather modeling, PDE, time-series, and biology). This performance boost is enabled by TKCC’s 252x higher experiment throughput compared to baseline agentic performance optimization systems. Together Compiler is serving trillions of tokens today.

Traffic is continually changing

As an inference provider, we see a variety of user behaviors based on regional patterns, new model releases, and burstiness.

  • Regional patterns: Users across the world may have different model preferences. We’ve observed traffic for one country’s working hours to have 1.4x longer prompts than another country (97k vs 70k).
  • Model releases: Users take time to figure out how to integrate new model releases into their workflows. First, they tend to opt for chat-based interaction and evaluation. This is swiftly followed by an 80% increase in prompt length just two weeks after the release as users shift towards agentic workloads.
  • Burstiness: Customers may send bursts of requests at random times throughout the day. Prompt lengths can suddenly double and cache hit rates can fall if not handled carefully.

It’s clear that we must adapt to ever-changing user behavior with specialized optimizations for each new deployment.

Overview of Together Compiler

TKCC takes as input the traffic shape, model, and hardware. TKCC uses agents to generate a series of optimizations for an inference engine.

Figure 1: Together Compiler recompiles as traffic drifts, with agents, a persistent engine and an ensemble in a loop.

The core insights in TKCC are as follows:

1. TKCC maximizes experimentation throughput and minimizes GPU idle time during agent optimization

‍Most existing agentic inference optimization systems require agents to launch and teardown engines like VLLM, SGLang, or TRT-LLM to test each new experiment. However, engine start times are tens of minutes, significantly impeding experimentation throughput (see table below). Instead, TKCC proposes a new paradigm of “persistent engines” where the engine starts up once and can hot-reload any candidate forward pass, without any restarts. To ensure that the persistent engines constantly have new optimizations to test, TKCC spawns multiple agents that continually generate ideas and communicate via a message board to parallelize their efforts.

PhaseStatus Quo (s)Together Compiler (s)
Process + worker init.93–
Weight loading50–
KV-cache sizing21–
JIT kernel warm-up93–
Autotuning193–
API server ready10–
RPC call + Together Compiler setup–1.7
CUDA-graph capture77.3
Total time to serving4679.0

Table 1: Engine startup is expensive

2. TKCC balances the tradeoff between measurement throughput and measurement fidelity

‍Existing agent optimization systems either iteratively relaunch the inference engine, suffering from low experiment throughput, or optimize standalone kernels in isolation, outside of the inference engine, suffering from poor measurement fidelity. Systems that optimize standalone kernels often evaluate them using random input data. However, with modern architectures using data-dependent primitives like MoE and sparse-k attention, input data distributions have a direct effect on which optimization strategies may win (see figure below). High-fidelity inputs are important for effective optimization. TKCC uses a tier of persistent engines to balance the throughput-fidelity tradeoff: “fast engines” load a few layers and are ideal for rapid iteration and low-variance timings, while “slower engines” load many layers and are ideal for testing whether optimizations hold-up on real data distributions.

Figure 2: Input data changes optimization strategies.

%20%C2%B7%20on-brand%20%23151630.png)

Figure 3: Together Compiler’s two-tiered architecture outperforms alternatives.

3. TKCC utilizes a custom cost model to select parallelism strategies (e.g., TP, EP, DCP, etc.) for agents to achieve the highest performance

Existing systems have sophisticated methods for selecting inference configurations under SLA requirements. However, selecting the ideal configuration faces the same throughput-fidelity tradeoff: it is intractable to measure each parallelism configuration, especially because software implementations are immature. A naive approach is to select a parallelism strategy based on raw hardware specs or micro-benchmarks. However, this insufficiently captures data dependent traffic properties like MoE expert imbalance or uneven prompt length distributions. We designed a cost model that uses a tiered measurement strategy involving hardware specs, microbenchmarks, and measured forward passes to construct a high-fidelity representation while rapidly pruning the configuration search space to support continual traffic drift.

Figure 4: Measured layouts beat the hardware spec’s pick, and the best layout shifts with concurrency.

Results

We evaluate TKCC against three different types of baselines: Hand-tuned megakernels, InferenceX engine configurations, and popular AI codebases from diverse domains like weather modeling, PDE, time series and biology models.

MegaKernel workloads

We start by evaluating the canonical MegaKernel workload: Llama 1B at batch size 1. This model architecture has been well-optimized by both human experts and traditional machine learning compilers. TKCC generates 1.7x higher TPS and continues to perform as sequence length increases.

Figure 5: Together Compiler outperforms megakernel and CUDA graph baselines on both H100 and B200

InferenceX AgentX workloads

We evaluate TKCC on the AgentX benchmark from SemiAnalysis. We start from the best-reported open source engine configurations for frontier models across inference engines and hardware platforms. TKCC consistently sets the performance frontier across all settings, outperforming highly-optimized baselines by up to 2.6x higher TPS.1

We also evaluate specifically on the low-latency use case at batch size 1 and set the state-of-the-art performance with 1111 TPS on MiniMax M3.1-Flash and 1205 TPS on DeepSeek v4.1-Flash. For these results, we use our cost model to select the parallelism configuration instead of using the InferenceX configuration. We observe speedups with this approach.

Figure 6: Together Compiler serves more tokens per GPU at the same speed per user on most models.

Figure 7: Together Compiler is faster per user than the best InferenceX configuration on all six model and chip pairs

Across AI workloads

We select popular open-source code bases across weather modeling, PDE, time-series, and biology. We show the geometric mean speedups of TKCC over simply using Claude Code with the /goal command, illustrating that the principles of TKCC generalize across domains. We have been using TKCC as a general purpose AI compiler beyond LLM inference.

Figure 8: Together Compiler finds larger speedups than Claude Code on three of four models

Polymorphic AI systems is the next frontier

For Together AI, the most exciting systems challenge has been Polymorphic Inference. Inference is no longer about optimizing for a single traffic shape for a single hardware platform and model, traffic is constantly and dynamically evolving, much like financial markets, and that dynamism has opened up a whole host of new research questions.

Check out our paper to learn more.

And if these frontiers of AI systems excite you, feel free to reach out to us!

1 Trainium2 was run on a synthetic multi-turn dataset (70k ISL, 3.5k new ISL 95% cached, 700 OSL) instead of AgentX since our implementation does not yet support higher concurrencies on the limited HBM capacity.

item.title: [Together AI] Polymorphic Inference: self-tuning inference for open models
item.content:encoded:
All blog posts

Company

Published 11/4/2026

From Static to Polymorphic Inference: A new era for production open-source inference systems

As of today, many of the models you run through Together AI endpoints are fully optimized by AI agents: the world’s first production-scale recursive self-improvement (RSI) inference system.

  • AuthorsBy Simran Arora (SVP of Research, AI Systems) and Dan Fu (Founding SVP of Research)
  • Table of contents40+ Models Chosen for Production...40+ Models Chosen for Production...40+ Models Chosen for Production...
  • Links in this articleTogether Compiler

Summary

At Together AI, we focus on making AI abundantly available to every individual user and organization. Our research team – the researchers behind FlashAttention, ThunderKittens, ThunderAgent, and more – has been a key driver behind our inference excellence. As the inference market grows exponentially, we’ve been focusing on how to scale our research capacity to enable abundant intelligence for all.

*This has required a shift in our thinking from Static Inference to **Polymorphic Inference – which is our response to the velocity of new model releases, diversity of model architectures, fast-changing workloads, and fast-changing hardware platforms. In this blog, we’ll highlight our research agenda for the Polymorphic Inference era – and how we are continuously using AI agents to optimize their own inference with Continuous Compilation**.*

What is Polymorphic Inference?

Over the past year, there has been a marked step change in the diversity of open-source models and the ways that these models are deployed in production environments. We see this step change as requiring a new approach that we call Polymorphic Inference.

Polymorphic Inference (inference in “many shapes” from Greek) is a response to a number of changes we are seeing across the industry, for us primarily defined by the convergence of a few trends:

  • Increasing velocity of model releases. Open-source models are coming out at a faster clip – and are far more diverse – than ever before. 80% of traffic on OpenRouter goes to models released in the last three months.
  • Increasing diversity of model architectures. All of the top-ten most popular OSS models in use today use different architectures (not to mention the many closed-source architectures served by our partners).
  • Traffic shapes that continuously evolve. We serve new users, organizations, and geographies every day across a broad range of workload shapes and SLAs. Product or algorithmic changes in harnesses, post-training of open-source models can all lead to changes to traffic shapes (e.g., a new post-train that increases the amount of tokens that a model spends thinking in exchange for higher quality).
  • Hardware that is changing faster and more frequently. We have seen major changes in inference serving capabilities from B200 to GB300, and are on the cusp of seeing the first Vera Rubin deployments (not to mention CPU-level optimizations, advanced storage systems, and alternative inference chips).

Polymorphic Inference is our response to these changes – inference that changes and adapts to these rapidly-changing environments.

We contrast this against the state of the world before the explosion of OSS inference – which we retroactively call the era of “Static Inference.” Whereas modern Polymorphic Inference takes on infinite different shapes, Static Inference is defined by closed models, traditional Transformer architectures, single-user, and single-hardware-platform inference.

From Static to Polymorphic Inference

One of our motivations behind writing this blog post is that a lot of the discourse around inference systems remains quite focused on the legacy Static Inference paradigm.

  • For example, the typical vLLM, SGLang, or InferenceX / AgentX recipe online is launched with a static hyperparameter-tuned inference engine configuration. A config optimized for one setting is not necessarily the best one for another setting.
  • Open-source kernels are frequently released assuming some static traffic shapes and design decisions that can be miscalibrated against real production traffic. A classic example is MoE kernels; an MoE kernel that works well against random tokens may not transfer to real production settings.

We take some of the blame here! For a long time, it has been possible to write kernels that are optimal for a variety of settings. FlashAttention, near and dear to our hearts, is still one of the best ways to run training workloads and many prefill workloads.

And nearly two years ago we wrote about megakernels for AI inference, a single kernel painstakingly designed around a single static shape (e.g., batch size one Llama 1B). But through the experience of putting some of the first megakernels into production for our customers last year, we learned an interesting lesson: megakernel fusion is actually not the right design goal for modern Polymorphic Inference! In the era of Polymorphic Inference, every variation – from model architecture (e.g. MoE), to workload (dynamic workloads larger than batch size 1) – requires different technical approaches.

Optimizing Polymorphic Inference for diverse, rapidly-changing conditions

At Together, we are systems and AI researchers at heart – so we view this as an incredibly exciting time to be rethinking our research agenda for this bright new future.

‍So, what’s the solution when your production traffic becomes ever more diverse? Get the AI agents to optimize themselves. This is the RSI moment for OSS models!

Achieving Polymorphic Inference requires solving a number of technical challenges in how we serve models. An ideal Polymorphic Inference experience is one that responds to the rapidly changing landscape of model architectures and workloads.

For example:

  • If your traffic shape changes – either through a product change or a change in user behavior – you should expect your inference system to adapt quickly.
  • If you are deploying workloads on a new model – you should expect your inference provider to approach ideal hand-tuned baselines as soon as possible.
  • If you have an existing product with stable user traffic, and you deploy it on a new hardware platform – you should expect performance to approach hardware bounds as quickly as possible.

These are lofty goals, but we believe that they are worth striving for. For us, one of the keys to achieving these goals is getting AI agents to help optimize themselves. The RSI loop is here for OSS models!

Continuous Compilation with Together Compiler

One of the projects that we’re announcing today as a first step towards achieving our goals for Polymorphic Inference is Together Compiler, a rapid AI-powered performance optimization RSI loop. Today, Together Compiler powers Continuous Compilation optimization loops across many of our top production inference workloads.

Together Compiler takes the classic challenge of optimizing inference workloads and recasts it from a traditional compiler translation problem to an agentic search problem. Together Compiler identifies a core set of key optimization patterns and pairs a swarm of agents with a high-fidelity persistent engine for fast iterations. This work was the result of many months of work by Together’s Frontier Performance team, notably from Reyna Abhyankar and Dylan Lim!

Together Compiler is running in production today on some of our most popular serverless endpoints, where it has found further gains on top of already highly optimized code.

Excitingly, Together Compiler gives us the ability to quickly adapt to rapidly changing model architectures and traffic workloads. We call this capability Continuous Compilation. Whereas previously new workloads would require new sets of hand-written kernels and optimizations, Continuous Compilation driven by Together Compiler means that we can automatically adapt to new traffic shapes and workloads.

What’s coming next from Together AI’s Research team

We’ve learned a ton scaling Together AI to serve trillions of tokens per day (and for the first time even serving more tokens than closed-source model labs on OpenRouter earlier in October!). This has informed our vision and research agenda for the Polymorphic Inference era. Here’s a little preview of some of the things coming up on our research agenda:

Self-serve Continuous Compilation with Together Compiler‍

Performance optimization needs to be a function of the workload deployment: the model, engine, traffic shape, and customer use case. Soon, our customers will be able to use Together Compiler to optimize their dedicated endpoints for their unique workloads at the click of a button.

Together Compiler is available to end customers in limited beta today – reach out if you want early access!

Shape-shifting speculative decoding

Inference engine configurations proposed in open-source repositories, VLLM, InferenceX, AgentX launch the engine with a fixed speculative decoding draft model and lookahead parameter. Speculative decoding needs to adapt per-domain, per-request, per-token and as a function of the traffic load.

ThunderAgent Router: Routing across heterogeneous deployments

Serverless inference endpoints serve an enormous number of users, each bringing their own traffic shapes and SLAs. This heterogeneity requires us to dynamically route requests across workers and deployment configurations across our clusters. We released ThunderAgent as an ICML 2026 Spotlight paper to share some early insights and have expanded on these foundations in production.

Together Post-Training

Several customers now want to incorporate open-source model backends into their AI applications. This requires choosing an open-source model, selecting and customizing the harness to the customer’s specific tool calls and use cases, and post-training the model to interact well with this harness. Our close partnerships with model labs including Moonshot, Minimax, and others allows us to help our customers customize open-source models for their own use cases and really own their intelligence stack.

TogetherLink: Workload-aware model routing

As OSS models improve, a key piece is getting them into everyone’s hands. The common perception is that a closed source model like Opus 5.5 is always best. But, as the history of AI has repeatedly shown us, ensembling a few pretty good models can definitely outperform using a singular great model, if combined in the right way. This builds on our roots in weak supervision at Stanford’s Hazy Research Lab (Ask Me Anything) and on our own work on combining models (Mixture-of-Agents, ICLR 2025).

Abundant intelligence for all

Inference is one of the most fascinating problems in AI Systems and we’ve unlocked a whole host of new insights through the scale at which we serve. To achieve our goal of making AI abundant for everyone we need our inference systems to continuously customize to each user and each workload in the Polymorphic Inference era. We’re excited to help close the loop and play a small role in making AI systems truly recursively self-improving.

If the ideas behind Polymorphic Inference ring true to your organization or your use case, please reach out for early access – we’d love to help you navigate these new complexities.

And lastly – if you want to help us tackle the challenge of Polymorphic Inference together, please take a look at our careers page – we’re hiring!
