item.title: [Amazon Bedrock] Bring structured and unstructured data together with Amazon…
item.description: Full title: Bring structured and unstructured data together with Amazon Quick
item.content:encoded:
Artificial Intelligence

Bring structured and unstructured data together with Amazon Quick

Organizations collect data in many forms. Structured data lives in databases and spreadsheets, whereas unstructured data sits in documents, reports, and files stored across file systems. Analyzing both together typically requires switching between multiple tools, running separate queries, and manually correlating results.

Amazon Quick addresses this with a unified experience. You can connect structured data through enriched datasets and unstructured data through S3-backed knowledge bases. You can then query both through a single conversational AI agent.

In this post, you learn how to:

  • Connect Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) as a data source and create a knowledge base.
  • Build a Space that combines structured and unstructured data.
  • Create and configure a custom chat agent that queries across both data types.
  • Ask questions that span structured and unstructured sources in a single conversation.

Solution architecture

The following diagram illustrates how each component connects to deliver a unified data experience through Amazon Quick.

Figure 1: Solution architecture for combining structured and unstructured data in Amazon Quick

The architecture has three layers:

  • Data layer: Your data exists in two forms. Unstructured content (documents, PDFs, reports) is stored in Amazon S3 and indexed through a knowledge base. Structured data (metrics, sales figures, and operational key performance indicators) is loaded as enriched datasets with semantic descriptions that the agent uses to translate questions into SQL.
  • Workspace layer: A Space brings both data types together into a single workspace. The Space references your knowledge base for unstructured queries and your datasets for structured queries. It can also include dashboards, file uploads, and action connectors. This is the layer where data from different sources converges into a unified context.
  • Agent layer: The custom chat agent links to the Space and uses it as its knowledge source. When a user asks a question, the agent determines whether to query the knowledge base, the dataset, or both, and returns a combined response with citations. Amazon Quick also applies built-in AI guardrails, such as content safety screening, to chat interactions.

With this layered approach, you can expand the solution over time. When you add a new data source to the Space, the agent linked to that Space can use it, and responses respect the permissions of the user who asks.

Prerequisites

To follow along with this walkthrough, you need:

  • An Amazon Quick account with an Enterprise subscription for the user who follows this walkthrough (creating datasets requires Enterprise). For details, see Amazon Quick pricing.
  • An Amazon S3 bucket for your business documents. To create one, see the Amazon S3 User Guide.
  • Amazon Quick access to your S3 bucket, granted by an Amazon Quick administrator. In the admin console, the administrator chooses Permissions, then AWS resources, selects Amazon S3, and chooses Select S3 buckets. Selected buckets have read-only permissions by default.
  • Permissions to create integrations, knowledge bases, datasets, spaces, and chat agents in Amazon Quick.

Prepare your sample data

This walkthrough uses two types of data:

Unstructured documents: Upload these to your Amazon S3 bucket for the knowledge base:

  • AnyCompany_Business_Review.pdf
  • AnyCompany_Market_Analysis_Report.pdf
  • AnyCompany_Product_Strategy_Memo.pdf

Structured data: Download this file to your computer. You upload it directly to Amazon Quick in Step 3:

  • Product_Sales.csv

Step 1: Create an Amazon S3 integration

Start by connecting Amazon Quick to your S3 bucket. From the Amazon Quick console, select Knowledge in the left navigation panel.

The knowledge page shows available connector types, including Amazon Q Business, Web Crawler, Amazon S3, and third-party options like Google Drive, OneDrive, and Microsoft SharePoint.

Under Amazon S3, choose Add. In the Create S3 knowledge base dialog, on the Connect S3 bucket page, provide the following details:

  • Name: A descriptive name for your integration (for example, “My Data Access Integration”).
  • S3 bucket location: Choose Quick Suite instance account to use a bucket in the same AWS account as Amazon Quick, or Other AWS account for a bucket in a different account.
  • S3 bucket URL: The S3 URI of the bucket containing your data. The bucket must be in the same Region as Amazon Quick.

Choose Next.

Figure 2: Create integration dialog showing the S3 connection fields

Step 2: Create a knowledge base

After the S3 integration is created, Amazon Quick prompts you to create a knowledge base. The knowledge base indexes your S3 content for AI-powered search.

Configure the knowledge base:

  • Name: “Business Knowledge Base”.
  • Description (optional): Notes about how the knowledge base will be used.
  • Content: Select “Add all content” to index everything in the connected S3 bucket, or “Add specific content” to specify the S3 prefixes for the folders and files to include (prefix filters are case-sensitive).

Next: Additional settings opens optional settings for document-level access control lists (ACLs) and a metadata files folder. Decide whether to use ACLs before you create the knowledge base, because you can’t change that choice later. This walkthrough uses sample data, so the default settings are sufficient. For details, see Set up and manage Amazon S3 integration.

Choose Create. A success banner confirms the S3 integration, and the knowledge base begins indexing in the background.

Figure 3: Create knowledge base dialog with the Business Knowledge Base name and content options

Step 3: Create and enrich a dataset

A dataset is your structured data file loaded into Amazon Quick. By enriching the dataset with semantic descriptions, custom instructions, and correct data types, the AI agent can interpret your data more accurately. It can then translate natural language questions into SQL queries.

Create the dataset

  • From the Amazon Quick home page, navigate to Data in the left navigation.
  • Choose Create dataset, then select Upload file.
  • Select the Product_Sales.csv file you downloaded earlier and choose Open.
  • On the confirmation screen, review the column names and data types. Choose Next to create the dataset.

Amazon Quick ingests the file into SPICE (the in-memory calculation engine) and the dataset appears in your dataset list.

The dataset takes its name from the uploaded file, so it appears as Product_Sales.csv in your account.

Enrich the dataset

Enriching your dataset with semantic information helps the AI understand your data in business context. The agent uses this context to translate natural language questions into more accurate SQL queries. From the dataset page, choose Edit dataset to enter the data preparation view.

Transform: Fix data types

In the Transform tab, update data types for columns that were auto-detected incorrectly. For this dataset:

  • Change Order Date and Date Key from String to Date.
  • Change Customer ID from String to Integer.
  • Change Sales, Discount, and Profit from String to Decimal.
  • Change Quantity and Unit Price from String to Integer.

Figure 4: Transform view showing data type changes applied to the Product_Sales.csv dataset

Output: Add semantic context

Select the Output tab to access the dataset-level enrichment fields. Here you provide context that helps the AI understand what your data represents and how to use it.

Description: Add a dataset-level description:

“Product sales transaction data for AnyCompany, covering orders from FY2024-FY2025 across North America, EMEA, Asia Pacific, and Latin America. Includes order details, customer information, product lines, and revenue metrics.”

Custom instructions: Add guidance for how the AI should query this data:

USAGE GUIDELINES:

  • Revenue values are in USD.
  • When comparing performance, group by Region (North America, EMEA, Asia Pacific, Latin America).
  • Order Date should be used for time-based trend analysis. The fiscal year matches the calendar year.
  • Date Key is a numeric YYYYMMDD representation of Order Date.
  • Sales = Quantity x Unit Price x (1 – Discount)

COMMON USE CASES:

  • Regional sales performance comparison.
  • Product line revenue analysis.
  • Quarterly trend identification.
  • Customer segmentation by industry and segment.

TAGS: Sales, revenue, orders, regional performance, product analytics

Column descriptions: Select each column in the left panel and add a description. For example:

  • Order ID: “Unique identifier for each sales transaction (format: REGION-YYYY-NNNNNN)”
  • Region: “Geographic sales region: North America, EMEA, Asia Pacific, or Latin America”
  • Product: “AnyCompany product name: Analytics Pro, Connect, Automate, AI Assistant, Data Catalog, or Integration Hub”
  • Sales: “Order revenue in USD after discount”
  • Segment: “Customer size segment: Enterprise, Mid-Market, or SMB”

Figure 5: Output view showing dataset details with Description and Custom instructions configured

Choose Save & publish to save your changes. The dataset summary now shows the columns with their correct data types and the descriptions you added.

Figure 6: Enriched Product_Sales.csv dataset summary showing all 16 columns, data types, and descriptions

This enriched dataset provides the structured data layer for your solution. When the agent receives a natural language question about sales data, it uses these descriptions and instructions to generate more accurate SQL queries. Combined with the knowledge base from Step 2, you now have both structured and unstructured data ready to bring together in a Space.

Step 4: Create a Space

Spaces in Amazon Quick act as unified data workspaces. A Space can hold file uploads, dashboards, knowledge bases, actions, and datasets, giving your chat agent a single location to query across data types.

From the left navigation, select Spaces and create a new Space. Name it “Business Intelligence Hub”.

Add your knowledge base and dataset to the Space:

  • Choose Add knowledge and select Knowledge bases from the list. Select “Business Knowledge Base” from the list.
  • Choose Add knowledge again and select Datasets from the list. Select “Product_Sales.csv” from the list.

The Space now shows both your knowledge base (unstructured documents) and your enriched dataset (structured sales data) linked as data sources. This is the central hub where both data types come together, giving your chat agent a single place to query across everything. Figure 7 shows the Space with both resources in the Ready state.

Figure 7: Business Intelligence Hub Space showing the Product_Sales.csv dataset and Business Knowledge Base

Step 5: Create a custom chat agent

Navigate to Chat agents in the left navigation and choose Create chat agent. Amazon Quick presents a prompt builder where you can describe your agent in natural language or choose from templates like Training Guide, Project Coordinator, and Onboarding Helper.

For this walkthrough, choose Skip to configure the agent manually.

Figure 8: Chat agent creation screen with the prompt builder and sample templates

Configure the agent persona

The configuration panel has several sections. Start with the Agent Persona:

  • Agent identity: “Business Intelligence Assistant”
  • Description: “An AI assistant that breaks down information silos by analyzing business data from your knowledge base”

For Agent Persona instructions, enter:

You are a Business Intelligence Assistant designed to help organizations break down information silos. Your primary functions are:

1. Analyze business data stored in S3
2. Retrieve relevant findings from the reports and memos in the knowledge base
3. Provide comprehensive insights that connect internal data with external trends
4. Generate clear, actionable recommendations based on data analysis

When answering questions, always cite your sources and explain how you arrived at your conclusions. Focus on delivering practical business value and highlighting patterns across different information sources.

A note appears confirming that your chat agent comes equipped with enterprise guardrails.

Figure 9: Agent persona configuration with identity and persona instructions filled in

Set communication style

Under Communication style, pick a response style preset. Options include Executive, Technical, and Creative. For a business intelligence use case, select Executive.

Link knowledge sources

Under Knowledge Sources, choose Link spaces and select the “Business Intelligence Hub” Space you created earlier. This gives the agent access to your S3 knowledge base and other data sources in that Space. When you link a Space, the agent answers from large language model (LLM) knowledge and the linked resources only.

You can also attach reference documents (PDF, TXT, HTML, MD, CSV, DOC, DOCX) directly to the agent for additional context. Amazon Quick extracts up to 100,000 characters of text from the reference documents that you upload.

Figure 10: Knowledge Sources section showing the linked Business Intelligence Hub Space

Customize the agent

Under Customization, configure:

  • Welcome message: “Hello! I’m your Business Intelligence Assistant. I can help you analyze your sales data and business documents and provide insights by comparing internal information with market trends. How can I help you today?”
  • Suggested prompts: “Summarize key insights from our reports” and “Analyze our quarterly sales performance”

Figure 11: Customization section with the welcome message and suggested prompts

Launch the agent

Choose Launch chat agent. The right panel shows a live preview of your agent with the welcome message and suggested prompts displayed.

Figure 12: Launched Business Intelligence Assistant with the welcome message and suggested prompts in the chat panel

Step 6: Query across structured and unstructured data

With the agent running, start with a question about your business results:

How did sales change by region in 2025?

For this question, the agent combines results from the Product_Sales.csv dataset with the documents in the S3 knowledge base. It returns a response with regional sales breakdowns, trends, and citations that point back to each source.

Figure 13 shows the response. Each citation marker links a figure back to its source document.

Figure 13: Chat agent response showing regional sales analysis from the dataset and the knowledge base documents

When you ask a question about structured data, the agent uses text-to-SQL to translate your natural language into a SQL query. It runs the query against the dataset and returns the results in a readable format. This means you can ask complex analytical questions without writing SQL yourself.

Next, ask about a specific document:

What are the key strategic priorities outlined in our product strategy memo?

The agent summarizes the strategic pillars, the FY2026 roadmap, and the investment requirements from the Product Strategy Memo, as shown in Figure 14.

Figure 14: Chat agent response summarizing strategic priorities from the Product Strategy Memo

Finally, ask a question that needs both data types:

How do our 2025 sales results align with the market trends identified in our analysis report?

The agent compares the trends in the Market Analysis Report with results from your sales data and cites each source, as shown in Figure 15.

Figure 15: Chat agent response comparing 2025 sales results with market trends from the Market Analysis Report

This is the core value of combining data types in a single Space. The agent can pull from structured CSV data and unstructured documents in the same response. You don’t need to know where the data lives.

Step 7: Generate artifacts and reports using natural language

The Business Intelligence Assistant can also generate formatted documents, including Microsoft PowerPoint presentations, Microsoft Excel spreadsheets, and Microsoft Word documents. Try these prompts in the chat agent:

  • “Create a PowerPoint presentation summarizing AnyCompany’s Q4 2025 sales performance by region, including key trends and recommendations.”
  • “Generate an Excel spreadsheet showing the top 10 orders by revenue with Order ID, Region, Product, and Revenue columns.”
  • “Create a Word document with a quarterly business review summary based on our annual review data.”

Figure 16: Chat agent confirming the request and preparing a PowerPoint outline for AnyCompany’s Q4 2025 sales performance

Figure 17: Generated eight-slide PowerPoint with a downloadable AnyCompany_FY2025_Sales_Performance.pptx file

Step 8: Share the agent

When you launch a chat agent, it remains private until you share it. After you test the agent, share it with your team:

  • From the left navigation, choose Chat agents.
  • In the Actions column for Business Intelligence Assistant, choose the menu icon, and then choose Share.
  • Enter the users or groups to share with, assign Owner or Viewer permissions, and then choose Share.

The agent returns permissions-aware responses, and a knowledge base is available only to its creator until you update its permissions. Make sure that the people you share the agent with also have access to the Space, the knowledge base, and the dataset. For details, see Custom chat agents.

What you accomplished

In this walkthrough, you:

  • Connected Amazon S3 as a data source through an integration.
  • Created a knowledge base that indexes unstructured business documents.
  • Created and enriched a Product Sales dataset for structured data queries.
  • Built a Space that serves as a unified data hub for your chat agent.
  • Configured a custom chat agent with a defined persona and linked knowledge sources.
  • Queried the agent across structured and unstructured data in a single conversation.
  • Generated a PowerPoint presentation from a chat prompt.
  • Shared the agent with your team.

Best practices

Use the following practices as you move from this walkthrough to your own data:

  • Organize your S3 data: Use clear folder structures and file naming conventions. A clear structure also makes it more straightforward to scope a knowledge base to specific S3 prefixes.
  • Write specific persona instructions: The more specific your instructions, the more consistent the agent responses. Include guidance on how to cite sources and handle ambiguous queries.
  • Use Spaces to control scope: Rather than giving an agent access to everything, create focused Spaces with only the data sources relevant to that agent’s purpose.
  • Start with suggested prompts: Suggested prompts help users understand what the agent can do. Choose prompts that demonstrate the agent’s range across both structured and unstructured data.
  • Test before sharing: Use the preview panel to test your agent with representative questions before sharing it with your team.

Security considerations

Under the AWS shared responsibility model, you are responsible for configuring access to your data, knowledge bases, and agents. Consider the following as you adapt this solution:

  • Grant least-privilege S3 access: Give Amazon Quick access only to the buckets that your knowledge bases need. Buckets that an administrator selects have read-only permissions by default. If you create knowledge bases through the API, you can provide a custom AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role for an individual S3 data source instead of granting account-wide S3 access.
  • Control document access: If documents require per-user or per-group access, enable document-level ACLs when you create the knowledge base. You can’t change this choice later.
  • Encrypted buckets: If your bucket uses AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) keys, follow the AWS KMS steps in the administrator setup guide.
  • Add only trusted content: The agent uses the documents in your knowledge base to form responses, so include only content from sources you trust.
  • Share selectively: Chat agents and knowledge bases are private by default. Share them only with the users and groups that need them.
  • Use guardrails as one layer: Amazon Quick includes built-in content safety screening, and administrators can add up to 50 blocked words or phrases. These controls help reduce risk but don’t replace your responsibility to configure access and permissions. For details, see AI guardrails in Amazon Quick.

Clean up

To avoid ongoing charges, remove the resources you created:

  • Delete the chat agent from the Chat agents page.
  • Delete the Space from the Spaces page.
  • Delete the Product_Sales.csv dataset from the Datasets page.
  • Delete the knowledge base and S3 integration from the Knowledge page.
  • If you created an S3 bucket specifically for this walkthrough, empty and delete it. Deleting a bucket and its objects is permanent, so back up any data that you want to keep.

Amazon Quick user subscriptions and account fees are billed separately from these resources. For details, see Amazon Quick pricing.

Conclusion

Amazon Quick helps you bring structured and unstructured data together. In this post, you connected S3 as a knowledge base, enriched a dataset, built a Space, and created a custom chat agent. Business users can now query both data types through a single conversational interface, without needing to know where the data lives or how to write queries.

About the authors

item.title: [Amazon Bedrock] ServiceNow on-behalf-of token exchange with Bedrock AgentCor…
item.description: Full title: ServiceNow on-behalf-of token exchange with Bedrock AgentCore Gateway
item.content:encoded:
Artificial Intelligence

ServiceNow on-behalf-of token exchange with Bedrock AgentCore Gateway

AI agents that interact with enterprise APIs on behalf of users need to maintain user identity throughout the request chain. Without identity propagation, API calls arrive at downstream services as the application itself rather than the user who initiated the action. This breaks audit trails, bypasses user-level access controls, and violates the principle of least privilege.

Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. This post shows how to configure AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, for an on-behalf-of (OBO) token exchange with Microsoft Entra ID. An AI agent can then call the ServiceNow REST API while preserving the calling user’s identity. You configure the token exchange on the gateway target, and AgentCore Gateway performs the exchange on each request. The pattern can be applied to other REST APIs protected by OAuth.

In production, you can additionally pair identity propagation with Amazon Bedrock Guardrails to filter harmful content and validate the agent’s inputs and outputs.

Solution overview

The architecture involves three key components connected through AgentCore Gateway:

  • An AI agent application, protected by Microsoft Entra ID through an OAuth application registration.
  • A Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, implemented using AgentCore Gateway, sitting between the agent and ServiceNow.
  • The ServiceNow REST API, configured with an inbound OAuth integration tied to Microsoft Entra ID.

The following figure shows the end-to-end solution architecture, including components within AWS, Microsoft Entra ID, and ServiceNow.

Figure 1: Solution architecture across AWS, Microsoft Entra ID, and ServiceNow

As shown in Figure 1, the user acquires a JSON Web Token (JWT) to invoke the agent 1. The agent authenticates to the gateway with a JWT token scoped to the agent’s own application registration 2. The gateway then exchanges that token, using the OBO flow, for a new token scoped to the ServiceNow API connector, with the original user’s identity preserved 3. ServiceNow receives a valid token whose preferred_username claim maps to an existing ServiceNow user and applies that user’s permissions to the API call 4.

How OBO token exchange works in this context

When the agent calls the gateway, it presents a JWT with an audience claim matching the agent’s client ID (for example, 3ff88e17-XXXX-XXXX-XXXX-XXXXXXXXXXXX). ServiceNow, however, expects a token with an audience claim matching its own API connector client ID (5d4a7a11-XXXX-XXXX-XXXX-XXXXXXXXXXXX).

The OBO flow bridges this gap. AgentCore Gateway sends the inbound token to the Entra token endpoint along with the agent application’s client credentials, the target scope, and a parameter requested_token_use: on_behalf_of. Entra validates that the calling user consented to the delegation, then issues a new token for the ServiceNow API with the original user’s claims intact.

Prerequisites

Before you begin, you need the following:

  • An AWS account with access to AgentCore Gateway.
  • A Microsoft Entra ID tenant with permissions to create application registrations. Your account needs at least the Application Developer role to register applications.
  • A ServiceNow instance with administrative access to configure inbound OAuth integrations. You can create a ServiceNow personal developer instance (PDI) at the ServiceNow personal developer instance signup page https://developer.servicenow.com/.
  • Two Entra application registrations: one representing the AI agent, and one representing the ServiceNow API connector.

Configuring Microsoft Entra ID

Start by creating an application registration to represent the ServiceNow API connector. The following screenshot shows the application registration page for the ServiceNow API Connector in Microsoft Entra ID.

Figure 2: Application registration for the ServiceNow API connector in Microsoft Entra ID

After creating, in the Overview page note the Application (client) ID.

In the navigation menu expand Manage and select Expose an API and add a scope named user_impersonation using the default Application ID URI. This scope is what the OBO flow requests when exchanging tokens. The following screenshot shows how to expose an API in Microsoft Entra ID.

Figure 3: Exposing the user_impersonation scope in Microsoft Entra ID

Next, create an application registration for the AI agent. The following screenshot shows the application registration page in Microsoft Entra ID for the ServiceNow Agent application.

Figure 4: Application registration for the ServiceNow Agent in Microsoft Entra ID

Note the Application (client) ID for the ServiceNowAgent.

Create a client secret on this registration. The gateway needs these credentials to perform the OBO exchange. The following screenshot shows how you can create a client secret on the ServiceNow Agent application registration in Microsoft Entra ID.

Figure 5: Creating a client secret on the ServiceNow Agent application registration

Then configure the agent application to have API permissions to call the ServiceNow API connector application. The following screenshot shows the API permissions that you need to configure on the ServiceNow Agent application registration in Microsoft Entra ID.

Figure 6: API permission configuration in Microsoft Entra ID

No changes to the Entra configuration are needed beyond what you would set up for any standard OBO integration between two applications.

Configuring ServiceNow

In the ServiceNow administrative console, navigate to System OAuth > Inbound Integrations and create a new inbound integration (Third party ID token issued by OIDC supporting identity provider). Specify the client ID from the ServiceNow API connector application registration you created in Entra. The following screenshot shows the configuration of the inbound integration in ServiceNow.

Figure 7: Configuring the inbound integration in ServiceNow

In the same screen, create a new OpenID Connect (OIDC) provider configuration and enter the OIDC metadata URL for your Entra tenant. Map the user claim to the appropriate user field. For example, if your Entra tenant places the user’s email in the preferred_username claim, map that to the Email field in ServiceNow. Clear JTI verification if your Entra tenant doesn’t include it in tokens. Entra uses an internal claim named uti on tokens it issues, which is equivalent to JTI. Consider mapping this uti claim to a jti claim to provide additional replay protection and denylisting. The following screenshot shows how to configure the OIDC provider in ServiceNow.

Figure 8: Configuring the OAuth OIDC provider in ServiceNow

Finally, in the same screen, create an auth scope for the integration (for example, APIConnector). The following screenshot shows how to create a new auth scope in ServiceNow.

Figure 9: Creating a new auth scope in ServiceNow

Limit the auth scope to the Table API, or whichever ServiceNow APIs your agent needs to access, as shown in the following screenshot.

Figure 10: Limiting the auth scope to the Table API in ServiceNow

After this configuration is complete, ServiceNow accepts authorization tokens with an audience of your API connector’s client ID and resolves the calling user from the preferred_username claim.

Configuring AgentCore Gateway

With Entra and ServiceNow configured, you can now set up AgentCore Gateway to handle the OBO exchange natively.

Step 1: Create an outbound auth configuration

Create a new outbound auth configuration (choose Build > Identity > Add Outbound Auth > Add OAuth client) in AgentCore and select Customized provider. Enter the client ID and client secret from your agent application registration, along with the Entra discovery URL as shown in the following screenshot.

Figure 11: Adding an OAuth client in AgentCore Gateway

Expand Additional configurations and select JWT authorization grant as shown in the following screenshot. This tells the gateway to use a JWT-based grant type for token exchange.

Figure 12: Configuring the JWT authorization grant

Step 2: Create the gateway with MCP version 2025-11-25

Create a new AgentCore Gateway (Build > Gateways > Create gateway). When defining the gateway details, expand Additional configurations — optional and select MCP version 2025-11-25 as shown in the following screenshot. This version is required for native OBO support. You can’t turn on native OBO for gateways created with earlier MCP versions.

Figure 13: Selecting MCP version 2025-11-25

Configure the inbound identity using your agent’s application registration (select Use existing identity provider configurations), as you would for any gateway that accepts Entra-authenticated requests.

Under JWT Authorization Configuration add the Application ID we documented earlier for the ServiceNowAgent as shown in the following screenshot.

Figure 14: Configuring inbound authorization in AgentCore Gateway

Step 3: Add a target with token exchange

Add a target to the gateway pointing to your ServiceNow REST endpoint. Define the schema inline. For example, to expose a tool called ListIncidents that calls the ServiceNow Table API, you can use the following OpenAPI specification (replace the server URL with that for your PDI).

{
  "openapi": "3.0.0",
  "info": {
    "title": "ServiceNow Incident API (Minimal)",
    "description": "A subset of the ServiceNow Table API for listing incident records.",
    "version": "1.0.0"
  },
  "servers": [
    {
      "url": "https://devxxx.service-now.com/api/now/table",
      "variables": {
        "instance": {
          "default": "devxxx",
          "description": "Your ServiceNow instance name."
        }
      }
    }
  ],
  "paths": {
    "/incident": {
      "get": {
        "operationId": "getIncidents",
        "summary": "List incidents",
        "description": "Retrieves a list of incident records from the ServiceNow instance.",
        "parameters": [
          {
            "name": "sysparm_limit",
            "in": "query",
            "description": "Maximum number of records to return.",
            "schema": {
              "type": "integer",
              "default": 10
            }
          },
          {
            "name": "sysparm_query",
            "in": "query",
            "description": "An encoded query string to filter results (e.g., active=true).",
            "schema": {
              "type": "string"
            }
          },
          {
            "name": "sysparm_fields",
            "in": "query",
            "description": "A comma-separated list of fields to return.",
            "schema": {
              "type": "string"
            }
          }
        ],
        "responses": {
          "200": {
            "description": "A successful response containing an array of incidents.",
            "content": {
              "application/json": {
                "schema": {
                  "type": "object",
                  "properties": {
                    "result": {
                      "type": "array",
                      "items": {
                        "$ref": "#/components/schemas/Incident"
                      }
                    }
                  }
                }
              }
            }
          },
          "401": {
            "description": "Unauthorized - Invalid credentials."
          }
        },
        "security": [
          {
            "bearerAuth": []
          }
        ]
      }
    }
  },
  "components": {
    "securitySchemes": {
      "bearerAuth": {
        "type": "http",
        "scheme": "bearer",
        "bearerFormat": "JWT"
      }
    },
    "schemas": {
      "Incident": {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {
          "sys_id": {
            "type": "string",
            "description": "Unique identifier for the incident."
          },
          "number": {
            "type": "string",
            "description": "Incident ID (e.g., INC0000001)."
          },
          "short_description": {
            "type": "string",
            "description": "A brief summary of the incident."
          },
          "severity": {
            "type": "string",
            "description": "The severity level of the incident."
          },
          "state": {
            "type": "string",
            "description": "The current state of the incident (e.g., New, In Progress, Closed)."
          },
          "sys_created_on": {
            "type": "string",
            "format": "date-time",
            "description": "The timestamp when the incident was created."
          }
        }
      }
    }
  }
}

The following screenshot shows how to configure the REST API target in AgentCore Gateway with the OpenAPI schema.

Figure 15: Configuring the REST API target with the ServiceNow OpenAPI schema

For the Outbound Auth configuration on the target, select OAuth as the outbound identity provider and choose the outbound auth configuration you created in Step 1.

Now expand the Additional configurations section and select Token exchange grant. Configure the following:

Scope: api://5d4a7a11-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx/user_impersonation

This is the scope you exposed on the ServiceNow API connector application registration in Entra.

Custom parameter (key-value pair): requested_token_use:on_behalf_of

This parameter is critical. Without it, Entra doesn’t perform the OBO exchange and the call to ServiceNow fails with an authentication error.

The final configuration is shown in the following screenshot.

Figure 16: Token exchange grant configuration on the AgentCore Gateway target

Step 4: Save and test

Save the target configuration. AgentCore Gateway now automatically exchanges inbound tokens for valid ServiceNow tokens, preserving user identity, with no custom code.

When an agent calls the gateway, the following happens transparently:

  • The gateway receives the agent’s JWT (audience: agent client ID).
  • The gateway sends the token to Entra’s token endpoint with the OBO grant type.
  • Entra issues a new token (audience: ServiceNow API connector client ID) with the original user’s claims.
  • The gateway forwards the request to ServiceNow with the exchanged token.
  • ServiceNow resolves the user from the token and applies their permissions.

The following code snippet shows a minimal chat agent that interacts with ServiceNow through the MCP server.

import sys
import strands
from strands.models import BedrockModel
from strands.tools.mcp import MCPClient
from mcp.client.streamable_http import streamablehttp_client

token = sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else sys.exit("Usage: python snow_agent.py <TOKEN>")
MCP_URL = "<GATEWAY_URL>"
mcp_client = MCPClient(lambda: streamablehttp_client(url=MCP_URL, headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {token}"}))
agent = strands.Agent(
    model=BedrockModel(model_id="global.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-6", streaming=False),
    system_prompt=(
        "You have a tool called 'target-snow___getIncidents'. "
        "When asked about incidents, call it immediately with no parameters. "
        "Never ask the user for credentials or instance details --- the tool is pre-configured."
    ),
    tools=[mcp_client],
)

while (user_input := input("\nYou: ")).lower() not in ("quit", "exit", "q"):
    print(f"\nAgent: {agent(user_input)}")

Troubleshooting

If you receive authentication errors from ServiceNow, verify that:

  • The preferred_username claim in the exchanged token maps to a valid user email in ServiceNow.
  • The auth scope on the ServiceNow inbound integration permits access to the API endpoints your agent is calling.
  • The agent application has API permissions to the ServiceNow API connector application in Entra.

Cleaning up

To avoid ongoing charges, delete the following resources if you created them for testing:

  • The AgentCore Gateway and its targets.
  • The outbound auth configuration.
  • The Entra application registrations (if created specifically for this walkthrough).
  • The ServiceNow inbound integration and OIDC provider configuration.

Conclusion

The native OBO support in AgentCore Gateway removes the need for custom AWS Lambda interceptors to perform token exchanges. You configure the token exchange directly on the gateway target, and the gateway handles it transparently on every request. This approach maintains user identity across the agent-to-API chain, supports ServiceNow’s user-level access controls, and eliminates custom code that would need to be maintained separately.

To get started with AgentCore Gateway, see the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore documentation. For more on Microsoft Entra’s OBO flow, refer to the Microsoft identity platform documentation.

About the authors

item.title: [Amazon Bedrock] How Gen Digital built Norton Revamp’s AI-curated News Engine…
item.description: Full title: How Gen Digital built Norton Revamp’s AI-curated News Engine with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Web Search
item.content:encoded:
Artificial Intelligence

How Gen Digital built Norton Revamp’s AI-curated News Engine with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Web Search

Your professional reputation now lives online first. Recruiters check LinkedIn before returning a call. Clients review your digital presence before booking a first meeting. For ambitious professionals, that shift is an opportunity: a well-crafted online voice can open doors that a résumé alone never could.

But standing out takes more than content generation. It takes real-time awareness of what’s happening right now. A professional building a reputation as a generative AI thought leader needs to react to today’s breakthroughs, not last week’s headlines. And with feeds flooded by AI-generated noise, audiences reward authenticity and timeliness more than ever.

Web Search on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore made that possible. We built Norton Revamp, a generative AI-powered professional reputation management platform. At its heart is an AI-curated News Engine, powered by AgentCore Web Search, that grounds every content suggestion, goal recommendation, and news feed item in current, cited web knowledge. The platform launched in March 2026, built by a small group of engineers.

In this post, we show you how the Gen team builds an AI-curated News Engine in Norton Revamp with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Web Search to help customers turn ideas into engaging social media posts.

The challenge: Real-time grounding for professional content

Unlike chatbots that rely on static knowledge bases, Norton Revamp needs to understand what’s trending right now in each user’s professional domain. A cyber security expert needs today’s threat intelligence. A marketing leader needs this week’s industry shifts. Traditional approaches (custom web crawlers, third-party news APIs, static content databases) each carry trade-offs: infrastructure overhead, stale data, vendor complexity, or data egress risk.

We evaluated three alternatives before choosing AgentCore Web Search. Custom crawlers require ongoing maintenance and lag real time. Third-party news APIs added vendor contracts, API key management, and data leaving our AWS environment. Static knowledge bases were perpetually stale. AgentCore Web Search eliminated these concerns. It’s fully managed with zero infrastructure overhead, operates entirely within AWS with zero data egress, and returns cited sources with URLs and publication dates. This makes personalized, real-time news feeds viable at scale.

How AgentCore Web Search powers Norton Revamp

Web Search on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a fully managed web search capability, compliant with the Model Context Protocol (MCP). It’s available as a managed connector on the AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. Our agent sends a natural-language query, and Web Search returns relevant snippets, source URLs, titles, and publication dates that the model uses to produce grounded responses.

This capability powers three core features:

AI-curated news feed

Every user gets a personalized content stream surfacing the latest articles and trending topics tied to their goal. If you’re building a reputation as a generative AI thought leader, your feed prioritizes AI breakthroughs, industry analysis, and emerging use cases, sourced in real time through AgentCore Web Search. Unlike a static RSS aggregator, the feed is a goal-aware discovery engine that refreshes with every session.

Smart content suggestions

Users receive AI-generated content ideas tailored to trending topics in their space, written in their own authentic voice, with optional AI-generated visuals. AgentCore Web Search grounds every suggestion on what’s happening today. A three-step coaching flow (Analyze, Refine, Post) walks users from initial ideas to published content on LinkedIn and X, with a feedback loop, so the AI gets sharper with every iteration.

Trend-aware goal setting

Users define a goal. The AI builds a personalized roadmap with weekly themes and milestones. AgentCore Web Search feeds real-time trend data into goal generation, so weekly themes reflect current industry movements. The system learns from the past four weeks of activity, refreshing recommendations as users grow.

Architecture and tech stack

Figure 1: Event-driven architecture of the Norton Revamp News Engine

The integration follows an event-driven architecture. When a user sets or updates their professional goal, Amazon Nova (through Amazon Bedrock) generates targeted search queries based on the goal, recent activity, and engagement patterns. The agent sends these queries to AgentCore Web Search, which returns cited results entirely within our AWS environment. Our AI Learning System ranks the results for relevance, recency, and source credibility. The ranked results then serve as grounding context for Amazon Nova Lite to generate content suggestions in the user’s authentic voice. Engagement data feeds back into query generation, making the News Engine progressively smarter.

Generative AI and machine learning stack:

  • Amazon Bedrock – Core generative AI engine for content generation, personalization, post analysis (batch mode), and content coaching.
  • Amazon Nova (Nova Lite) – Primary large language model (LLM) powering content generation, goal creation, and trend analysis.
  • Web Search on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore – Real-time web retrieval powering the News Engine, content grounding, and trend discovery through an MCP-compliant managed connector.
  • Stability AI – Image generation.
  • Claude (through Amazon Bedrock) – Additional LLM capabilities for complex reasoning tasks.

Infrastructure: React, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS on the frontend. Node.js, Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS), AWS Lambda, Amazon DynamoDB (multi-table with composite key patterns), Amazon API Gateway, Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS), Amazon EventBridge, Amazon CloudFront, Amazon CloudWatch, and AWS Secrets Manager on the backend. Infrastructure managed through Terraform with blue-green deployment for zero-downtime releases.

Processing pipeline: The platform runs four pipeline stages:

  • Full Scan – Pull up to 1,000 historical posts, store in Amazon S3, run Amazon Bedrock batch analysis for reputation impact.
  • Daily Scan – Amazon EventBridge-triggered incremental analysis.
  • Weekly Goal Generation – Lambda generates goals considering past engagement data plus real-time trend data from AgentCore Web Search.
  • Content Coaching – Synchronous Amazon Bedrock calls through the Analyze, Refine, Post flow, each step grounded with AgentCore Web Search results.

Engineering with an AI-native development mindset

We embedded generative AI from day one, as both the product and the development methodology. The human-AI responsibility split was deliberate: human-owned architecture decisions, security reviews, business logic, and personalization algorithms. AI handled code generation, documentation, test scaffolding, refactoring, and UI component creation.

With Claude, we produced 10 or more design variants per concept, compressed design-to-prototype time from weeks to hours and generated 70 percent of UI code with AI. We tested five pricing models in the time previously needed for one. The gamification system went through eight iterations before launching.

The measurable impact: 3x faster feature implementation, boilerplate generation accelerated by 90 percent, documentation by 80 percent, test creation by 70 percent, and UI component generation by 65 percent. The trade-off: AI output review consumed 20–30 percent of our time.

AI helped with personalization algorithms, the DynamoDB multi-table architecture (which needed experience-based judgment), security implementation, and Amazon Bedrock batch processing optimization. The key insight: AI accelerated implementation, but humans designed how the AI Learning System should adapt to user goals. Product generative AI (Amazon Bedrock, Amazon Nova, AgentCore Web Search) and development generative AI served different purposes, and we kept them separate.

Testing, security, and quality assurance

We achieved 85 percent code coverage through automated test generation. Critical test areas included content generation quality, AgentCore Web Search result relevance and freshness validation, engagement tracking accuracy, gamification logic, and news feed relevance to user goals.

For a product carrying the Norton brand, compliance is non-negotiable. Security checks spanned static code analysis, dependency vulnerability scanning, authentication flows, user data encryption, access control logic, generative AI model output validation, and content filtering. Our security team reviewed all AI-generated recommendations: AI accelerated identification, and humans made final decisions.

The result: 99.9 percent uptime since launch with real-time monitoring of generative AI content quality and user satisfaction.

Best practices for AgentCore Web Search integration

For teams considering AgentCore Web Search for real-time grounding:

  • Invest in query generation – Well-structured queries yield better results than open-ended ones, so we focused on our prompt engineering there.
  • Cache strategically – Real-time freshness is the point, but some queries don’t need to re-execute every session. We cache results with time-to-live (TTL) values that match freshness requirements.
  • Build feedback loops – Track which web search results users engage with and feed that signal back into query generation. Our News Engine’s relevance improved over the first 90 days.
  • Validate source quality – AgentCore Web Search returns source URLs and publication dates. We built a lightweight credibility scoring layer to prioritize authoritative sources.

Conclusion

Building Norton Revamp proved that a small, generative AI-augmented team can deliver enterprise software in months. It also proved that Web Search on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore can serve as the real-time intelligence backbone for products that need to stay current with the world.

We launched a generative AI-native professional reputation management platform in months, with personalized goal setting, AI-driven content suggestions, real-time curated news feeds grounded by AgentCore Web Search, adaptive learning, gamification, and Norton-grade security. A small group of engineers achieved 99.9 percent uptime.

Generative AI doesn’t replace engineers. It amplifies them. Pairing that amplification with fully managed services like AgentCore Web Search removes entire categories of infrastructure complexity. Humans designed the vision. Generative AI through Amazon Bedrock, Amazon Nova, and AgentCore Web Search accelerated bringing it to life, grounded in real-time, cited web knowledge.

“Web Search on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore eliminates the complexity of building and maintaining our own web retrieval infrastructure. It lets our Norton Revamp News Engine deliver real-time, personalized content grounded in what’s happening in each user’s professional domain, with zero data egress and Norton-grade privacy. We went from concept to production in months, and AgentCore Web Search was a key enabler.”

To learn more about Web Search on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, visit the AgentCore documentation. Check out Norton Revamp.

About the authors
